en: Preface to the Publication of the *Fogu Ji* (Record of Restoring the Ancient Text) of the *Huayan Wujiao Zhang*:
Regarding the *Wujiao Zhang*, there exist both the Tang edition and the Japanese edition with differences between them.

However, since this present commentary and sub-commentary are based on the Tang edition, the chapter texts recorded in Dauting’s *Yiyuan* have been used to correspond with the text of this commentary.
Regarding the sequence of the chapters in this instructional text, the middle fascicle of the original edition has been combined with the lower fascicle of the Tang edition;
furthermore, the section beginning from "the two vehicles turning their minds" is placed at the very head of the compilation. Those who peruse this book should first discern this distinction.
Regarding the instructional texts and commentaries, I previously published them as separate works;

fearing that students might grow weary of consulting them all at once, I have now arranged the topical outlines (ke) above each chapter and appended the sub-commentaries (ji) beneath them, so that the meanings of the text and the divisions of the chapters may shine forth with clarity.
The punctuations in this instructional text were added by the venerable Hye-hae, a high-ranking disciple of Master Go-jeong. This is confirmed by the aforementioned colophon.
Although various editions have been collated and corrected, instances of redundant text or displaced passages may still remain; it was while I was traveling to Gao... [text ends].
The manuscript collated by Yue Longbian at the mountain hermitage is the most precise and detailed; therefore, I have now followed that version.
The original record consisted of three fascicles, which I have now divided into six; I have thus used the characters for the "six aspects" (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) to indicate their sequential order.
On a day in the third month of spring in the year of the Dragon, the Jihou cycle, the ninth year of the Kwanbun era,
the śramaṇa Fuhatsu of Gangoji on Mount Godaisan in the western part of Rakuyō respectfully inscribed this preface to the Record of Restoring Antiquity.
My late teacher, Venerable Ketang, applied himself to the commentaries on the Avatamsaka Sūtra from his youth, almost forgetting to sleep or eat.

Whenever there were textual or doctrinal points he could not fully penetrate, he would study them with tireless diligence, seeking only the most definitive explanation before ceasing. Though his mind was exhausted and his body worn out, he never for a moment desisted.
He was particularly proficient in the *Kongmu zhang* (Chapter on the Essential Categories), which he had recently been studying while residing at Bodhi Temple.
One day at dawn, while Master Qin was opening a scroll, he suddenly felt as though he had attained something.
Seeing that the Master’s countenance was extraordinary, Qin asked him in surprise, "Have you perhaps obtained the Dharma of the Venerable One? The Master explained the reason for this in detail.
Qin joined his palms in praise and urged the Master to compose writings based on what he had seen, so that he might elucidate the principles of the Complete and Sudden Teaching. The Master declined.
Lacking the leisure to know the difficulties of the author’s work, I did not dare to abruptly alter the Master’s text. When he was sixty-five years of age, he first began composing this record;
however, before reaching the section on the "Delimitation of the Severance of Delusions," his efforts were suddenly cut short as he passed away.

On his deathbed, he made a vow, saying: “You should complete it for me. I, Shanxi, am ashamed of my late arrival and did not dare to hastily continue the previous work; yet even now, [time] has encroached upon it.
Upon reflection, I find that the year this work was begun coincides with the year my late teacher passed away.

Fearing that life is as fragile as a candle in the wind and may suddenly perish, I would be failing the legacy of his final instructions. Therefore, disregarding my own lack of skill, I have taken what I previously heard from my teacher and appended it to the end of his work, completing it in three volumes.
Yet, for one of mediocre craft to attempt the carving of a master artisan—how could such a thing possibly succeed?

Regarding the reproach of "soiling one's face with blood-stained fingers," my late teacher exclusively employed ancient meanings for his exegesis, and thus he named this work *Fugu* (Restoring Antiquity).
On the first day of the first month of autumn in the year of Renzi of the Shaoxi era, the disciple and successor in the teaching, the bhikṣu Shanxi, respectfully records this.
*Huayan Yicheng Jiaoyi Fenzhizhang Fugu Ji*, Scroll One (Part One of the Upper),
composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Hui of Yufeng.
*Huayan Yicheng Jiaoyi Fenzhizhang*.
Within this single title, there are two layers of subject and object. First, the "Chapter" (*zhāng*) is the signifier (*nengquán*), while all that precedes it is the signified (*suòquán*;
i.e., the delineation of the causes and fruits of the One Vehicle through profound words and wondrous phrases).
Second, "Huayan" (Flower Adornment) is the signifier, and the subsequent six characters are the signified; that is, the inexhaustible ocean of teachings elucidates and reveals the One Vehicle.
The two great categories of cause and effect are profoundly deep; this chapter now clarifies this meaning.

The title of the chapter is established by following the ultimate intent from its verbal expression, adopting the name of another [text] in a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound. The meaning of the sutra’s title is fully contained within the *Great Commentary* (*Daisho*);

although its inexhaustible varieties cannot be fully detailed here, I shall now briefly set them forth. Since the subtle words of the Perfect Teaching must exhaust the Dharma-realm, they are already complete.
The Tathāgata’s power of discernment pervades each pore of space throughout the oceans of lands until the end of the future; he speaks such teachings all at once and constantly.
How could one limit such a corpus to a fixed number of fascicles? Now, based on the scriptural text, I shall arrange these from the narrow to the broad into ten categories:
first, the Abridged Original Sūtra; second, the Lower Version Sūtra; third, the Middle Version Sūtra; fourth, the Upper Version Sūtra.
1. The Sūtra of the Five Universal Eyes; 2. The Sūtra of Common Exposition; 3. The Sūtra of Diverse Exposition; 4. The Sūtra of Principal and Retinue; 5. The Sūtra of the Retinue;

6. The Sūtra of Perfection. The commentary explains: Although each of the aforementioned sūtras individually elucidates the scope of the One Vehicle teaching, if they are categorized according to their commonality or distinctness, the first eight constitute the distinct teaching (*bhedadeśanā*), for although they mutually serve as principal [teachings],...
Because its retinue consists entirely of the inexhaustible ocean of Dharma, the meaning of this ninth single sūtra should be understood as belonging to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-naya*).
It merely provides a partial exposition according to a specific direction and according to the capacities of beings; it serves only as a skillful means (*upāya*) and is not the primary sūtra itself.

Therefore, within the Shared Teaching that follows, starting from the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and extending through the Two and Three Vehicles, all other sūtras are listed together as the retinue (*parivāra*) of this ninth [sūtra].

This is precisely because they are subsumed by these skillful means; thus, the derivative does not depart from the fundamental, as it is established in reliance upon the fundamental and accords with the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, it enters into the subsumption of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). For this reason, the teaching of commonality (*sāmānya-deśanā*) is both threefold and one.

As for the tenth scripture, it universally synthesizes all the fundamental texts into a single, perfectly interfused wheel of boundless teaching; that is to say, it subsumes the preceding various [teachings] through the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).

Since each and every teaching of the three vehicles and all other dharmas is fundamentally the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), just as the hundred rivers in the ocean are none other than the sea itself, they are either the Perfect (Yuan) or the Distinct (Bie). Alternatively, within the Perfect, one may distinguish the aforementioned Shared (Tong) and Distinct.
One should know that what our school venerates—the Perfect-Sudden (Yuantun)—encompasses the entirety of the inconceivable ocean of the Tathāgata’s teachings; in brief, it is called thus.
The title of this work is established because the *Avataṃsaka* universally reveals the two great categories of the One Vehicle’s teachings and meanings;
other alternative titles are merely listed briefly here for the time being.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Jianfu Monastery in the Capital.
I shall now expound the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teachings of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi).
"Tathāgata" refers here to the Tathāgata of the ten bodies. "Sea-seal" refers to the meditative concentration upon which this sutra relies.

Because the One Vehicle—whether in its universal or particular aspects—necessarily arises based on the Sea-Seal Samādhi, it differs from the Three Vehicles, which rely on the wisdom established by the Dharma.
Therefore, the *Sāgarāmudrā-samādhi* is cited to establish its central tenet. This samādhi receives its name from a metaphor:
when the Tathāgata realizes perfect wisdom and reaches the fullness of the ocean of fruition, he gives rise to great, non-directional functions. Briefly stated, these comprise the ten great samādhis;
this particular gate corresponds precisely to the arising of function based upon the essence, whereby an inexhaustible cloud of bodies is manifested, pervading everywhere.

Because this sutra is expounded all at once throughout time and space, it is called the "basis" (*āśraya*); because it is that which is realized, it is devoid of the characteristics of entering or exiting.
As explained extensively in the *Bhadramukha-parivarta*, the Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated here as "right reception" (*samyak-pratigraha*) or "equipoise" (*samyak-dhāraṇī*).
It refers to right contemplation and so forth. The "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) is precisely the non-dual Mahāyāna Dharma. Nāgārjuna said: "Great..."
This is the perfectly round ocean as taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, also called the "Single Flavor" Mahāyāna or the "Great One" (*Mahātman*).
Within it is the "Nature-Arising Tree-Treasury," which internally adorns the One Vehicle and externally arrays the Three Vehicles, as well as the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and so forth.
There is but one gate of awakening; beneath the Bodhi tree, there are only two positions: cause and fruit—namely, the Buddha and Samantabhadra alone.

Opening the vision to establish the great framework of the teachings for those sentient beings who can be transformed, and so forth—this takes as its essence the perfect fusion of principle and wisdom, as well as the universal and particular aspects of practice.
To speak of "oneness" means that what is not one is one; "one" means all, and "all" means one.
One is all, and all is one; all is not all, and one is also not one. This is the nature of all dharmas.

Because all phenomena mutually interpenetrate, manifesting the characteristics of non-obstruction between thing and thing—wherein they enter one another and are identical to one another, all being harmoniously fused as the single Dharma-realm—it is thus that the totality of all dharmas constitutes the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Only this accords with the essential purport of the Sūtra.

As Guishan said: "To comprehensively gather them without distinction is called 'One'; to contain and fuse them so as to carry them forward is called 'Vehicle' (yāna); it refers to both the teaching and the principle."

Since both practice and its fruit possess the sense of "carrying across," they are collectively termed the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Because there is not a single dharma that is not subsumed within this vehicle, it is not that other names do not exist;
however, "one" refers to non-duality, and "one" refers to equality. The meaning of the teaching will be explained below.
Briefly composed in ten sections: 1. Establishing the One Vehicle; 2. The Comprehension and Benefit of the Teaching’s Meaning; 3. The Ancient and Modern Establishment of the Teachings; 4.
The Classification of Teachings and the Opening of the School; 5. The Opening and Closing of the Vehicles and Teachings; 6. The Chronology of the Arising of the Teachings.

What are these ten? They are: (1) the establishment based on the equality of the dharma-realm; (2) the establishment based on the equality of the lineage (*gotra*); (3) the establishment based on the equality of the purification of the basis (*āśraya-pariśuddhi*); (4) the establishment based on the equality of the manifestation of the fruit; (5) the establishment based on the equality of the absence of distinction between the vehicles; (6) the establishment based on the equality of the single vehicle; (7) the establishment based on the equality of the ultimate; (8) the establishment based on the equality of the non-differentiation of the path; (9) the establishment based on the equality of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); and (10) the establishment based on the equality of the non-abandonment of the great compassion. This means that because all phenomena are equal in their nature of being devoid of self, they are equal in the dharma-realm. Because they are equal in the dharma-realm, they are equal in the lineage. Regarding the statement "first clarifying the establishment of the One Vehicle" (*ekayāna-pratisthāpana*): it means that our Patriarch, using the manifest brush of his great hand, inscribed this Way to show it to future generations;
because he first distinguished this meaning, it is called "first clarifying. Regarding "establishment," the *Kongmu* states:
"The dharma-meaning of the One Vehicle is established by the Buddha and Samantabhadra’s vows and practices, so that sentient beings may rely upon it and abide therein."

Because sentient beings who uphold the teachings and meanings of the Three Vehicles, as well as their karmic actions, establish Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, upon whom they rely for sustenance, the Sūtra says:
"The vow-power of Vairocana Buddha pervades the Dharma-realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel.
Some say that it was our Patriarch who established this, but that is incorrect; furthermore, regarding the Buddha and Samantabhadra...
The path realized by the worthy ones must await the Patriarchs to be established.
This doctrinal framework of the One Vehicle is divided into two gates: first, the Separate Teaching; second, the Common Teaching.
However, this One Vehicle is the inexhaustible universal Dharma that is the very substance of dependent origination.
As for the meaning of the verbal teachings, they consist of the two great aspects of cause and effect discussed below. Regarding this, there have been many ancient explanations;

some say that the teaching which expresses is the causal portion (*hetu-bhāga*) and the meaning which is expressed is the resultant portion (*phala-bhāga*). Our Patriarch said, "This explanation is extremely superficial. Furthermore, Zhenguó said:

This deviates from the intent of the text; since the Chongguan era, those who have produced commentaries and sub-commentaries to explain this chapter, as well as the various schools of exegesis, have all followed this interpretation, yet they still cannot avoid error. To rectify this, the *Kongmu* (Outline) states:

"The 'division of cause' refers to the Greatness of the Teaching (*jiao-da*), while the 'division of fruit' refers to the Greatness of the Meaning (*yi-da*); therefore, the meaning of 'Greatness of Meaning' is explained in reference to the fruit."

The term "result" (*phala*) signifies the stage that has been attained; the term "greatness" (*mahat*) signifies the dharma that has been realized. Because these stages are analogous, they are correlated to clarify the underlying reason.

Regarding the correlation through the cause (*hetu*), "cause" signifies the stage capable of producing [the result], while "teaching" (*deśanā*) signifies the skillful means (*upāya*) that serves as the designation.
Because these stages are analogous, they are correlated to clarify the teaching. Thus, the two aspects of virtue consist of the teaching and the realization.

Because its measure is not small, it is called "Great"; because the aspect of realization (pramāṇa) transcends words, it is the ultimate destination for those who set out on the path, and is thus called "Meaning.
Master Yuǎn also accepted the verbal teaching, but our Patriarch rejected it. Qingliang said: "The later interpretation does not accept the expressive [words].
His intention was this: even if the seven verses of the sutra clarify the Great Meaning, how could they be without the expressive [words]?
Because its application is profoundly deep, it is termed "meaning" (*artha*); because it can be conveyed through words and speech, it is termed "teaching" (*deśanā*).
The essence of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is not separate from these two. As for the boundaries of this [teaching], the causal gate and the resultant gate encompass all phenomena without exception;
only the wisdom of Samantabhadra can exhaustively fathom its depths, which encompasses the great void, transcends the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, because it is inexhaustible and cannot be exhausted by calculation or analogy, it is termed "limitless" (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, this scriptural teaching revealed in the text transcends the three vehicles, surpasses the provisional and gradual, and stands in stark contrast to other schools; it encompasses all that is profound, subtle, and inconceivable.
To open this into two gates means that the inconceivable universal Dharma, which transcends the emotions and is free from views, initiates these two gates.

To demonstrate this, it is said that one reconciles the two gates of the principle and the practice of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through two categories: first, the distinct teaching (*pṛthagdeśanā*), and second, the common teaching (*sāmānyadeśanā*).

This corresponds to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s distinction between the common and the uncommon. Therefore, the essential question asks: "What are the boundaries of the doctrinal meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*)?
The answer is: "The teachings of the One Vehicle are of two kinds: first, the common teaching; second, the uncommon teaching. The Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) is [the latter]."
The meanings elucidated throughout its every phrase and every sentence are each complete with all [teachings]; this is the uncommon teaching (*asādhāraṇa-śāsana*), as explained in the *Avataṃsaka*.
Furthermore, it is said that the single volume of the *Avataṃsaka* is the uncommon teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Qingliang [Zongmi] stated:
"The 'distinct' (*bīe*) refers to the uncommon, the sudden, and the ultimate reality. He further stated: "It is utterly different from other teachings," and "uncommon in three ways."

Because it is based on the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), the *Kongmu* states that the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is distinguished in order to clarify its differentiation according to the capacities of sentient beings;

it does not mean that they can be differentiated by their own intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). It is discussed as having distinct characteristics according to those capacities, and each of these distinct aspects possesses ten [aspects].

The reason for speaking of "ten" is to manifest the immeasurable; thus, it is the universally harmonious and perfect teaching (*samantabhadra-dharma*) which is utterly transcendent and distinct, and is therefore called "distinct" (*bhedaka*). Second, the commonality.

The Teacher asks: Regarding the "Shared Teaching," although the names are the same as those in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, their meanings are entirely different, as is extensively explained in various Mahāyāna sūtras.

Therefore, within the Shared Teaching, starting from the One Vehicle up to the Infinite Vehicles, all are listed therein as a collective summary drawn from other sūtras; hence it is called "other sūtras" in the context of the Shared Teaching.
Because the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Lesser Vehicle all rely upon it together; furthermore, the *Kongmu* states:

"As for the 'Gate of Common Teaching' (*tóngjiàomén*), its meaning is the same as that of the Three Vehicles, yet because wisdom is redirected and thus enters the inclusion of the One Vehicle, the treatises and the question-and-answer sections refer to it as the 'Common Teaching' (*gòngjiào*).
Moreover, 'common' (*gòng*) means 'the same' (*tóng*); thus the various patriarchs state that the origin of the 'Common Teaching' lies in wisdom."

The broad dissemination of this treatise throughout the various texts of our school—both those that agree and those that differ—begins from this point. As for superficial talk and arbitrary assertions, they are not worthy of esteem;
these have been fully distinguished within the *Tongjiao Wenda* (Questions and Answers on the Shared Teachings). In the course of the word-by-word commentary, I shall briefly set them forth.

The first two sections of the beginning—the single nature and the fruit-stage of the ocean—should be understood as having an ineffable meaning. Why? Because they do not correspond with verbal teaching;
rather, they are the self-realized realm of the ten Buddhas.
The "beginning" and "middle" refer to the two divisions of cause and effect within the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*). Why are these two distinguished?
The *Yunhua* (Cloud Flower) states that the *dharmadhātu* of the sovereign dependent origination of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) does not transcend its own essence as either cause or fruit;
therefore, they must be distinguished. The "fruit division of the ocean of nature" refers to the ultimate, quiescent, and perfect fruit of one's own essence. Is this not so?

That which can be described as the meaning refers to the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*), which transcends all characteristics of description; therefore, it cannot be elucidated through verbal expression.
Why is this so? If one asks what reason there is for its being unspeakable, it is because it does not correspond with the teachings (*śāsana*).
Since it does not correspond, it cannot be manifested through words. The Treatise says: "This Dharma is supremely subtle and profound."

Because it is profoundly and uniquely honored as being free from the limitations of sensory faculties (*indriya*) and free from the constraints of verbal teaching, and because its virtues surpass those of other Buddhas, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (the Great Root Flower Adornment Scripture) speaks thus: "The ocean of perfect and perfect merits of these Buddhas is supreme;
all other Buddhas cannot achieve such a perfect and perfect ocean, for they are inferior. This applies to both Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles.
It is the same for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); thus, the ocean of the perfection of their innate virtue is precisely the self-realm of the ten Buddhas.

Regarding this, Yunhua said: "The realm of the ten Buddhas is one and yet all. This refers to the ocean of the worlds of the ten Buddhas, which clarifies the meaning of the ten Buddhas as explained in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), namely: the Unattached Buddha (*asaṅga-buddha*), the Vow Buddha (*praṇidhāna-buddha*), and so forth. (4)
Since the teachings of the three vehicles all lack this [nature], it is said that the ultimate fruit is entirely ineffable.
Thus, the *Dilun* states: "The causal aspect may be spoken of, but the fruitional aspect cannot be spoken of. This is precisely what is meant.

Regarding the *Dilun* and other treatises, Qingliang states: "If one looks directly at the intent of these treatises, they take the 'Greatness of Meaning' (*yì dà*) as the resultant aspect (*guǒ fēn*);

therefore, it cannot be said that the 'Greatness of Teaching' (*jiào dà*) constitutes the causal aspect (*yīn fēn*), though it can be so described. *Tàn xuán* states: "These two meanings of 'greatness' are briefly explained through four sections:
first, defining the names; second, distinguishing their characteristics; third, clarifying what is expressible and what is inexpressible; and fourth, providing an exegesis."
Because it is that which is expressed at the beginning and middle of the text, it is called "meaning" (*artha*). Because it is profound, it is called "great" (*mahā*);
because it is extensive, it is called "great. Since meaning itself is great, it is termed "Great Meaning" (*Mahārtha*).

Because it expresses meaning, reveals the objective realm, and is called "teaching" (*deśanā*), and because one attains that meaning by means of this teaching, the instruction is also called "great" in accordance with that which it expresses. This...
Because it is the teaching of the Great (Mahā), it is called the "Teaching of the Great"; this is the explanation of its name. Below, the characteristics are distinguished as follows:
within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are six essential points: first, the ocean of the fruit upon which they rely, which is like the great void;
second, the tenfold Dharma-realm realized by the stage-wisdom, which is like all that can be encompassed within the void; third, the fundamental stage-wisdom capable of realizing [the former];...

1. The Dharma-realm as the nature of the exhaustion of that which can be supported; 2. The four stages where subsequent attainment arises in accordance with phenomena through the practice of compassion and wisdom, remaining in neither [extreme];
3. The five stages where the preparatory practices give rise to the conduct of resolve as the means for proceeding to the stages; 4.

The manifestation and establishment of the distinctions between the stages by means of the dharmas, namely the ten wholesome paths, the factors of dhyāna, and so forth; 5. The integration of the first three [categories] as the meaning of the "Great" (mahat) at the end.
The three combined are explained as the "Great" (*mahat*); this refers to the essential characteristics of the two aforementioned "Greats.

Since that [text] is a commentary on the *Bhūmi-vibhāga*, it takes the initial wisdom within those stages (*bhūmi*) and unifies it with the ultimate, perfected fruit as its meaning of "Greatness. Master Qingliang’s sub-commentary states:
"Furthermore, when seeking the meaning, there are briefly two types: first, explaining it solely in terms of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), taking realized wisdom (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) as the fruit."

The *Fenfangbian* (Distinction of Expedient Means) and the *Jifa* (Entrusting the Dharma) are both categorized as the "Causes" (*hetu*). This section is divided into two parts based on the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood in contrast to the cause of Samantabhadra.
Now, we shall address the latter meaning. The *Kongmu* (General Index) and the present chapter likewise take the quiescent, perfect fruit of the self-substance (*svabhāva*) as their primary meaning.

Since the *Dacheng Yizhang* (Great Vehicle Meaning Chapter) and the *Benji lun* (Treatise on the Original Ground) both expound upon the Great Perfect Cause of Samantabhadra, I shall now cite them here.
Furthermore, in the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundity), it is clarified that there are two great categories regarding the meaning of what can be spoken and what cannot be spoken;
each of these two categories possesses three meanings. Regarding the three meanings of what can be spoken and the one meaning of what cannot be spoken:

the former refers to the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*), which may be generally indicated so that people may know its name—this is called "what can be spoken"—yet it cannot be pointed out or demonstrated by name, which is called "what cannot be spoken," and so forth. These details are fully set forth therein.
As it is with that, the second is the causal portion of conditions, which is the realm of Samantabhadra. Regarding the two causal portions of conditions:
this refers to the cultivation of the means of conditions, wherein the essence is perfected and the stages are fulfilled; this is precisely Samantabhadra.

Now, according to the provisional teachings (*kyōjō*), because the arising [of phenomena] is distinguished by relying upon their own essential characteristics (*jittaisō*) in relation to conditions, it is called "conditioned arising" (*engi*).
Because it is manifested within the gate of causes, it is called "the objective realm" (*kyōkai*). Furthermore, these teachings are broadly categorized into three types:

first, the greatness of the accomplishment of the cause, meaning that compassion and the power of vows serve as the foundation for initiating practice; thus, they are termed the "cause. Second, the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause... [text continues].

The wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) serve as the causes for supramundane wisdom; because their arising is not instantaneous, they are termed "gradual.

The three teachings speak of the accomplishment of cultivation, which refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). True cultivation accords with reality, and because it can be expressed through verbal designations during the process of correct realization, it is called "taught" (*deśanā*).
The two characters "taught" (*jiao-shuo*) specifically distinguish this from the "greatness of meaning" (*artha-mahattva*), which does not refer to the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
Since they can be explained, all the stages (bhūmis) contain these three. If one considers them in terms of seeing and hearing, one cannot distinguish between the two greats of teaching and meaning;
however, if one considers them in terms of Samantabhadra’s practice, realization, and meaning, then one may say that there are the two greats of teaching and meaning.

Furthermore, if one contrasts seeing and hearing with Samantabhadra’s realization, one may also say that seeing and hearing constitute the greatness of the teaching, while realization constitutes the greatness of the meaning.
"Meaning" (yi) is the "Great Meaning" (yida).
These two are non-dual, their entire substance encompassing all; it is like waves and water—consider this and it will become clear.
Both Patriarchs used this single category as a name to teach: that teaching is non-teaching, and non-teaching is teaching; they are non-dual.
Because they are fused together, it cannot be said that the ineffable is not different from the expressible, for the ultimate truth is all-pervasive;

nor can it be said that the expressible is not different from the ineffable, for conditioned cultivation is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Although the scriptural text speaks of only a partial meaning, this is by no means insignificant.
As the Treatise says: "Because it is grasped as being fulfilled according to reality," it is therefore said that the whole is universally subsumed within it.
It is like waves on water: the entirety of the wave is the water, and the entirety of the water is the wave.
Within the gate of Samantabhadra, there are further two gates: first, the gate of distinct characteristics, and second, the gate of comprehensive inclusion.

Regarding the term "Universal" (Puxian): although it first arises from the perfection of wondrous virtue, because its renown pervades everywhere, Mañjuśrī is omitted and only Samantabhadra is mentioned.
The reason for establishing two gates is that by distinguishing their characteristics, the provisional and the real are revealed;
by encompassing them, the correct teaching is demonstrated without exception. It contains all streams as its vastness and stands out like a solitary peak among the many mountains as its loftiness.
How majestic and vast! It may be said that while it is profoundly distinct from other schools, its comprehensive synthesis does not differ from them.
As for the "Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics" (*fenxiang men*): this gate distinguishes the differences between the characteristics of the three teachings and the one teaching.
This refers to the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle (biejiao yicheng) as distinct from the Three Vehicles.

Regarding how the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle differs from the Three Vehicles, Zhizang states: "Based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the distinctions between the realm (*dhātu*), essence (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), skillful means (*upāya*), and the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*) are not the same.
Thus, the *Tanyan ji* says: "Alternatively, it is opened into two, namely: the One Vehicle."

Although within the various teachings prior to those of the Three Vehicles there exist differing approaches—some preserving the three and some merging the two—all are nonetheless categorized as "teachings of the Three Vehicles" because they all serve as gateways for entry into the Three Vehicles.
The subsequent [teaching] directly reveals the fundamental Dharma and does not accommodate the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is exclusively "One.
Qingliang (Zhiyi) said: "Alternatively, only the final one is the uncommon One Vehicle," and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* points to this [as such].
Because it is taught in common with the *Mahāvaipulya* and other *Mahāvaipulya* sūtras for those of the Two Vehicles, it also accords with the Four Vehicles. The subsequent chapter states:
"The last one is the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle; the intermediate three teachings may collectively be considered as one, namely the teaching of the One and Three Vehicles.
Since these are all attained by the three types of persons, they are also termed the "Teaching of the Fundamental Dharma" that adapts to the capacities of beings.
The Final Teaching is sometimes called the Vehicle of Ultimate Perfection (*niṣṭhā-yāna*) or the Vehicle of Expedient Means (*upāya-yāna*). Regarding the five teachings, there are two theories:

first, that the preceding four teachings constitute the Three Vehicles while the final one constitutes the One Vehicle; this is briefly as cited previously, and is explained in detail in the *Kongmu wen答* (Questions and Answers on the Key Points), the *Soutan erxuan* (Exploring the Two Mysteries), and various other chapters. Second, that the initial Small Vehicle constitutes the Three Vehicles while the latter three [teachings] constitute the One Vehicle.
This is for the sake of the One Vehicle, as explained in the *Huayan yuanjue shuchao* and other such works.

The reason for this is that while the virtuous masters of previous generations merely distinguished the provisional from the real within the various teaching gates and differentiated between skillful means and the direct vehicle, they held up the *Avataṃsaka* as the sudden, perfect, and ultimate teaching, asserting that only this Dharma possesses the realization of the supreme fruit; apart from this universal Dharma, there is nothing else.

Those who attain Buddhahood perform all actions solely as skillful means (*upāya*); thus, only the final one [the *Tathāgatagarbha* teaching] constitutes the ultimate, perfect One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The preceding four teachings are all provisional, partial explanations suited to specific capacities.

Even when they speak of the true, eternal merits of the *tathāgatagarbha*, they do not actually incorporate the provisional skillful means; these are fundamentally categorized within the Three Vehicles. Since the Zhenguan era, Xuanzang...
When the Master returned to the West, his successor, Master Ki, inherited his lineage by asserting that the five natures and three vehicles were the reality,
while the one vehicle and one nature were provisional. His teachings obscured the One Vehicle, yet as its path flourished throughout China,

[the author] refuted it through works such as commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith* by means of categories such as "words" and "teachings," "completeness" and "deficiency," thereby clarifying that the One Vehicle and one nature are the reality, and the three vehicles are provisional.
The five natures are provisional, whereas both the final and sudden teachings discuss the single nature; therefore, they are judged to be included within the One Vehicle.

Qingliang (Zongmi) inherited this tradition, and Guifeng (Huiyuan) followed in his footsteps; thus, they taught that the latter three [teachings] constitute the One Vehicle while the former two constitute the Three Vehicles.
This present chapter is a transcription of the bequeathed words of Yunhua, compiled into a formal literary structure; therefore, it treats the preceding various teachings as follows:

All three [vehicles] are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). Those of old, being unacquainted with the essential categories (*kaṅmuk*), failed to investigate the two mysteries through question and answer;
they lost the core meaning of the chapters and merely confused later worthies.
For example, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three carts pointed out outside the gate within the house are used to entice the children so that they may emerge.

These are the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). The ox-cart bestowed on the open ground outside the enclosure is the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as seen in passages such as those in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the delimitation of the application of these teachings, it is said: "Now, based on the sevenfold classification of teachings, we shall establish the textual and doctrinal boundaries of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The sutras referred to are the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Śrīmālādevī*, the *Ratnakūṭa-vaipulya*, and the *Bodhisattvagocaropāyaviṣayavikurvaṇanirdeśa*."
The two treatises—the *Brahmajāla-sūtra-avatāra-tathāgata-viṣaya-acintya-sūtra* and others;
the three commentaries—the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; the four chapters; the five commentaries; the six question-and-answer texts;
and the miscellaneous *Kongmu*—all have their words and meanings in accord, and may be cited in full.

However, regarding the distinctions between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, there are briefly ten explanations found within the various sacred teachings. [The interlocutor] asked the Patriarch: "You have recorded the subtle words and wondrous purports of Master Wuye to compose the *Yiji* (Record of Meanings), and in works such as the *Kongmu*, you have merely cited scriptural evidence according to the specific points established therein.
