In ancient times, there were only the two schools of *dharmatā-śūnyatā* (emptiness of phenomena) and *tathatā-śūnyatā* (emptiness of suchness), which together discussed the equality of the single flavor;

thus, it was easy to hear and believe, and there was no need to wait for the foundation of realization. However, masters such as Xuanzang and others held the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) to be real and did not believe in the existence of the One Vehicle (*eka-yāna*), being so firm in their conviction that they were difficult to turn back.
Therefore, one must cite the *Juechao* in full: "The difference between the Mahāyāna and the One Vehicle is that in the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* school..."

Because many people did not believe this, Master Huayan Zang composed the *Wujiaoyi Fenqizhong Wen* (The Text on the Delimitation of the Meanings of the Five Teachings), in which he analyzed the ten distinctions between the Mahāyāna and the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), citing more than twenty sutras and śāstras as evidence.
Thus, one knows that those whose learning and knowledge are shallow and limited cannot avoid slandering the Dharma; for this reason, Guifeng wrote this work.

The instruction does not state that this chapter was composed for this specific purpose alone; it singles out the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school but does not exclude the *paryanta* (ultimate) or *dharmatā* (perfect teaching) schools.
Is it not erroneous to claim that Guifeng [Zongmi] described the intent behind our Patriarch’s composition in such a way?

Furthermore, Buddhatara followed in the footsteps of various virtuous predecessors who all revered the *Avataṃsaka*, producing extensive commentaries and works—could these also have been intended solely for those students of the *lakṣaṇa* school?
Ah! Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real:
this distinction between the provisional and the real is explained in terms of ultimate skillful means. As for "skillful means": [it refers to...]
"Provisional" (*quán*) refers to the application of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), which is precisely the "opening of the gate of skillful means" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Among the five teachings, the last one is the ultimate vehicle; it is also called the "original teaching" (*běn jiào*) and the "correct vehicle" (*zhèng chéng*). The preceding four teachings are the provisional vehicles;

they are also called the "derivative teachings" (*mò jiào*) because they are provisional. Since they are provisional, they are the ultimate [in their own context]. Question: Is the final teaching (*zhōng jiào*) also called...?
Question: Since the Real Teaching (Shijiao) and the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao) are both called "Real," why are they considered provisional? Answer: Because their substantial reality is insufficient;
they do not teach that all beings possess the Buddha-knowledge and vision. Therefore, they belong to the Three Vehicles.

Even when discussing the One Vehicle or the One Nature, these refer only to the nature of the cause (*hetu-svabhāva*), as they lack the nature of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*). This present chapter concerns the fruit; therefore, it teaches that all are empty.

Furthermore, because one must abandon the vehicle of skillful means (*upāya-yāna*) and proceed toward the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*) before attaining Buddhahood, it is not ultimate but rather provisional.
[The interlocutor] asks Qingliang: "If there is reality and one does not stagnate in skillful means, why do you not acknowledge this?
What do you mean by saying that 'proceeding toward the True Vehicle' is itself a skillful means? He replied: "The Patriarch merely said that one does not stagnate in the direction."
Thus, he did not say it was not a skillful means (*upāya*). Although there was no need to wait for the faculties [of beings] to ripen, they naturally returned [to the teaching].
It is like staying at an inn; although one is not sent for, one goes there of one's own accord. Qingliang said:
"Although there was the Mahāyāna in the past, it spoke of the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, Nirvāṇa, and the Dharmakāya as being truly eternal, yet it never explicitly revealed this."
All sentient beings are fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; [the Buddha] appears in the world for this one purpose alone and not for any other.
Thus, while the One Vehicle and Three Vehicles were provisional in the past, they are now realized as the ultimate reality.

Because this principle illuminates and penetrates all, Master Zhiyi said: "As for the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras, there is no depth that they do not reach to the utmost; therefore, those who seek the Way rely upon them."
The Great returns to that which encompasses all; thus, those who ride it employ this for their movement. Yet, in its general outline, it takes adaptation to transformation as its foundation.
Within the gates of exhortation, one cannot help but employ skillful means (*upāya*) as its function.

That the transformation effected by such means—though vast in its awakening of beings—is ultimately insufficient when compared to the ultimate reality, and that everything belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, is indeed appropriate. It is truly fitting.
Thus, it was previously established that the three carts collectively belong to the category of expedient means (*upāya*).
Among these three, the ox-cart is likewise a provisional device used to lead the children out of the house;

therefore, at the gate, all three carts were presented as the opening of the door of expedient means, while it was only upon reaching the crossroads that the Great White Ox-Cart was specifically bestowed.

To demonstrate the true nature [of the teaching], regarding the phrase "by means of the three [vehicles]": the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavāda) does not believe that there is anything outside the three [vehicles].

Because they confused the ox-cart outside the gate with the one on the open ground and failed to distinguish between the two oxen, the present judgment states that among the three, the ox-cart is identical to the sheep and deer carts.
Both belong to the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*). The great carriage on the open ground represents the mark of ultimate reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
The *Kongmu* states that this refers to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), because outside the triple world (*tridhātu*), one separately seeks the carriage drawn by a great ox.

If, among those three [vehicles], the ox-cart were also real, then when the elder was leading his children out from within the house, he would have pointed to that ox-cart as being right outside the gate;

they should have come out and been able to see the cart immediately. Why then, after having gone out and reached the very place where the cart he had originally pointed out was located, did they not find it and subsequently seek for it again?
Regarding those [three carts], the King said: "The goat and the deer are empty pointers; one cannot board them once they have gone outside the gate.
If the ox-cart were real, one would indeed board it upon leaving the gate. Now, since all the sons seek them, it is clear that all three are empty pointers.
Previously, when the three vehicles were pointed out as being outside the realm, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) exited the triple world, yet there was no true realization of bodhi."
Since the Bodhisattva has emerged from the triple world, how could there be a true realization? Since both are equally without true realization, it is called "not mounting the carriage.
It is clearly known that all three vehicles are merely provisional expedients.
Furthermore, one cannot say that seeking the carriage outside the triple world applies only to the two vehicles, for the sutra does not state that they seek the ox-cart.
Furthermore, since people obtain those ox-carts as soon as they go out the gate, it is not said that those ropes previously promised the carts; this is because there are only two vehicles.

The phrase "nor can it be equal" is used because one might fear the opponent's defense: that these are merely the two vehicles who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] obtaining the carts upon exiting.

Therefore, it is said that because the sūtra does not speak of [the vehicles] and so forth, and since one cannot obtain the chariots, it is clear that they all lack intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*); for there is nothing to be obtained.

The elder’s empty pointing toward the three vehicles is actually the wisdom of the non-exhaustible and the non-arising; this is the substance of the vehicles of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The shallow wisdom of the six-foot [Buddha-body] is the substance of the ox-cart. Since the wisdom of the two vehicles is not ultimate reality, how could the shallow wisdom of the six-foot [body] possibly be?
Because they exist in reality, we know that [the father's] search was the same [as his sons'].
Therefore, when the sons had emerged from the house and reached the open space, each addressed their father, saying:
"Father, please grant us at this time the playthings you previously promised—the goat-drawn carts, the deer-drawn carts, and the ox-drawn carts. From this, it is known that there are three carts.
"Similarly, they seek.
Since the sons have already sought ox-carts, it is clear that [the carts] lack intrinsic substance; therefore, the text merely restates their seeking.

Regarding this "seeking of the carts," which is a metaphor for the Dharma, there have been many ancient interpretations, but they can be summarized into two points: first, seeking by means of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*), and second, seeking by means of speech.

Regarding the term "rope and pulley" (jīsuo): those of the three vehicles, having exited the suffering of the triple world through the gateways of the Buddha’s teachings, consider this to be the ultimate;

they do not realize that the rope and pulley have already been refined and tempered, and that the capacity for the One Vehicle has been awakened. When the appropriate conditions arise and they strike upon the holy meaning, they merely speak of the "rope.
The Buddha, knowing their capacities were mature, gathered them at Vulture Peak to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*, the principle of the single extreme. This is...

"Each of these sons is granted one great carriage and two mouthfuls of rope. Having assembled at Mount Ling, those of the three vehicles and the three faculties all spoke forth, seeking the Dharma and seeking a prediction;
this is the "seeking of the carriage. To preach for them and grant them predictions so that they may cultivate and realize [the truth] is the "equal granting.
In the Preface of Maitreya, the doubts of the fourfold assembly are set forth to question the Buddha regarding the definitive causes.
Regarding the meaning of this passage, Mañjuśrī said: "If there are those seeking the three vehicles who have doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them so that none remain.
Having thus granted his consent, at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, it says:
"I tell the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas: 'I have caused you to be released from the bonds of suffering and to attain nirvāṇa. The Buddha—
By the power of skillful means, [the Buddha] manifests the teaching of the three vehicles to instruct sentient beings who are attached in various places, leading them to escape from this state;
this is the disclosure of the provisional. Furthermore, it says: "Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas are not different.

Regarding the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, you should give rise to great power of faith. After a long time, the World-Honored One must surely proclaim the ultimate truth. This is precisely [the disclosure of the real].
The revelation of the truth and the opening of the provisional means—having already briefly bestowed [the teaching] and granted it to Śāriputra through his three requests for the Dharma-exposition;
the initial raising of doubts and petitioning the Buddha for the explanation of the parables of the carts in the "Parable" chapter;

and the presentation of doubts by Maitreya and the request for the explanation of the fruit-cart in the "Emergence" chapter—the subsequent disclosure of knowledge and vision, the preaching of the Buddha’s lifespan, and so forth, constitute this very [revelation].
"Equally bestowing the three roots and seeking a prediction" means requesting the vehicle; "the Buddha granting predictions to all" means equally bestowing [the fruit] upon the bodhisattvas;
"when the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of doubt is entirely removed" refers to their joy;
and "the twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas" is the meaning of "bestowal. Therefore, the metaphor is combined to say: "causing all these sons to pass day and night for kalpas..."
He constantly enjoys playing together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, riding this precious vehicle directly to the site of enlightenment;
for this reason, it is known that all three vehicles are sought and all three vehicles are bestowed.
Among these, the three vehicles refer to the fruits sought by those of the three vehicles.

Regarding the term "middle" here, Zhenguó stated: "Because the fruits of the three vehicles are not ultimate, it is necessary to turn back and enter the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) before there can be the realization of the fruit;
this is precisely the meaning of the 'differentiation of characteristics' in this chapter. This is first clarified.
The "Great Meaning" (*yidam*) is the ultimate fruit-dharma of the Buddha; for apart from the Universal Dharma (*sarvadharma*), there is no principle by which other vehicles can achieve Buddhahood.
Thus, the *Yanyi* states: "Within the preceding four causes, there is [the potential for] the ultimate fruit, yet it is entirely absent [in others].

It further states: "Regarding the fruit, the causes of the three vehicles are harmonized so that they all return to the single fruit. From this, one should know that it is because the three vehicles lack the fruit that [this teaching] is spoken.
The three vehicles are a provisional indication.
This is because they are the goals pointed out by this intention.
"By means of this intention," etc., refers to receiving the teachings, practicing them, and aspiring to seek the fruit.
Question: Since the followers of the Two Vehicles each attain their respective minor fruits, why do they seek further beyond the boundary?

Once the aspirations of the followers of the Two Vehicles are directed toward Arhatship and they have already exited the boundary to individually realize their minor fruits, it would logically be improper for them to seek more;
how then can it be said that they seek it?

Answer: According to the Hīnayāna, it is said that there are teachings, practices, and fruits; however, according to the Mahāyāna, it is said that in the past there were only verbal teachings and no actual practice or realization of the fruits.
Therefore, it is said that the three vehicles were empty and non-existent.
According to their own schools, such as the Āgamas and other scriptures, it is said that there is a teaching received from which one initiates practice,
and by means of this practice one proceeds toward the fruit and attains the two types of nirvāṇa. However, according to definitive Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
it is said that in former times there were only empty words of skillful guidance, and they were unable to truly cultivate the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) accordingly.
Because that which is attained through unreal practice is not true, and because there is no real fruit, it is said that the three vehicles are empty and non-existent.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states that one departs from the suffering of the triple world by means of the Buddha’s gate of teaching; thus, it says there are "only verbal teachings.

Furthermore, the essential intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* lies in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), yet our Patriarch [Zhiyi] merely classified it as belonging to the gradual teaching, restricting it to the five [vehicles].
Because it was taught gradually at that time, Zhenguó stated: "The perfection of the *Avataṃsaka* is the perfection within the sudden teaching;

the perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the perfection within the gradual teaching. While the meanings of the gradual and the sudden differ between these two sutras, their methods of perfect transformation do not differ.
All commentaries on the *Vajraśekhara*, the *Māṇḍala-prakaraṇa*, the *Qǔmù wèndá*, the *Yuánjué*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and so forth, are entirely consistent with this."
All are judged as the One Vehicle of the Common Teaching (tongjiao yicheng) and the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao yicheng), and so forth.
If, from the perspective of one’s own school, [beings] all attain the fruit, then how could they fail to transcend the world if they do not?

Now, when it is said that "neither attains [the fruit]," this is because it is viewed from the standpoint of the One Vehicle; therefore, when the Real (shi) reflects upon the Expedient (quan), the characteristics of the expedients are exhausted, and thus [they are so described].
There is nothing to be attained.

Originally seeking to exit the realm of boundaries, now that one has already exited, it is not that there is no attainment; rather, one remains within what is being led, and thus all are without attainment when viewed from the perspective of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Ying" (reflecting) means concealment; when the real is manifested, the provisional conceals itself of its own accord. This is the method.
Thus, through skillful means appropriate to the occasion, they are led back to the single reality; once this single reality is revealed, provisional characteristics vanish.
Therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of expedient means are exhausted.
Because one wishes to turn those three types of people toward the One Vehicle, the Mahāyāna also speaks of "turning."
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of desire and so forth," some scholars maintain that since there was already a true principle of uniting the two [vehicles] into one, the meaning is clear;
however, we maintain that the three vehicles were provisionally established to guide beings according to their capacities, and as all three lack inherent substance,
even the Mahāyāna is said to involve a turning back.
If it were not so, then those people seeking ox-carts, having already exited the boundary, would not be the same as ordinary worldlings;

yet, because they do not seek sheep- or deer-carts, they would not be the same as those of the two vehicles; and since they have not yet obtained the great white ox-cart on the open ground, they would not be the same as those of the One Vehicle.
If they are not among these three types of Mahāyāna practitioners, what kind of person could they possibly be?
If they are not equal, having already transcended the three realms, they are certainly not ordinary beings; they do not regress from the Two Vehicles, nor do they advance toward the One Vehicle.
Those who seek the ox-cart should know that such people are followers of the Mahāyāna.
Because they reach the ultimate stage of their own respective positions, they subsequently all enter the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle.
Their "own positions" refer to the stages attained by each of the three vehicles; the "ultimate stage" refers to the destination reached through the cultivation of causes.
Since they have subsequently all entered the dwelling place of the vehicle of fruition, and that place is entirely empty and non-existent, one should then equally bestow the great white ox-cart.

The inexhaustible Dharma-gate of the vehicle is the perfect fruit; thus the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities) states that Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, through long periods of cultivation within that teaching, deepen their understanding until they exhaustively penetrate the source of the *xingbu* (distributed) teaching.

At this point, they shall attain this Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra, for there is no other path by which one can achieve Buddhahood apart from this universal Dharma. Therefore, it is said that they "enter" [it].
Question: Are the three vehicles at the gate real or unreal?

Regarding whether they are real or unreal, from the perspective of one's own school (svayūthya), they are real as they lead to the attainment of the fruit; yet from the perspective of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), they are empty and there is nothing to be attained.
Thus, are those three vehicles real or unreal?
The answer is "real" and "unreal";
it is an answer that is both real and unreal. Why is this so?
What follows explains the reason for this:

because it is a skillful means (*upāya*). It is by means of this skillful means that the child is led out; it is not that he is not real. Because he is led out by means of this skillful means, he is not [merely] real.
These two are non-dual, possessing only a single characteristic.

Regarding the phrase "because this is a skillful means" (upāya), it is shown in general that by means of these skillful means, beings are led out from the three vehicles (*triyāna*), yet they are not unreal.
Because they are led out by these skillful means, they are not real when viewed from the perspective of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Although there are these two meanings, there are no two distinct dharmas; therefore, reality and unreality are of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

Second, the distinction between the teaching (*śāsana*) and the meaning (*artha*). "Teaching" refers to the greatness of the cause; "meaning" refers to the greatness of the fruit. Because cause and fruit are not the same, they are said to be distinct.
Even the ox-cart at the gate is identical to the sheep- and deer-carts in that it possesses only a name; when compared to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), both are merely teachings.

Therefore, within the boundary (sīmā), it is universally admitted that although the three carts are permitted [to leave], they do not actually board the ox-cart when exiting; since they all equally seek [the same goal], it is said that they possess only the name [of being distinct vehicles].

As for those who claim both are merely "teachings" (upadeśa), from the perspective of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), these are merely causes, while the fruit is empty and merely pointed out. Thus, as stated in the following passage:
It is said that the Three Vehicles constitute the teaching (*śāsana*) while the One Vehicle constitutes the meaning (*artha*); thus, one knows their distinction.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "By means of the Buddha’s gateways of teaching, one exits the suffering of the triple world.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the Buddha’s words refer only to the Two Vehicles, because the Sūtra does not make such a restriction; for they seek the [true] cow.
When people seek the teaching and arrive at its meaning, it is likewise not attained by those of the Two Vehicles;
thus, the meaning is as explained previously.

Third, regarding the distinction of what is aimed for: because that One Vehicle is not within the realm [of the Three Vehicles], whereas the Three were previously permitted [within it], it therefore exists outside the realm.
When [the Buddha] bestowed the vehicles upon his sons at the crossroads, they all said it was not what they had originally hoped for.
Because that One Vehicle had been kept secret and undisclosed for over forty years, it was not something permitted within the [three] realms;
the three carts were only revealed and manifested at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when he finally bestowed the great carts. Therefore, it is said "at the crossroads."

Bestowing [the vehicle] at this time was not what was expected; the "four crossroads" (catur-mahāpatha) immediately refers to the realm outside [the burning house], which is unlike the interior of the burning house where paths lead in all directions.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the sons each mounted a great vehicle, obtaining what they had never before experienced—this was not what they had originally expected."

Nor can it be said that this was not their original expectation; for since the Sūtra does not exclude the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), there is no fault in the words of the Sage.
Each of these denials is made because the tenets of those [opponents] are so stubbornly held that they cannot be turned back.

This is because that which was promised within the gate is now entirely unattainable; the ox-cart in the open space was not originally what was hoped for, and thus the present attainment is said to be "not what was originally expected.

Regarding the distinctions in the measure of the four virtues: when pointing from inside the house toward the outside, one speaks only of the ox-cart and does not mention the other virtues, yet it is in the open space [that they are revealed].
The great chariot of the seven treasures bestowed by the Earth is adorned with immeasurable varieties of jewels, such as jeweled nets and bells;

this refers to the excellence of its essential substance (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, while that [previous] passage mentions only the oxen without describing other characteristics, this one states that they are "white oxen, fat, strong, and powerful, swift as the wind," which refers to the excellence of their function (*kāritra*). Moreover, it says they are attended by a vast retinue of servants.
The "provisions for the journey" and so forth refer to their retinues.
Regarding the phrase "within the house" and so on, it mentions only the carts of sheep, deer, and oxen, but does not speak of other virtues;
thus, unlike the great jeweled cart which is adorned with the seven treasures and so forth, the practice, function, essence, and virtues of those three vehicles are entirely incomplete.

This is the difference between the two schools regarding the distinctions of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). If that is so, does it mean that those [other vehicles] lack stages, positions, levels, and so forth?

The *Kongmu* states: "Furthermore, the stages, levels, and the sequential characteristics of the dharmas elucidated in the various sūtras and śāstras of the three vehicles are all explained in this manner from the perspective of the gate of faith and understanding (*adhimukti-mukha*). It further states: "Practice and understanding (*caryā-adhimukti*) also enter [into this]."
Since this is a chapter on the gate of liberation, it now distinguishes those who lack these qualities by focusing on the excellence of their practice, virtues, and functional applications.
These various distinct characteristics are all clarified as differences based upon the Common Teaching (tongjiao) of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Regarding the "Common Teaching" (tóngjiào): because it does not yet manifest the inexhaustible [aspects of reality], it is not the "Distinct Teaching" (biéjiào).
As Master Tànxuán’s *Tàn xuán* (Probing the Profundities) judges, saying: "The Common Teaching means that its meaning is the same as this.
It is called "common" because it shares the same [doctrinal content] as the three vehicles (*triyāna*) of the preceding teachings; thus, it is termed "common."
Furthermore, among those three [vehicles], the ox-cart is unique because that school clarifies it as a single-phase expedient (*upāya*) lacking both a principal and its retinue;
this case, however, is not so, for it is fully endowed with a principal and its retinue, encompassing immeasurable virtues. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"I have such great seven-jeweled carts, their number being immeasurable. These immeasurable jeweled carts do not refer to just one; this reveals the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The inexhaustible teachings are explained extensively in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of those meditative attainments (*samāpatti*): within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), they are the state of perfect luminosity and the full possession of all virtues;

within the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), they are merely isolated gates of a single characteristic. Thus, one knows that the tenets of the Two Vehicles differ; now, by means of this, we shall distinguish the skillful means (*upāya*) of the single characteristic.

The subsequent passage states that teachings are given briefly according to the capacities of beings, such as the principles of "one mark," "one stillness," and "one flavor," rather than being exhaustive expositions.

The *Kongmu* (Pivot of the Teachings) states: "The ultimate teaching of the Three Vehicles—'stillness-illumination and illumination-stillness,' 'one-mark True Suchness,' and even the categories of the conditioned and unconditioned—all these schools differ in their meanings and their principles are each distinct. From this, we know that the ultimate teaching of the Three Vehicles and so forth [are distinct].

This is merely a skillful means of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇopāya*). Now, it is clarified that there is a distinction because the immeasurable jeweled chariots are fully endowed with both the principal and the attendant elements.
Such ancestral texts are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; one must not dogmatically cling to them, for they do not conform to what is called "the one.
This demonstrates the Dharma which is the object of our school's adherence. *Avataṃsaka* is the expressive medium (*vācaka*).
Regarding the teaching, an ancient said: "The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* encompasses two aspects. Such a statement is already erroneous;

to say that its words may be applied here is likewise erroneous. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* school, the principle of "harmonizing the three" (*hui san*) should be understood as the "concordant teaching" (*tongjiao*), for the school does not take "inexhaustibility" as its primary tenet.
It is simply because the sūtra text contains these two meanings that they are cited in this chapter.
The seventh and eighth gates, concerning the establishment [of the teachings], are both of the same teaching (tongjiao).
These are distinguished only by way of the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
The preceding four gates all rely on the meaning of the four vehicles in the *Lotus Sūtra*, as explained in the first gate.

Fifth, regarding the distinctions of the stages of provisional assignment (*prajñapti-sthāna-viśeṣa*): according to the *Bunyō-kyō*, the *Ninnō-kyō*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *She-da-cheng-lun* (Treatise on the Compendium of the Mahāyāna) translated during the Liang dynasty, and other texts, the first, second, and third stages are provisionally assigned to the mundane world; the fourth through the seventh stages are provisionally assigned to the supramundane;
and from the eighth stage upward, they are provisionally assigned to the ultra-supramundane. Within the supramundane, the fourth and fifth stages are provisionally assigned to the Śrāvakas.

In those sūtras and śāstras, the various stages (*bhūmi*) are distinguished by associating them with the four vehicles: the Dharma of the *ṣaḍbhūmi* (six stages) is associated with the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle; the Dharma of the seventh stage is associated with the *bodhisattva* vehicle;
and from the eighth stage upward, they are associated with the *ekayāna*. Now, however, we shall treat these stages according to their respective levels.
This reveals that there are distinctions among the various vehicles (*yāna*).

If the Mahāyāna were identical to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), then the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) would already be the supramundane transcendence, and the One Vehicle should not be situated in the eighth stage.
Therefore, one should know that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, those of the three vehicles seek the three carts.
"Going out to the gate" refers to the ultimate realization of one's own station within the world-transcending [path] common to all three vehicles;
this corresponds to the stages from the fourth bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi herein.

"Bestowing the great white ox-cart at the crossroads" refers to that which lies above the world-transcending, and is thus the One Vehicle of the super-world-transcending; this corresponds to the eighth bhūmi herein.
The above is the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Question: If this is so, why does the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) translated during the Liang dynasty state that "the goodness of the two vehicles is called 'transcending the world,' while from the eighth stage upward until the stage of Buddhahood it is called 'transcending the transcendent'? Since it does not say that the three vehicles are "transcending the world," how can you make such a claim?

It is said that the fourth and fifth stages constitute the stage of the Śrāvaka, the sixth stage constitutes the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, and from the eighth stage onward is the supramundane. As for that seventh stage, who is it?
Therefore, one should know that what those of the two vehicles call "supramundane" refers to both the Great and Small Vehicles; for both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are termed "Small."
Therefore, the names of the two vehicles are applied universally, as will be explained below.
Regarding the statement that "the names of the two vehicles are applied universally, as will be explained below," this is the same as in the section on the "Teaching of the Same" (同教).
Sixth, regarding the distinctions in entrustment (*parindanā*), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In a future age, if there be good sons or good daughters..."
To those who believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* so that they may hear and know it, for the purpose of enabling them to attain the Buddha’s wisdom.

If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept it, you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by means of other profound teachings of the Tathāgata. If you are able to act in this way, you will be repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
The passage from "At the time when [the Buddha] has not yet descended" down to "attaining the wisdom of a Buddha" is the entrustment of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The passage from "If there are those who have descended" down to "instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening" is the entrustment of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). The passage beginning with "You all" is the general entrustment.

The commentary explains that "other profound dharmas" refers to the Mahāyāna; because it is not the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), it is termed "other," yet because it is not the Hīnayāna, it is termed "profound.

"Other" signifies that which has not been fully exhausted [by other teachings]. As stated in the *Kongmu*: "This refers to the limited scope of the transformative ritual according to a single aspect."
Regarding the statement that it is not an inexhaustible teaching, it is as the sutra says: "This is a teaching with remainder (*śeṣa-vacana*), not a supreme teaching.
Therefore, although it is called the Mahāyāna, it is termed "remainder"; yet, because it is not a teaching for the ignorant, it is termed "profound" (*gambhīra*).
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the Hīnayāna serves as a "remaining profound dharma," for the Lotus Sūtra precisely refutes the Hīnayāna;
how then could it be praised as being "profound"?
Since the Lotus Sūtra refutes the Hīnayāna to reveal the One Vehicle, it cannot be praised as being profound.
Therefore, one should know that the specific intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* lies precisely in the One Vehicle (Ekayāna); it is for this reason that this entrustment is made.

Although the doctrinal tenets of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* concern the One Vehicle, even though the Two Vehicles and others are here entrusted [with the teaching], one should know that its true intent lies precisely in the One Vehicle.
The seventh is the distinction in the objects of the faculties (*indriya*) and their reception.

This means that there are differences among those who receive and practice according to their faculties, capacities, and conditions; that is, the two types of capacities—the universal and the particular—elicit two different types of teachings, the universal and the particular, respectively.
As it is said in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta*) of this sutra: "O Son of the Buddha,

if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the six *pāramitās* and cultivate the roots of goodness of the factors of enlightenment for immeasurable billions of *nayuta* kalpas, yet have not heard this sutra— or having heard it,
do not believe, accept, uphold, or accord with it— such individuals are still merely 'provisional' bodhisattvas."

The commentary explains: This clarifies that because the faculties of the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles have not yet matured, even though they have practiced in this manner for so many kalpas, there are those who do not believe in or hear this sūtra of the One Vehicle.

It should be understood that these are precisely those whom [the Buddha] previously, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, instructed, benefited, and gladdened through other profound dharmas; this is in anticipation of the ultimate dharma of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, it is said that they are designated as "provisional names"; yet, from the perspective of our own school, they are also real.
The meaning of this passage clarifies that the *Avataṃsaka* is the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which differs from those [other teachings].
Regarding the statement that "words are provisional designations," this chapter clarifies that because words refer to the One [Vehicle], they are called provisional designations;

yet, in relation to their own school’s tenets, they are also real. *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities) states: "A 'provisionally named Bodhisattva' is one who practices solely according to the provisional teachings and is thus obscured from attaining the true practice of the One Vehicle.
This is not the case for those prior to the first stage or those on the stages themselves. If it were so..."
One cannot distinguish between the two schools [of thought] based on this alone.
Eighth, the distinction between that which is difficult to believe and that which is easy to believe:
as stated in the "Bhadrapāla Chapter" of this sutra, "Among all classes of sentient beings in all worlds, there are few who desire to seek the state of a śrāvaka."
Those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas are even fewer still; those who seek the Great Vehicle are extremely rare.
While seeking the Great Vehicle may yet be considered easy, being able to have faith in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult.

To cultivate faith in the Three Vehicles is already difficult, let alone that of the One Vehicle, whose manifest texts shine brightly and whose provisional and ultimate teachings possess clear evidence.
The commentary explains: because this chapter correctly elucidates the final mind of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), it encompasses all stages and the attainment of Buddhahood.
Since such matters as these transcend the three vehicles, they may be difficult to believe and accept; therefore, the three vehicles are cited for comparison to resolve this.

"The final mind of the stage of faith" refers to the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-bhāga*) at the completion of the ten faiths, wherein one attains all stages up to the Buddha-ground and so forth;
thus it is said that "one becomes a Buddha. This is actual accomplishment (*bhūta-niṣpatti*), not transformational accomplishment (*nirmāṇa-niṣpatti*); it is not [the case] of the three [vehicles].
Regarding the "Vehicle of the Realm" (Cheng-jing-ji): even if there were those who heard it, they would surely find it difficult to believe and accept.

To this day, some say that the "Provisional" (Ji) refers only to the contemplative practice of names and is not the "Ultimate" (Jing). Fearing that such a teaching might be difficult to believe, the scripture uses the three vehicles to provide a comparative resolution, thereby clarifying the differences between the two schools.

Question: Previously, it was explained that the fruit-virtue (guo-de) transcends all characteristics of verbal expression; how then can it be said that [the fruit] is reached at the end of the ten stages of faith (shi-xin)?

If the mind itself possesses the functional virtue of the fruit of Buddhahood, and if those in the stage of the ten faiths were identical to that fruit-virtue, then the fruit-virtue would be a phenomenon that can be described;
how then could it be called "ineffable"? Answer: To manifest the fruit-virtue while still in the causal stage is intended to show that this fruit-virtue is ineffable.
Therefore, the words praising its virtues state: "The Bodhisattva, while abiding in the first stage, universally encompasses [all stages]."
This refers to the merits of all the stages (*bhūmi*).
Ninth, the distinction of revealing the principle according to the capacities of beings:
as the first verse at the beginning of the ninth stage in this sutra says, "If there are sentient beings who are inferior and whose minds are weary and despondent... [it] reveals...

By means of the path of the śrāvaka, one causes them to emerge from the manifold sufferings. Furthermore, if there are sentient beings whose faculties are slightly clear and sharp, and who find joy in the dharma of dependent origination, one preaches for them the path of the pratyekabuddha.
If there are persons whose faculties are clear and sharp, who possess great compassion, and who benefit all sentient beings, one preaches for them the path of the bodhisattva.

This explains that if one proceeds toward the Dharma-gate by relying on provisional means (*upāya*), there are two senses in which it is generally described as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*):

Second, because it serves as a provisional means for that ultimate, perfectly penetrating One Vehicle.

Regarding the general meaning:

Second, it is explained that there are three types of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyāna*).

Question: Since the initial teaching speaks of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*), there are three vehicles; yet in the final and sudden teachings, they discuss the single reality together. How is this so?

This constitutes the first section, which correctly elucidates the fundamental meaning.

Among these, that which is "small" while penetrating the "great" is not the teaching for those of dull faculties who penetrate the small; nor is that which is "great" while penetrating the "small" the One Vehicle.

The three meanings—the beginning, the end, and the sudden—are each explained differently, yet all are the Three Vehicles. When the Lesser Vehicle is considered alone, it constitutes these three meanings;
for this reason, the Liang Dynasty *Lun* (Treatise) makes such a statement. Since this chapter clarifies this meaning from beginning to end, it says, "Based on these three meanings," and so forth.
Including both the *Kongmu* (Comprehensive Catalogue) and the *Wenda* (Questions and Answers), the total count is one hundred.

In more than forty locations, this meaning is discussed; searching through the texts of the two mysteries (the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*), both the upper and lower sections, the selection of the three vehicles also clarifies this meaning.
However, there are also instances where the meaning of the single nature (*ekadhātu*) is used to select the five natures (*pañcadhātu*), though these are mentioned only sparingly.
Second, if one uses the final three teachings—Sudden, Complete, and Perfect—to subsume the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), within that framework, they are likewise opened as being identical.
If one distinguishes them, the Final and Sudden [teachings] are considered the same, while the Perfect Teaching is considered distinct.

This is because the Final and Sudden teachings speak of the single nature (*ekadhātu*) and subsume the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), whereas the Characteristics School (*lakṣaṇavāda*) speaks of the five natures (*pañcadhātu*) and maintains the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Therefore, these two teachings are opened up to enter into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and are subsumed under the school of the single nature.
Of these, the former two are not yet harmonized and are thus the "same teaching" (*samānaśāsana*), while the latter one is perfectly interfused and is the "distinct teaching" (*viśeṣaśāsana*).
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), within the One Vehicle school, there are no dharmas other than those that are either identical or distinct;

therefore, none of the patriarchs established two types of "identical teaching" (tongjiao) in contrast to the "one distinct teaching" (yibiejiao). Taking the Initial Teaching as the Three Vehicles and the teaching for the ignorant as the Hinayana constitutes three distinct schools.
This is also corroborated by the *Liang-lun* (Treatise of the Liang Dynasty); one should know that this treatise was composed in that region and thus cites it.
The sūtras and śāstras used in this land contain many points, yet their applications differ; thus, there is no impediment to the formation of three schools.

One should know that the white ox is one, the three carts are three, the "fools in the teaching" (yūfǎ) is the small [vehicle], and the three birds leaving the cage or the three beasts crossing the river are all general meanings from that region. How could it be that those alone are permitted for exclusive use?
Is this not something that can be cited? Future scholars should deeply contemplate this.

If it is argued that when the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras were taught, there were those who attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle through diverse understandings of a single sound—thereby establishing the existence of the Three Vehicles—then why was there no such diverse understanding leading to the attainment of the Lesser Vehicle when the *Avataṃsaka* was taught?
Furthermore, why was there no such [diverse understanding] when the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and other texts were taught?
One can realize the great fruit;
therefore, one should know that the principles of the three schools are each distinct and beyond doubt.
Thus, there is no doubt regarding the principles of the One Vehicle school, the Three Vehicle school, and the Hinayana school, even for those who might harbor disbelief.
For this reason, it is indicated repeatedly.
Second, regarding the three vehicles—Mahāyāna, Madhyamāyāna, and Hīnayāna—there are three meanings:

first, because the One Vehicle is integrated into Mahāyāna and the "Dharma for the Ignorant" (fo-fa) is merged with Hīnayāna, there are only three. This can be understood through both teaching and principle; this [point] concerns the One [Vehicle].
Regarding the "vehicle" (yāna), there are two types: within the Mahāyāna itself there are three vehicles as described above;
likewise, within the Hīnayāna there are also three, such as the Śrāvaka-dharma, Pratyekabuddha-dharma, and Buddha-dharma found within the *Kṣudrakavibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Here, the Buddha-dharma differs from the two vehicles solely in its practice of compassion, loving-kindness, and so forth.

This has three meanings. Regarding the first, the analysis according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*): because the Mahāyāna distinguishes itself from the Two Vehicles, those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) must turn their minds [toward the Great].
This is explained in terms of universal capacities; thus, one knows that the analysis is made according to the One Vehicle.

Second, within the Mahāyāna itself there are three types, as mentioned above—namely, the *Puxu* (Universal), the *Chao* (Transcendent), and the *Pin* (Grade)—as taught in such texts as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Furthermore, there is a version of the *Liang-lun* (Treatise of Liang).
"Taking the three vehicles as the Great Vehicle" refers to the school of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna). "Three" means that within the Small Vehicle there are also three;

however, as for the differences such as compassion and so forth, these merely involve thirty-four moments of mind to sever the fetters and become a true Buddha—this refers to the school of the Small Vehicle.
Fourth, regarding the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*), there are likewise three interpretations: first, the four are defined as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*);

this is because the One Vehicle is distinguished from the Three, while the Śrāvaka vehicle is subsumed within them. Second, the four are defined as the One Vehicle, the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), and the human and celestial realms;
this is the general interpretation. Third, the four are defined as the Three Vehicles and the human and celestial realms; this may be understood by reference to the above.
The first refers to the "lower combination," meaning that those śrāvakas who are deluded regarding the Dharma and have likewise turned their minds [toward enlightenment] are combined.

The second refers to the "general opening" below, which, concerning the three worlds, opens up the human and celestial realms within the world into four. The third refers to the "three vehicles" below, which constitute the three.

Fifth, regarding the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), there are likewise three ways of enumerating them: first, the one vehicle (*ekayāna*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*) constitute the five;

second, the three vehicles together with humans and devas constitute the five; third, the Buddha, the two vehicles, devas, and Brahmās also constitute the five—all of which may be understood according to the preceding explanations.
The first three [categories] are threefold, thus making five; the second refers to the division of humans and devas; the third refers to the lower [realms], all of which are visible.
The sixth refers to the "immeasurable vehicles," meaning all dharma-gates; therefore, this sutra says: "In a single world..."
This refers to hearing within [the teaching] the sounds proclaiming one vehicle (*ekayāna*), or two, three, four, five, or even immeasurable vehicles.
While all dharma-gates can lead one into the Way, there are two meanings here; in this context, it merely distinguishes between the various vehicles.
The classification of vehicles has been completed above.

It should be understood that the teachings of the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as those of humans and devas, all enter this gate precisely because it is a skillful means; because the meaning of the Dharma-realm is universal;
and because the Perfect Teaching is profoundly deep, vast, and inconceivable. Thus, both the common and the distinct are each subsumed within it.
Because the Dharma is exhaustive, my Patriarch said: "This ocean of teaching is vast and profound, encompassing all without exception.

To speak of its horizontal inclusion and total inclusion, it embraces all five teachings, even including those of humans and devas, leaving nothing uncontained; only thus is its depth and breadth revealed. Furthermore, to speak of its breadth, it clarifies the immeasurable vehicles;
to speak of its depth, it reveals only the One Vehicle. One should know that this ocean of teaching is entirely deep and entirely [vast]."

It is extensively capable of both excluding and including; yet there are those who do not know which dharmas are entirely excluded and which are entirely included, being truly ignorant of even a few words and phrases.
Second, as for the fusion of the fundamental and the derivative:
Regarding the fundamental and the derivative, they are subsumed within the same unity; the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles are interfused and non-dual.
This interfusion of the various vehicles of the "Teaching of Commonality" (tongjiao) into a single, non-dual Dharma-realm has two gates.

This "teaching of commonality" refers to those within the various vehicles—whether categorized as three or one—who are free from the obstruction between the provisional and the real, or who establish the provisional and the real in opposition to one another yet mutually complete each other, and are thus collectively termed the One Vehicle. This is fundamentally because the response to the dharma-realm possesses two gates;
because there are these two gates, the two schools stand side by side. Because they respond to the dharma-realm, the non-obstruction of the three and the one all enter herein.
For this reason, our Patriarch said: "Alternatively, it is also universally inclusive because the fundamental and the derivative are perfectly interfused and there is not a single characteristic;
because it encompasses skillful means; and because all are one Dharma-realm. Therefore, that which is attained by humans and devas is also contained therein. He further said:

"If one includes those who employ skillful means, then all the various teachings mentioned previously are likewise contained within this. Thus, it is called the "Sameness Teaching" (tongjiao) One Vehicle.
To first differentiate the various vehicles and subsequently clarify the integration of the fundamental and the derivative is an error.

It is like the Master [Zongmi] saying: "This text, while existing within the Three Vehicles, also functions as the One Vehicle. Why is this? Because by observing the Dharma through this [lens], its function applies everywhere in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus, Yi Jian’s analogy of splitting firewood to suggest that they will become one within the single Dharma-realm and thereby receive the name of "teaching of sameness" (tóngjiào) is mistaken.

Furthermore, because this text pertains to the *dhātu* (element/realm), and because it is not fully revealed in other systems of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) or the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), one should know that if there were no ultimate, inexhaustible One Vehicle alone, [it would not be so]. Why? Because it corresponds to the *dharmadhātu*.

If, according to the characteristics of the text, the distinct characteristics are those of the Three Vehicles, one should know that this explains how the distinctions of the Three Vehicles lead to entry into the One Vehicle. As...
It is said: "This text belongs to the Three Vehicles, yet its meaning penetrates the One Vehicle. Why? Because it accords with the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, it is said:
"This text belongs to the Three Vehicles, yet its meaning penetrates the One Vehicle; this is because its function arises from the same *dharmadhātu*. Moreover, it is said:
"This text belongs to the Three Vehicles, yet it reaches ultimate fulfillment in the One Vehicle. Why? Because it is designated as the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, it is said: "All..."
The various distinctions in meaning are all the doctrine of the Common Teaching of the One Vehicle (tongjiao yicheng). Why is this so?

Because they establish the Universal Dharma (pufa) and are themselves established by the Universal Dharma; thus, the meanings are extremely clear. The name "Common Teaching" arises merely from the combination of the three [teachings] into one.

1. The gate of submerging the provisional to return to the real is the teaching of the One Vehicle; 2. The gate of gathering the real to form the provisional is the teaching of the Three Vehicles and so forth.

Regarding "submerging the provisional" and so on: because the three disappear and the one is revealed, there is only the One Vehicle; regarding "gathering the real to form the provisional": [the same applies].
Thus, one [vehicle] is hidden while three remain, distinguishing the capacities [of beings] such that they do not see the Universal Dharma (pūrvadharma) but see only the Three Vehicles.

In the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), there is only the first gate; the Three Vehicles alone possess the latter gate. The Shared Teaching (tongjiao) possesses both gates, encompassing the "One" within the "Three.
As for the statement that it is "the same as the teaching of the Shared [Vehicle]," its meaning is seen here.
At the beginning, the provisional is not destroyed and is immediately subsumed; thus, the three vehicles are identical to the one vehicle without obstructing the three.
At the end, the real is not different and is immediately the provisional; thus, the one vehicle is identical to the three vehicles without obstructing the one.
Therefore, the one and the three are fused and integrated, their essence being non-dual.
In the first case, because there are four phrases below regarding "not being able to destroy" and so forth, the one does not obstruct the three.

In the latter case, it is like a river branching out from its source: while the branches form the particular, the source remains unmoved. Therefore, while the provisional (upāya) is identical to the ultimate reality, it does not obstruct the single essence;
these two are non-dual. As my Patriarch said: "Division is not outside of perfection; every division is perfect, thereby forming [the whole]."
The parts are not outside the circle; the circle is formed by encompassing the parts, and this is precisely the circle within the parts, which are themselves within the circle.
Because water moves, it forms waves; because the water is still, it remains water. What duality could there be?
Question: If this is so, and both gates are equal, why do you further speak of the provisional and the real?
Since they are equal, the three and the one are mutually fused and their essence is non-dual.
Answer: Because the gateways of meaning differ, the provisional and the real always exist; yet because the principle universally penetrates all, the entire body is non-dual.

If one follows the gate of principle (*artha*), then the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*bhūta*) are ever-present within the Dharma-realm; their principle is perfect and their essence is non-dual. Why is this?
It is said that when the provisional arises, it invariably relies upon the real; therefore, by grasping the real, the real is not lost.
However, the real does not invariably depend upon the provisional; thus, when the provisional is extinguished, the provisional does not stand.
What is meant by "the gates being different while there is both the provisional and the real"? This refers to the provisional explanation that follows.
It is not that there is water without waves, for waves necessarily depend upon water; nor is it that there is one without the three, for the three must be gathered from the one.

Because they rely on the root to be formed, and because the branches collectively constitute the particular, the One Buddha Vehicle is distinguished and taught as three; thus, the reality is not lost.
Where there is a wave, there is water; since the wave is entirely moist, when the wind ceases, the water remains. Therefore, by grasping the reality, the reality is not lost.
When one realizes the underlying stillness of the water, it does not depend on the waves; thus, realizing the reality does not rely upon the provisional.
Once the provisional is subsumed, the characteristics of skillful means are exhausted. To cross the river and then burn the boat is the point where the provisional is no longer established.

Therefore, although the three vehicles (triyāna) appear to exist and perish, they are ultimately one; and although the one vehicle (ekayāna) appears to be hidden or manifest, it is ultimately ever inexhaustible.

The three vehicles are provisional constructs to guide sentient beings, yet their essence is fundamentally one. This is explained according to their functional meaning as existing or perishing, while their intrinsic nature is fundamentally [one].

From non-existence to existence, the single vehicle’s universal Dharma naturally flourishes in profusion; because those of small wisdom do not know this, it is said that the Dharma-body has hiddenness and manifestation, yet its essence is inexhaustible.
Through this integration, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, "only the single vehicle," as in the Separate Teaching; second, "only... [the text continues].
The three vehicles are like the three vehicles because they do not know the One; thus, they may be three, or both one and three, as in the teachings of commonality;
or they may be neither one nor three, as in the ocean of the ultimate fruit of cessation.
"Melted" (*yōng*) means that affairs enter into principle and are thereby dissolved; thus, they are harmonized into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, "only the One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*):
the universal Dharma stands alone, independent, and devoid of all else. This is as explained above regarding the Separate Teaching (*pratyekadeśanā*). Second, "or only the Three Vehicles":

this is taught as a provisional skillful means (*upāya*), because it conceals the One Vehicle. Those whose faculties are inferior do not know the One Vehicle; because they do not know it, it is said to be "concealed."
Therefore, one must not raise objections based on the capacity for the One Vehicle alone.
Third, "both three and one" refers to the same teaching as before, wherein the three and the one are harmonized and unified, returning the three to the one.
Fourth, "neither three nor one" refers to the ultimate perfection of the nature and its fruit, as previously explained.
Within these four meanings, each individual gateway fully encompasses the entire essence of the Dharma;
therefore, whether the various vehicles are preserved or subsumed, they do not obstruct one another—this can be understood through careful reflection.

Because the nature of the Dharma-realm is interfused such that both the partial and the perfect manifest simultaneously within the complete inclusion of all dharmic bodies, the various vehicles—whether they persist or dissolve—are both provisional and ultimate;
yet, this is spoken from the perspective of the Three Vehicles. Therefore, they do not obstruct one another.
By reflecting deeply according to this principle, one may attain understanding.

The remaining explanations regarding the names, essence, and other attributes of the vehicle are all as explained elsewhere. The above concludes the clarification of the establishment of the One Vehicle.
The details concerning its nature as a conveyance and so forth are extensively discussed in the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Separate Record*, the *Tanxuan ji*, and other commentaries.

Therefore, this is now demonstrated. This section has two parts: first, distinguishing the scope of the doctrine and its meaning; second, clarifying the scope of the encompassing benefit.
First, regarding the differentiation of the scope of the teachings and their meanings, this clarifies the differences in the respective scopes of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.

The beginning and middle also have two parts: first, showing the characteristics; second, opening and synthesizing them. Within the first part, there are three meanings.

Therefore, the *Kongmu* (General Overview) states that the meaning of the "ten numbers" contains two gates: first, the gate of the perfected round teaching; second, the gate of the unperfected round teaching.

Now, when comparing the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and others with the original *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] such as the *Neizang jing* and the *Baolun jing*, the "ten numbers" therein are merely single and distinct, lacking all aspects of the round [teaching];
thus, they are subsumed within the three vehicles (*triyāna*) because they do not fully possess the ten meanings.
There are also two kinds of enumeration: first, it refers to the three vehicles, causing people to understand and analyze them;

second, it refers to the one vehicle, which is manifested in contrast to those of inferior capacity. Now, because the perfect number is employed, it says "ten times ten," as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This indicates the teaching that serves as the means of expression (*upāya*), thereby elucidating the meaning of the superior teaching. *Yunhua* says: "For now..."

Regarding this single scripture, the *Avataṃsaka*, its fundamental tenet clarifies that the dependent origination of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) does not transcend its own essence as cause and fruit;
this is the immediate classification [of its doctrine].

Second, regarding the "three carts at the gate," there is an inherent distinction between teaching and meaning: within the realm [of birth and death], it is shown as the teaching; transcending the realm, it is the meaning.

Nevertheless, the meaning of the teachings is without distinction; this should be understood according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other texts, which explain it as the teaching of the Three Vehicles.
As for the presentation of one's own teachings and meanings within one's own school, it is like holding up an empty fist to demonstrate the teaching.
To entice a child is merely to have words without substance; to lead them out is the meaning of "righteousness" (yi).

To rush toward fire is difficult to realize as being truly the three vehicles. If one asks: are the Buddhas of the Small Vehicle and the Buddhas of the Three Vehicles both Buddhas according to the Āgamas?
If their doctrinal meanings are not distinct, then "leading them out" constitutes the meaning, while "enticing and leading them" constitutes the teaching. These two are [distinguished].

Because they are non-dual, they are said to be "without distinction. This refers to the teachings of the Three Vehicles—that is, the three intermediate teachings—within which there are both provisional and ultimate aspects, yet these are collectively considered as the single vehicle of the Three Vehicles. Other sutras include the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Samantaprabhā-samādhi*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and so forth;
as well as treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Questions of Maitreya).
Third, taking the three carts at the gate as the provisional teachings (*upāya*) and separately bestowing the great ox-cart outside the realm as the revelation of the true meaning:
this corresponds to the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding those who open the gates of the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*): because the stages of understanding and practice (*adhigama-pratipatti*) of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*), as well as their respective grounds (*bhūmi*), are all means for entering the One Vehicle (*eka-yāna*), and because the dharmas of cause and effect therein are all merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) within the *āgama*, they are all categorized under the heading of "Teaching. It is said:
Furthermore, the gates of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), the stages, and the sequential order of distinctions elucidated in the various sūtras and śāstras of the three vehicles—

Furthermore, it is stated within the context of the gate of faith and understanding (*adhimukti-mukha*) that if one relies on the practice of the Dharma, even those whose understanding enters the realm beyond the gate, such as those on the open ground and others who are granted the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*), are all given a prophetic assurance (*vyākaraṇa*). This is precisely what is shown to be the true meaning.
This corresponds to the "Identical Teaching" (*tongjiao*) of the One Vehicle; it is the essential point of the aforementioned Identical Teaching, which is both threefold and one.
Question: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a scripture whose central doctrine is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Because the Three Vehicles accomplish their practice within the triple world (*tridhātu*), whereas the One Vehicle exists beyond the triple world and serves as the object of seeing and hearing for those within it, many of our own school’s patriarchs have regarded the *Lotus Sūtra* as the "Provisional One Vehicle" (*tongjiao ekayāna*). This chapter itself contains more than ten such instances.
The text states that this "teaching of commonality" refers to the teachings of the Final and Sudden [vehicles].
Second, regarding the opening and closing [of the gates], there are two parts: first, the specific, and second, the general.
Within the specific section, each of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles has three phrases.
Regarding the "three phrases of the three vehicles": first, they may refer to both teaching and meaning as explained according to the specific tenets of the three vehicles;

second, they may refer to teaching alone and not meaning as explained according to the common teaching of the one vehicle; third, they may refer to neither teaching nor meaning as explained according to the distinct teaching of the one vehicle; for these are the respective designations applied to them.

As listed in the text, "that which is designated" (the object of designation) refers to what is being pointed out; for example, if the *samādhi* of the profound emptiness (*gaganasamādhi*) is designated as belonging to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it belongs to the One Vehicle;
if it is designated as belonging to the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), it belongs to the Three Vehicles.
Now, since each [aspect] is perfectly interfused as that which is designated by the One Vehicle, there is no further distinction between this and the One Vehicle itself. Thus:
One’s own school has lost the meaning of the teaching. "Mu" (目) is the form of the eye; it designates the eye.
When Huan Wen was at Shitou, he said to the gentlemen: "If you can designate this city, I shall present you with two concubines.
Kong Mu replied: "The teaching is the expedient means for designating. He further stated: "The teaching that names designates the meaning of what is named," and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of the limits of the teachings:
as for the "One Vehicle and three phrases," they may refer to both teaching and meaning when explained according to the distinct teaching (*biete jiao*);

or they may refer to meaning alone, not teaching, when explained according to the common teaching (*tongjiao*); or they may be neither teaching nor meaning, referring solely to the Three Vehicles, because they conceal the inexhaustible teaching and meaning of that [One Vehicle].

The various phrases are easy to understand; as for "concealing the meaning of that teaching," it refers to the distinctions among the three capacities [of sentient beings]. Because those of small wisdom do not see or hear the Great Dharma, it is said to be "concealed.

Regarding the general analysis: either both the teaching and the meaning are concealed—whereby the Three Vehicles are viewed from the perspective of the One Vehicle—or both the teaching and the meaning are revealed.

Because the One Vehicle is contrasted with the Three Vehicles, these two phrases may be taken together as an explanation according to the "teaching of commonality" (*tongjiao*); alternatively, both teaching and meaning may be fully present, each being explained according to the specific distinctions of its own school.
The general discussion consists of three parts. Regarding the third phrase, "or possessing," "possessing" refers to possessing both the teaching (*śāsana*) and the meaning (*artha*);
the Three Vehicles constitute the teaching, while the One Vehicle constitutes the meaning. The remainder of the text is self-evident.
Second, as for the "comprehension and benefit," there are three sections within it.
Regarding the classification of realms, there are two types of practitioners—internal and external—and the benefits they receive differ accordingly.
First, some may only encompass those with internal capacities, leading them to attain supramundane benefit and regarding this as the ultimate;
this is explained according to the specific tenets of the Three Vehicles, as also clarified in works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
This refers to the drawing forth [of beings] by means of the three vehicles.

Second, there is the case where those with capacities outside the realms are gathered and led to attain the benefit of supramundane transcendence, which constitutes the ultimate goal; this has two types.
This is a general designation based on the capacities of beings.

If one first causes others to attain liberation through the three vehicles and subsequently employs skillful means to lead them to the single vehicle, this is a teaching that harmonizes the single vehicle and the three vehicles;
thus, it belongs to the category of the "Teaching of Commonality" (tóngjiào) and is also called the "Teaching of Returning the Three to Enter the One.

This is as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If, however, one has already established understanding and practice regarding the single vehicle and subsequently realizes it through supramundane embodiment, [this is the Teaching of Returning the One to Enter the Three].
That dharma belongs to the classification of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as explained in the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics" (*Xiaoxiang pin*).

If it says "previously equal" (*xiansheng deng*), this refers to the "Previously Shared Teaching" (*xiantong jiao*) of the "Returning the Three to Enter the One" (*huisan ruyi*); "Shared Teaching" is simply another name for it.

If the *Kongmu* states, "The Sūtra says that the three are brought together to return to the one; thus we know they are the same," this points to the phenomenal characteristics (*xingxiang*) of the teaching.
The explanation of the "Common Teaching" (*sāmānya-dharma*) does not mean that the convergence of the three vehicles into one constitutes a "common teaching";
rather, it is called "common" because the three and the one share a common basis. The *Lotus Sūtra* is the sūtra upon which this Common Teaching of the One Vehicle relies.

The explanation of the five teachings and three vehicles universally clarifies that all the Buddha-dharma manifested by Śākyamuni Tathāgata through the Ocean-Seal Samādhi does not transcend the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, or the Small Vehicle.

Riding upon the three schools, they encompass all; do not grasp them through mere sentimentality. If one first practices the Distinct Teaching and subsequently achieves understanding and practice, this pertains to the mundane realm;

the "penetration" of seeing and hearing and the "understanding and practice" leading to supramundane realization refer exclusively to the stage of entry through seeing and hearing. Since both entry and realization are based on the One Vehicle, they belong to the Distinct Teaching.
As for the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics," it concerns the threefold sudden and perfect [teaching] for the heavenly son in hell.
Third, there are cases where [the teaching] universally encompasses both types of capacities to bring about two kinds of benefits; this also has two aspects.
The two benefits refer to the two kinds of benefit: supramundane and ultra-supramundane.

If one first leads others out by means of the three vehicles and subsequently causes them to attain the One Vehicle, this is also a case of the "same teaching" (*tongjiao*), because it combines the three and one to encompass two capacities and accomplish two benefits;
this is as taught in the *Lotus Sūtra*. Whether it be within the realm [of the mundane] where one sees and hears the supramundane to attain the Dharma, or attains realization beyond the supramundane;

or whether it be within the realm where there is both seeing, hearing, understanding, and practice, while in the supramundane there is only understanding and practice—[these all fall under the same category].

The supramundane [teaching] consists solely of the realization and entry into these [stages]; this belongs to the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle (*pratyekayāna*), as explained in the *Avataṃsaka*.
The initial gateway can be seen therein: while within the realm, the lower [stages] do not conjoin with the three [higher vehicles], and thus they belong to the Separate [Teaching].

The differences in meaning arise from whether one considers the stages of seeing, hearing, practice, and realization within the mundane and supramundane realms, or includes the transcendence of the supramundane—just as described in the *Avataṃsaka*.

That which Vasubandhu (Yan) distinguishes—the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*), its doctrine, its meaning, its inclusion of capacities, and its accomplishment of benefit—is all that is "expounded" (*saṃprakāśita*);

as the sūtra says, this refers specifically to the "expounding" (*deśanā*) of the teaching. Third, the presentation of the systems for establishing the teachings according to ancient and modern [scholars].
The various teachings established by the sages of antiquity and the present are not uniform; for now, I shall briefly enumerate ten schools to serve as a model for reflection.

Regarding those who established these teachings throughout history, the first two chapters have already distinguished the vehicles of the Dharma they expounded, how they encompass sentient beings, and the benefits they achieve.

The three [categories] are not identical, yet their sameness and difference are also distinct; intending to reveal that the scriptures and treatises which serve as the expressive means have varying depths, and to demonstrate the ultimate principle of the school one follows, it is appropriate to classify the teachings and establish the fundamental tenets. To this end, I shall first recount the exemplary models of past and present masters;

thus, this section is titled "The Opening of the Gate by the Wise and Distinguished," for there have been many who have opened and classified [the teachings], and I shall here recount ten schools to provide a standard for guidance.

First, based on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts, Bodhiruci established the doctrine of "one sound" (*ekasvara-dharma*), asserting that all sacred teachings are of one sound, one flavor (*ekarasa*), and one rain (*ekavarṣa*). However, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings differ, they understand these differently according to their respective capacities;
thus, although there appear to be many varieties, when examined at its source, it is solely the Tathāgata’s single, perfect sound-teaching. As the Sūtra says:
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their respective types; this is the same principle.
Bodhiruci, who arrived in China during the Later Wei dynasty, established the "Single-Voice Teaching" based on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

"Single voice" refers to the "single flavor" (*ekarasa*) in the *Vimalakīrti*, while "single rain" refers to the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which speaks of the three [vehicles].

Grasses and trees are different, yet they equally receive the moisture of a single rain; the five natures and three vehicles are distinct, yet the Dharma-rain is of one flavor without differentiation.
