Thus, this single sound is sometimes called the root of the teachings and sometimes called the fusion of the root and the branches—a great skillful means of the Dharma.
Yet Guishan claims that the Perfect Teaching subsumes the preceding four, such that each and every one is identical.

In the ocean of perfection, the hundred rivers are none other than the sea itself. It is sometimes called the Great Vehicle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-mahāyāna*), or the Vehicle of Infinite Perfect Penetration and Sovereignty;
this is precisely the Great Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka* that fully subsumes all teachings.

In the present chapter and in the *Tanxuan ji*, [the author] uniquely cites Bodhiruci as evidence for the "one-sound teaching" (*ekasvara-dharma*) and quotes the preceding verse from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
"By preaching the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind; all say that the Tathāgata speaks in their own language.
This is a spiritual power, an uncommon dharma. Sengzhao says: "The secret mouth uses a single sound, yet those of different kinds have diverse understandings.

*Tanchuan* says: "First, regarding types: for the sake of the assembly of devas, he may manifest a single celestial sound, which is able to encompass the various distinct [understandings] of the other types."
It is the same for those who attain understanding through dialogue; it is likewise for all other categories. Qingliang said:

"The Tathāgata’s single voice simultaneously responds to the ten thousand beings, large and small, appearing together; the profound texts and the dual currents flow forth. Quoting from Kumārajīva, following the sutra with a verse:
"When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand according to their own capacity, and all universally obtain [enlightenment]."
To receive and practice [the teaching] and thereby obtain its benefits constitutes the uncommon power of spiritual efficacy (*abhijñā-dharma*). Zhaò says:
"The Buddha speaks a single Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each receive and practice it according to their own inclinations. *Tàn xuán* says: "The second point concerns the Dharma;

whether for the sake of sentient beings he speaks of giving, this 'single voice' also causes people to understand the precepts, meditative concentration, and so forth. *Qīng liáng* says: "The Buddha’s one perfect [voice]."

The voice is equal, non-dual, and without thought, universally responding to the capacities of beings; while there are differences in what is heard, this does not mean that the voice itself originally manifests in large or small forms.

Furthermore, it is said that initially the Buddha’s voice possesses various distinctions, but later, according to the capacities of sentient beings, each attains the perfect voice (*sambhinnabuddhakṣetra*).
Any claim that this differs from the teaching of Qingliang [Chengguan] is an error.
Second, following Dharma Master Tan and others, based on scriptures such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, two types of teaching are established: the gradual and the sudden.

This refers to the "gradual" teaching, which involves first practicing the Hīnayāna and subsequently proceeding toward the Mahāyāna; because the Great [Vehicle] arises from the Small, it is called "gradual," and because both the Small and the Great are presented together, it refers to teachings such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The "Small, Medium, and Large" [teachings] arise to correctly demonstrate the meaning of gradualism; progressing from the small to the large, and presenting the small and large side by side, is why they are called "gradual.

As for *Nirvāṇa*, it gathers together those whose capacities remain residual; it proceeds from the small to the large. It delivers those who have attained the fruit of the ten *ṛṣis* and enables them to realize *arhatship*;
thus, its classification as belonging to the Three Vehicles in the preceding text is correct.
Because bodhisattvas such as those who proceed directly (*ṛju-gāmin*) do not pass through the small [vehicle] but enter directly into the great, it is called "sudden" (*tun*);

furthermore, because there is no small [vehicle], this refers precisely to the *Avataṃsaka* teaching. Since they proceed directly to the great, there is no textual mention of returning from the small; thus, it is established from the outset as the sudden teaching.
Because they can be brought together, it is said that there is no "Small" [Vehicle] and that [the teaching] is sudden.
Dharma Master Yuan and other virtuous masters of later generations mostly agree with this view.
Dharma Master Yuan of the Sui dynasty and Liu Qiu of the Qi dynasty also established these two [categories].
Third, relying on Master Guangtong, three types of teaching are established: namely, the gradual (*jiàn*), the sudden (*dùn*), and the perfect (*yuán*).
Master Guangtong was a preeminent disciple of Buddhata Tripiṭaka. His formal name was Huiguang; he was the patriarch of the Nanshan school and the founder of the Vinaya lineage.
He frequently lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, for which he composed two commentaries, an extensive and an abridged one. These are the teachings he established.
The Master Zhixiang thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries and transmitted these teachings for our use;

he was the first in this land to judge the *Avataṃsaka* as the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*bījaikayāna*), and people to this day all receive his bounty—he was no ordinary man. The definitions and meanings of the Three Teachings are as explained in the original commentary.

Master Guang explains the underlying intent as follows: because the faculties [of sentient beings] have not yet matured, he first teaches impermanence and subsequently teaches permanence; he first teaches emptiness and subsequently teaches non-emptiness.
Since these profound and subtle meanings are taught in such a gradual sequence, it is called the "Gradual Teaching" (Anupūrva-vinaya).

Because their faculties were not yet mature and they were not yet capable of hearing the teachings in their entirety, he first taught [the provisional doctrines] such as those mentioned above, following the sequence of the five periods or three periods of teaching.

Regarding permanence and impermanence, this is like contrasting *prajñā* with *nirvāṇa*; regarding emptiness and non-emptiness, this is like contrasting *prajñā* with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such texts.
For those whose faculties are mature, all Buddha-dharmas are fully expounded within a single dharma-gate;
because both the permanent and the impermanent, as well as the empty and the non-empty, are taught simultaneously without any gradual progression, it is called "sudden."

It is called "sudden" (*tun*) because it expounds [the teaching] in its entirety. Regarding these two aforementioned teachings, both the *Shiyi tantan xuán* (Profound Commentary on the Meaning of the Sūtra) and the *Zhou shu* (Commentary by Zhou) provide this explanation;
my own patriarch has here briefly summarized their meaning to compose this text. If one follows those commentaries, the *Souxuan* (Exploring the Profound) employs them in full.
As for the gradual teaching (*jianjiao*), it explains the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*), translating their names and distinguishing their characteristics; that text states:
To distinguish the beginning and end of the single transformation according to its categories, there are three gateways of teaching: first, the gradual; second, the sudden; and third, the perfect.
Within the initial gateway of the gradual, because there are three subjects to be expounded, the teachings are threefold;
because there are two purposes, the teachings are twofold. Regarding the threefold division: first, the Sūtras; second, the Vinaya; and third, the Abhidharma.
The teachings of the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* and other such treatises establish two categories, namely the Great and Small Piṭakas (Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna).

The reason this is so is truly because the Three Piṭakas expound the Three Studies (*triśikṣā*), encompassing both those that emphasize them directly and those that do so indirectly; whereas these two Piṭakas do not expound the Three Studies.

Within these two Piṭakas, the Great [Vehicle] is not spoken of in the Small, and the Small is not discussed in the Great. Since they collectively encompass the gradual sūtras of a single lifetime, they are said to come first.

Regarding "emptiness later and non-emptiness first," "impermanence later and the teaching of permanence first," and so forth, he further states that the two types of sudden teaching are as described in the *Sutra*:
"If there are sentient beings who are inferior and whose minds are weary and submerged, he shows them the path of the śrāvaka to enable them to emerge from all sufferings;
if there are again sentient beings whose faculties are slightly dull yet sharp, who delight in the dharma of causes and conditions..."
It is taught that for Pratyekabuddhas, if there are persons with sharp faculties who benefit sentient beings and possess great compassion, one should teach them the path of a Bodhisattva;
if they possess the unsurpassed mind and are determined to delight in the Great Matter, one should reveal the Buddha-body to them and teach the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma.
By this text, it is known that there is the One Vehicle, the Sudden Teaching, and the Three [Vehicles].
Regarding the distinction of vehicles (*yāna*), because these four vehicles are employed simultaneously within this text, it is said that they are "fully expounded.
This means that while the pedagogical methods (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*) differ, the Dharma taught is not distinct;
pointing to the *Awakening of Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuanjue*) as the sudden aspect of the pedagogical method is identical to this principle.

Because it is for those who have reached the higher stages and aspire to the realm of the Buddhas that this "Secret Dharma Gate of the Sovereign Perfection of the Ultimate Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Unhindered Liberation" is taught, it is called "Complete"; this very sutra is it.

The "Upper Attainment" (shàngdá) encompasses both the stage prior to the earth (xián dì) and the stages within the Buddha-realm (fó jìng dì). This is fully detailed in the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Shūsòng*) and the *Explanatory Notes* (*Yìchāo*).

Furthermore, later masters under the lineage of Guǎngtǒng, such as Zūntǒng Shī and other virtuous ones, all likewise followed and upheld this interpretation, which accords with the Great Same (Dàtóng).
Zun and his peers were the eminent disciples of Master Daoyuan; their dignity and reverence surpassed even that of their teacher.
At one time, the various virtuous masters, including the Great Dharma Master Dacheng, established the four religious teachings (sijiao) in order to comprehensively encompass all [Buddhist doctrines].

The first category, the school of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), refers to the Sarvāstivāda and other Hīnayāna sects. The second, the school of provisional names (*prajñapti-saṃjñā*), refers to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the Sautrāntika, and others.
The third, the school of unreality (*atattva*), refers to the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras which clarify the principle of emptiness, stating that all phenomena are not direct realities and so forth.
The fourth, the school of reality (*tattva*), refers to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and others, which clarify the Buddha-nature and the true *dharmadhātu*.
The principles and so forth are established; the textual passages for the four tenets are quite clear.
Fifth, based on the Dharma Master Hugen, five types of teaching are established; three of these teachings are the same as those previously mentioned by the Master [Heng]. The fourth name is...
The True Teaching refers to the Nirvāṇa and other sutras that clarify the Buddha-nature, the true principle, and so forth;
the fifth is called the Dharma-realm School (Faxie Zong), which refers to the Avataṃsaka’s teachings on the dharma-gates of the sovereign and unobstructed Dharma-realm.
"Guarding the Body" (Hushen) is the name of the monastery itself; however, from among the first four [schools], the *Avataṃsaka* is singled out as the Dharma-realm school (*fajie zong*).
Regarding the six schools established by Master Qisheshi: the first two are identical to those of the former master;

the third, the School of Non-Reality (*buzhen zong*), clarifies that all Mahāyāna teachings generally explain all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations; the fourth, the School of Reality (*zhen zong*), clarifies the specific explanations...
The fifth, the Constant School (*nitya-nikāya*), clarifies the meaning that the principle of the emptiness of all phenomena and the *sands-of-the-Ganges* of merits are eternally constant;
the sixth, the Perfect School (*pariniṣpanna-nikāya*), clarifies that the free and unimpeded functioning of the dharmadhātu’s dependent origination is perfectly complete,
which refers to the *Avataṃsaka* dharma-gate and others.

Gṛdhrakūṭa is also named after its location. Third, [the teaching that] all phenomena are not real and so forth is spoken solely in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), where all dharmas are like illusions.
Fourth, it is spoken in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), where the principle of emptiness is the true reality. Fifth, it is spoken in terms of the eternal nature of inherent virtue.
Sixth, it is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-zong*) because the merit and function of the *Avataṃsaka* are fully perfected.
Seventh, based on the teachings of Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue and Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, four teachings were established to encompass all the Buddhist doctrines transmitted to the East.
The first is called the Tripitaka Teaching; because it refers to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it cites the Lotus Sūtra itself, which says: "One shall not [be permitted to] approach..."
Because he was a scholar of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Hīnayāna is the Tripiṭaka teaching and the Mahāyāna is the Mahāyāna Piṭaka;
these two names refer to the "Shared Teachings," meaning that the teachings expounded in various Mahāyāna sūtras benefit those of all three vehicles,
as well as those stages common to both the Great and Small Vehicles, such as the ten stages beginning with "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) found in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*.

It is also called the Gradual Teaching (Jianjiao), thirdly the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao)—referring to those principles elucidated in various Mahāyāna sūtras that do not apply to the Hīnayāna—and also called the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao).

Fourthly, it is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which refers to the sovereign freedom of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) wherein all inexhaustible dharma-gates are fully present; in which one is all and all is one—such as the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
It is also called the "Secret Teaching" because it is not seen or heard by the Śrāvakas and others.

As for the passage where he cites a sūtra himself, he refers to this teaching as "Small Supervision" (小監); thus, it is said that he cites it himself. The names and meanings of the four teachings are summarized here;
they are explained in detail in the *Yanyi* (Exegesis of the Meaning) and according to that school's own tradition.

Eighth, according to Dharma Master Min of Jiangnan, two teachings are established: first, the Śākyamuni Sūtras, which are called the "Teaching of Crookedness" because they follow the capacities of beings and break attachments by conforming to their conceptualizations, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others;
second, the Vairocana Sūtras, which are called the "Teaching of Levelness" because they preach with sovereign freedom according to the nature of phenomena, namely the *Avataṃsaka*.
The establishment of the two teachings is as explained in detail in the *Yanyi* (Exposition of the Meaning).
Ninth, Master Yun of Guangzhai Monastery during the Liang dynasty established the doctrine of the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*).

He held that the three carts offered at the gate represent the three vehicles, while the great white ox-cart bestowed upon [the children] at the crossroads constitutes the fourth; this is because the ox within the gate...
The chariot is likewise [unreal], as neither the sheep nor the deer can be obtained; thus, the remaining meanings are as explained above in the *Bianyi* (Discrimination of Meanings).
The meaning is as set forth at the beginning of the chapter, with further details as found in the *Tanxuan* (Exploring the Profundities) and the *Yanyi* (Explication of the Meaning).
Later, the Master Xinxing, relying on this school, established two teachings: namely, the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles. As for the Three Vehicles:

This refers to the distinct liberation and distinct practice, as well as the distinctions between the three vehicles, and those who first practiced the Hīnayāna and subsequently proceeded toward the Mahāyāna.

As for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), it refers to universal understanding and universal practice, which is exclusively the One Vehicle; it also includes the Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka* and the "Direct Advancement" (*ṛju-vakra*) and so forth.

"Differentiated understanding and differentiated practice" means that the practices and understandings of each of the three vehicles proceed individually, with distinctions in their objects of truth (*satya*), conditions, and perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Prior cultivation" refers to the Great Vehicle arising from the Small, as well as the simultaneous presentation of both the Great and the Small.
"Universal understanding and universal practice" means that one possesses all within a single [practice]; this does not exist outside the *Avataṃsaka* school. Other schools lack it.
Tenth, based on the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, who established three types of teaching—
namely, the three wheels of Dharma— relying upon the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra, and the Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra.

The first is called the Wheel of Turning the Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), which refers to the initial period when he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park; this is the Dharma of the Hīnayāna.

The second is called the Wheel of Illumination (*āloka-dharmacakra*), which refers to the intermediate period when, within the Mahāyāna, he spoke with intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*) regarding the emptiness of all phenomena and so forth.
The third is called the Wheel of Sustaining the Dharma (*dhāraṇa-dharmacakra*), which refers to the final period when, within the Mahāyāna, he spoke with explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).
The three natures, suchness, and the principle of non-emptiness, and so forth.
First, the turning of the wheel of Dharma refers to the wheel of the four truths with its three spheres. Second, the illuminating wheel of Dharma refers to using emptiness to illuminate existence;

thus, in order to destroy the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it was spoken with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*) of "emptiness," without yet explicitly teaching "existence. Third, the sustaining [wheel]...
The "Dharma-wheel" refers to the simultaneous maintenance of the preceding two [natures]. The three natures—emptiness, directness, and suchness—are all explained in terms of principle (*li*).

"Non-emptiness" refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as being existent; according to their own school, they only admit an existence that is immutable and eternally abiding, rather than an existence that arises through conditions (*pariṇāma*).
Among these three wheels of Dharma, only the Hīnayāna and the two teachings—the initial and final—within the Hīnayāna are subsumed;
the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle is not subsumed. Why is this? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught at the beginning and is therefore not of the Hīnayāna;
the wheel-holding Dharma was taught later and is therefore not the *Avataṃsaka*. For this reason, it does not include the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-gate.
Furthermore, these three wheels of Dharma encompass only the Hīnayāna and so forth; however, from the small to the great, they encompass the gradual teachings of a single lifetime.

Because the beginning, middle, and end—small, intermediate, and great—are combined and designated as "gradual," and because the meaning of the three wheels is pervasive, it is as Paramārtha [the True Meaning] has explained.

Those of the Dharma-nature school (Faxingzong) within the Tripiṭaka also establish these three wheels based on scriptures such as the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*; thus, they maintain both nature and characteristics (*dharmatā* and *lakṣaṇa*).

Consequently, they subsume the three wheels within the three teachings. However, this is not the intention of the Characteristics school (Xiangzong); for the Characteristics school maintains that while the object is empty, the mind exists, thereby maintaining both [nature and characteristics] only to that extent.

The ten masters mentioned above, who established these teachings, were all Dharma generals of their time whose brilliant insights were peerless; they served as luminous models throughout successive generations, and their spiritual stages remain unfathomable.

For instance, the wonder-working responses and spiritual communications of Master Si and Master Zhiyi—whose traces reached the ranks of the [Bodhisattva] stages and who heard the Dharma on Vulture Peak even now—are still remembered today.
Other miraculous manifestations are as extensive as recorded in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*). Furthermore...

The Dharma Master Ruyun followed this [tradition] to establish his school and lecture on the Lotus Sūtra, moving the heavens to rain down flowers and manifesting other such divine traces as recorded in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*).
Furthermore, his various virtues, conduct, and profound understanding that surpassed his contemporaries are likewise detailed in the *Monastic Biographies*.
How could these various virtues be merely a fondness for novelty? Rather, having thoroughly exhausted the Tripitaka and beheld these divergent vehicles, I could not help but distinguish them.

Consequently, I have relied upon the teachings to establish the schools, striving to preserve their comprehensive unity so that deep-seated doubts and stubborn obstructions may be dissolved and clarified.
Although the sacred teachings appear to differ, it is appropriate that each finds its own accord.
The fourth section concerns the opening of the school’s tenets (*kāya-vibhāga*).

As for one who opens the school and judges the teachings: unless they are a great talent born for the age, possessing the correct eye that penetrates the Dharma, having exhausted the mastery of the Tripiṭaka, encompassing the insights of a hundred schools, and relying on the reality while entrusting themselves to expedient means—elevating the fundamental while appearing humble in their traces—who could possibly accomplish such a task? In the past...

This is indeed commendable; yet, while it is applied with rectitude, the underlying principle may not yet be fully realized. To establish a new perspective, ten schools are first presented as a comprehensive mirror from which to draw lessons.

Among these, there are two parts: first, the classification of teachings according to their methods (*dharma*), wherein there are five categories of teaching; second, the opening of the schools according to their principles (*tattva*), wherein the schools are...

There are ten [points]. Regarding the classification of the teachings according to the Dharma: "Dharma" refers to the teaching that expresses [the truth]. Within the entirety of the teachings throughout this lifetime, they are categorized by their common characteristics;
thus, there are five streams. Therefore, the subsequent text asks: "The holy teachings differ in ten thousand ways, yet essentially there are only five. What are these?
Question: Now, your family uses the meaning (*artha*) to judge the teachings; where does this principle rest? Answer:

If one does not rely on the meaning that is expounded, how can one know that the Buddha’s teachings consist of five categories? It is because our Patriarch, with his eye of perfect and penetrating wisdom, observed those holy teachings:

when they expound the practices and fruits of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), he classified them as the Small Teaching (*hīnayāna-śāsana*). This is because there exist distinctions in terms of provisional versus real, and partial versus perfect.
Because they are identical, they are divided into those teachings; thus, the text below states: "This is a division of teachings based on the Dharma.

If one proceeds from the meaning of the Dharma, as will be separately distinguished below, this division concerns the differences among the five teachings that express [the truth], while what follows distinguishes the differences among the five categories of that which is expressed.
Regarding "illuminating the principle to establish the school," this refers to the differences in the principles favored by various individuals.
Briefly, there are ten [categories].
Regarding the first gate: although the holy teachings differ in myriad ways, they essentially consist of only five: (1) the Hīnayāna teaching; (2) the initial Mahāyāna teaching;
(3) the final teaching; (4) the sudden teaching; and (5) the perfect teaching.
The myriad differences within the Holy Teachings refer to the many categories of the one period of transmission in the East; these Holy Teachings are generally classified into five types.
"Small" refers to those that follow one another as small [teachings], without distinguishing between the number of fascicles, sizes, or scrolls.
The same applies to the remaining four [categories]. It is like a person holding a ruler to measure silk, dividing the silk into five sections; one simply speaks of them as such.

When dividing silk, one does not speak of inches and so forth, yet it is not that the inch is not used; likewise, classifying [the teachings] into five according to the system of Chu is not done without recourse to principle.

The first [category] refers to the two vehicles of the ignorant dharma, while the last refers to the One Vehicle of the Separate Teaching; these are designated as "good" within the original text of the sutra.
This name was established because it accords with what the Crown Prince taught as the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*.

The first [category] refers to the teachings for the two vehicles of the "foolish dharma" (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas); that is to say, within these teachings, one only severs the afflictions (*kleśa*) to realize the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*), but does not sever the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) nor realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). They are "foolish" regarding all dharmas, such that an Arhat does not recognize red salt.
Zhenyuan says: "I do not explain [the characters] 'yin' and so forth for ordinary and ignorant people. The subsequent downward-pointing gesture refers to the Jin edition of the sutra;
because this is a chapter and not a commentary, it is titled the *Pūrṇavartanī-sūtra* (Sutra of the Perfect Wheel of Causes).
As for the establishment of this name, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is based upon it.
The three intermediate [teachings] possess three meanings.

These three intermediate ones refer to the initial, the final, and the sudden. When the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundity) opens up two [categories], it first distinguishes the One Vehicle of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), while the preceding four are treated as the Three Vehicles.
Within the three [categories] of the middle, the Lesser [Vehicle] is opened out as the Hinayana, and the three intermediate teachings are [treated as such].

The common teaching of the Three Vehicles is entirely identical to this; at the beginning of the chapter, the distinct teaching distinguishes the Three Vehicles by placing those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant within the inner precincts as Hīnayāna, while those in the intermediate stage are designated as the Three Vehicles. Who, then, would say that the final and sudden teachings are not distinguished?

First, "either taken collectively as one" refers to the single teaching of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), because all of these are attained by the three types of persons, as stated in the citation above.
That is to say, the three teachings are combined in their entirety to form the single teaching of the Three Vehicles; this [section] below explains the reason why there are three.
The teachings are generally categorized into two vehicles because these three teachings are all attained by the three types of practitioners;

"attainment" refers to the fruit obtained through the cultivation of causes. This is because, although these Mahāyāna sūtras contain both provisional and ultimate aspects, they universally expound the three dharmas and universally benefit the three capacities. Those cited above are precisely the Three Vehicles.

In scriptures such as the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, the assemblies of the three vehicles are gathered together to universally expound the Dharma of the three vehicles, whereby one fully obtains the benefits of the three vehicles;

"obtaining benefit" refers precisely to what is attained. If it is claimed that those of the *Sudden* and *Gradual* [teachings] alike attain a single fruit and all achieve Buddhahood, or if one cites near differences to prove distant similarities, these are all mere conjectures. Furthermore, in the Initial Teaching (*Ādikarmika-yāna*), one attains the three fruits.

Ultimately, one attains the single fruit; this can explain the distinction between "preserving three" and "extinguishing two," which were previously divided into two parts, but are now unified as one.
Second, they may be divided into two, namely the gradual and the sudden.

Regarding the gradual and sudden [teachings] distinguished within the three vehicles above: the *Kongmu wen答* (Questions and Answers on the Essential Gate) and the present *Jiaozhang* (Treatise on the Teachings) both judge the scriptures upon which the various teachings rely to be those prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

For instance, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* distinguishes between correct understanding and practice (*samyag-dṛṣṭi-caryā*) and false understanding and practice (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi-caryā*), applying this to the teachings of the three vehicles; likewise, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and others do so as well.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (specifically the *Nāgaśrī-bhāgīya-parivarta*), and others belong to the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*).

The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* belongs to the Initial Teaching of the Three Vehicles (*san-sheng shi-jiao*). Therefore, the present text distinguishes between the Sudden and the Gradual within the Three Vehicles, and further differentiates between the Initial and the Final [teachings].
Because all the understandings and practices of the two teachings— those of the beginning and those of the end— are situated within the stages of verbal expression,
following a sequence of cause and effect that proceeds from the subtle to the manifest, they are collectively termed "gradual."

Regarding those that are equal in terms of beginning and end: although the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) speaks of the provisional establishment of stages and positions, it still relies on verbal expression and thus differs from the Sudden Teaching (Dun jiao).
Therefore, these two teachings together constitute the Gradual Teaching (Jian jiao).
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The gradual is like the ripening of a māluka fruit, which occurs gradually and not all at once"—this is what that refers to.

As for the sudden teaching (*tundajiao*), it means that verbal expression is suddenly cut off, the principle of nature is suddenly revealed, and understanding and practice are suddenly perfected; the non-arising of a single thought is itself Buddhahood, and so forth.
When verbal expression is suddenly cut off, it is like remaining in direct silence; when the rational nature is suddenly revealed, it is because the dharma-nature has neither quantity nor dimension.
When the practice of understanding is suddenly perfected, the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* states: "At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying:
"This is truly entering the gate of non-duality. The Patriarch said: "If there were no silence from Vimalakīrti, there would be no non-duality."
Regarding the principle that "all dharmas are not established" and "not a single thought arises," if even a single moment of deluded mind does not arise, how could one not be named Buddha?
Qingliang (Cleansing Coolness) says: "Only when all conceptualization is utterly stilled can it be called 'non-arising.

When stillness and illumination manifest before one, is this not being named Buddha? Furthermore, because True Suchness is non-discriminative emptiness, a single thought-moment immediately constitutes Buddhahood.
Furthermore, a single thought-moment is what is called "no-thought. In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there is no such thing as attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The sudden is like an image appearing instantaneously in a mirror; it is not gradual"—this is precisely what that means.

Because all dharmas are fundamentally and originally correct, they do not depend on verbal expression nor upon contemplative wisdom; they are manifested through silence, just as in the case of Vimalakīrti.
Furthermore, because the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* also speaks of it as being named "Sūtra of Sudden Teaching" (*tun-jiao xūduluó*), this name is established based on that;
it is one of the four types of sudden teaching, while the mango fruit is one of the four types of gradual [teaching]. All subsequent sections are abbreviated.

The reason for demonstrating that verbal expression is suddenly cut off is to achieve self-correction; because all understanding and practice are ineffable, they do not depend on contemplative wisdom.
This silence reveals the non-dual principle of suchness itself. The name "Ratnakūṭa" (Jewel Heap) is derived from the subsequent section.

Third, it may be expanded into three; that is, within the gradual teaching, the two teachings of the beginning and the end are distinguished, namely the latter two among the three wheels of Dharma mentioned in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other such texts.

Since the Mahāyāna is characterized by being shallow at first and profound later, it is divided into two assemblies. As for the "Profound and Secret" (Saṃdhinirmocana), it subsumes the gradual teachings within three periods.

Regarding the five periods, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras—which teach the wondrous doctrine of eternal permanence—are extracted from the latter period to constitute the fourth and fifth periods.
Now, by merging these five into three, the third period encompasses a very wide range of sūtras; furthermore, this includes those who uphold the Dharma.
The meaning of "wheel" (cakra) also applies here. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* likewise speaks of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as a wondrous existence;
however, the Master Xuanzang’s primary tenet was that it is an unchanging, serene existence. Now, based on this general sense, I shall briefly distinguish the teachings.
Based on this meaning, in the *Dharmabherī-sūtra*, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is established as the beginning and the gate of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*) as the conclusion.
Thus, that sūtra states: Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "In many Mahāyāna sūtras, the meaning of emptiness is extensively taught.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "All sūtras concerning emptiness are teachings with remainder (*sāvasesa-vāda*); only this sūtra is the unsurpassed teaching, not one with remainder."
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like King Prasenajit, who every year in the eleventh month convenes a great assembly for almsgiving.
First, he provides food for hungry ghosts, the solitary, and those who beg out of greed; next, he bestows sweet delicacies and various flavors upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas according to their desires.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise act in this same manner, providing for all sentient beings according to their various inclinations and pleasures.

He expounds various sūtras and dharmas; yet if there are sentient beings who are indolent, transgress the precepts, and do not diligently comply with or abandon the Tathāgatagarbha—the wondrous scripture of eternal abiding—and instead delight in practicing and studying various sūtras on emptiness, and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding this meaning, it relies upon the two teachings whose beginnings and ends differ. Taking emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as the beginning and non-emptiness as the end—this is so.
These five teachings were first conceived by Emperor [Gaozong], followed and developed by Zhixiang, and refined by Xianshou.
Thus, they were opened and distinguished prior to the return of Master Xuanzang; furthermore, [the views of] Zhu Fatai...
At that time, the newly translated *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and the teachings on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) were practiced in parallel, each conforming to its own school’s tenets.

Consequently, within the Mahāyāna, the two teachings of "existence" and "emptiness" were followed by successive sages, leading to a distinction between the provisional and the real. Our school’s fivefold taxonomy encompasses all traditions;
thus, it takes emptiness as the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna and non-emptiness as its culmination. "Initial" refers to the very beginning.
"End" (*anta*) refers to the ultimate limit. "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) and "non-emptiness" (*aśūnyatā*) are the principles revealed by the two teachings;

they are not the causes for establishing names. Nevertheless, this sequence of beginning and end merely reveals a single principle wherein emptiness and existence are viewed in relation to one another.

As Guifeng briefly distinguished in his *Ten Pairs*, their relative depth and shallowness differ. Yunhua stated: "Furthermore, within the gate of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), there are two kinds."
Regarding the "beginning gate" (*ādimukha*): as stated in the *Śata-dharma-vyākhyāna*, the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are subsumed within all phenomena;

only upon realizing the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena does one enter the category of emptiness. One understands that suchness (*tathatā*) does not surpass the two emptinesses, and thus the two emptinesses are superior.
Regarding the "concluding gate" (*paryantamukha*): in the "Disciples' Chapter" of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it says, "Non-arising and non-ceasing is the meaning of impermanence," and so forth.

"Vajra-dust is not dust," and so forth; it further states that in the initial teaching (the *Hīnayāna* or *Āgama* gate), True Suchness (*tathatā*) is merely the meaning of emptiness, which differs from the Final Teaching (*paryantayāna*).
In the Final and Second [teachings], both the gates of emptiness and existence are fully present. One may ask:

Did Master Xuanzang himself, while in India, maintain the position of those with fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) and the icchantikas as never attaining Buddhahood? Therefore, regarding the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the third...
The second and third periods are combined to form the Initial Teaching (*śāstrīya-ādi-deśanā*), so called because there are those who do not attain Buddhahood; it is also named "Partial" (*bhāga*).
Furthermore, it is the meaning of the *tathatā* revealed by the initial gateway of the Mahāyāna, which is identical to the hundred dharmas. The answer is provided to demonstrate this meaning.
Next, the passage below cites an analogy, and the subsequent section correlates [the analogy] with the teaching to reveal its significance, as can be seen in the text.

The commentary explains: This refers to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), which is designated as such because it relies on the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while leaving something remaining; and the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), which is designated as such because it relies on the Tathāgatagarbha as eternally abiding and unsurpassed.
"Leaving something remaining" means that there is still more to be exhausted; only the wondrous scriptures of the eternally abiding [teaching] fully exhaust the discourse.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, the ineffable *tathatā* (suchness) is revealed through the gate of the sudden teaching (*dun-jiao*),

while the verbally dependent *tathatā* is explained through the gate of the gradual teaching (*jian-jiao*). Within the verbally dependent [tathatā], two types of *tathatā*— the empty and the non-empty— are taught according to the two teachings of the initial and final stages.

Since there are three aspects of the *tathatā* (suchness) thus revealed, the teaching is established as threefold. Those who harbor doubts regarding its function should know that the sūtras and śāstras contain many meanings;
they differ according to their specific application. Although it is opened up into three, all of them are nonetheless the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
This is a classification of the teachings based on the phenomena [dharmas] themselves; however, if one proceeds according to the meaning of these phenomena, it will be distinguished separately below.

"As distinguished separately below" refers to the section where, within the differentiation of the signified meanings (*vācya*), the teaching that signifies (*vācaka*) is first analyzed, followed by the analysis of the signified meaning itself.
This meaning consists of the three categories of principle (*tattva*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruition (*phala*).
Second, the presentation of the ten tenets according to their principles.
First is the tenet that both the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) exist; this has two parts:

(1) the Vehicle of Humans and Devas, and (2) within the Hīnayāna, schools such as the Vātsīputrīya. They establish three aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*): first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

There are three aggregates: the aggregate of two [conditioned things], the aggregate of three [unconditioned things], and the aggregate of neither. Of these, the first two are phenomena (*dharma*) and the latter one is the self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, five dharma-treasuries are established: first, the past; second, the future; third, the present; fourth, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); and fifth, the inexpressible (*avaktavya*).
This last one is the self, because it cannot be said to be either conditioned or unconditioned.

Regarding the twenty sub-sects of the Vātsīputrīya school within the Hīnayāna, their respective tenets concerning the similarities and differences among the six philosophical systems (ṣaḍ-nikāya), as well as the detailed explanations of the number and scope of these schools, have been fully set forth in the *Yanyi* (Exposition of the Meaning) and need not be listed here again.

Second is the school that asserts "the existence of phenomena and the non-existence of a self" (*dharmāstitva-pudgalanāstitva-vāda*), such as the Sarvāstivāda and others; they maintain that all phenomena are comprised of two categories: first, [conditioned phenomena]; second, [unconditioned phenomena].
They are said to be subsumed under either two categories of matter or four categories—namely, the three time periods and the unconditioned—or five categories: first, mind; second, mental factors;
third, matter; fourth, non-associated formations; and fifth, the unconditioned. Therefore, all phenomena are entirely and truly existent.
Third, the school that maintains that dharmas have neither past nor future— namely, the Mahāsāṃghika and others— asserts that there exist present dharmas and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas,
because they hold that the essence and function of the past and future do not exist. Fourth,
the school that maintains that the present encompasses both the provisional and the real— namely, the Prajñaptivāda and others— asserts that there is no past or future, but only the present.

Among these, those dharmas that exist within the aggregates (*skandha*) are real; those that exist within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are conventional (*prajñapti*), as the case may be. Whether these various dharmas are conventional or real is not fixed.
This is also the position of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) and other masters of the Sautrāntika school.
The fourth consists solely of the Hīnayāna.
The fifth is the school of the conventional, the false, and the real— namely, the Lokottaravādins and others— who maintain that all worldly phenomena are merely provisional and false,
whereas supramundane phenomena are real and not false.

Sixth, the tenet that all phenomena are merely names refers to the Ekavyāvahārika school, which holds that all persons and phenomena possess only provisional names and have no substantial essence whatsoever;
this corresponds to the beginning of the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna). Based on this, one may infer [the other schools].

The *Yanyi* (Exegesis) states: "The five and six [categories] encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles; the five 'lesser' ones resemble half of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, while the former [five] generally pertain to the beginning of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*).
Regarding the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*) within the gate of the Gradual Teaching, there are three gates: first, the Gate of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-śāsana*);
second, the Gate of the Initial Teaching; and third, the Gate of Worldly Knowledge. Within this third [gate], there are again three gates, beginning with the Initial Gate."

Regarding the "terminus of the ultimate gate" (*kyōjūmon*) which encompasses both humans and devas as well as the two vehicles of the ignorant dharma, the *Śāstra* commentary states that all phenomena possess only names—
that is, they are merely conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), designations (*nāman*), and mental constructions (*manasikāra*). Because this serves as the proximate expedient means for the Mahāyāna,
it is called the beginning of the Initial Teaching (*shikyō*).
Seventh, the school that asserts that all things are empty refers to the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, which states that all phenomena are entirely true emptiness;
however, because they transcend emotional attachments and are free from conceptual discrimination, as in the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others.
Regarding the "Initial Teaching" (*shijiao*) and so forth, the meaning is as analyzed in the section on the classification of teachings (*fenzhiao*).

However, this teaching encompasses both the meaning of the differentiated teaching (*fenbie jiaoyi*) and the meaning of the non-differentiated teaching (*wufenbie jiaoyi*). The meaning of the non-differentiated teaching refers to the realization of *tathatā* (suchness);

the meaning of the differentiated teaching refers to the fact that the meaning of the teaching is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Here, because we are referring to the profound [aspect], it is called "non-differentiated. As for "Prajñā," it refers to...
This is the scripture upon which they rely; Huiguan, Daoshi, Zhizang, Fotudeng, Zhu Fatai, and others all made this same judgment.

The eighth is the school of the non-emptiness of true virtues, which refers to the final teaching (*zhōngjiào*). It holds that the various scriptures teach that all phenomena are solely True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Tathāgatagarbha;
because they possess real virtues, because they have their own intrinsic substance, and because they are endowed with inherent qualities of nature.

This refers to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*) and others, which state in the aforementioned eternally abiding wondrous scriptures that the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with untainted intrinsic virtues (*anāsrava-guṇa*), each possessing its own substantial reality.

As for the ninth, it is the school where both signs and conceptualization are utterly transcended; like the "teaching that transcends words" within the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*), it reveals the principle that transcends words.
This should be understood by analogy with the silence of Vimalakīrti and similar cases.

Regarding the "sudden teaching" (dun-jiao) and so forth, the *Kongmu* states: "This is like being beyond all teachings; because both meaning and characteristics, as well as conceptualization and perception, are utterly unattainable."

The tenth, the school of the Perfectly Illuminating Endowment of Virtues (*daśa-samantaprabhā-guṇa-yukta-naya*), refers to the dharma-gates manifested by the complete and inexhaustible mastery of the principal and its attendants within the One Vehicle of the Separate Teaching (*bhinna-śāsana*).

Such categories as these follow the sequence of the five teachings as previously established in the *Fenjiao* (Classification of Teachings) section, and this chapter likewise follows the order of the five teachings according to the *Tongtanxuan* (Comprehensive Exploration of the Profundities).
Following this principle, I have arranged the sequence of the various schools and provided their exegeses.

Among them, the National Teacher Qingliang’s seventh school is named the School of the Three Natures as Empty and Existing, and his eighth is named the School of True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics; his ninth is named the School of the Unobstructed Interpenetration of Emptiness and Existence.
This was done by using "nature" (*xing*) to distinguish from "characteristics" (*xiang*), shifting the Great Dharma Master’s seventh school to the eighth position to accord with the Dharma.
The nature (svabhāva) follows the characteristics of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa) because it is profound; thus, it does not accord with the sequence of the five teachings.

Furthermore, because the emptiness of nature (svabhāva-śūnyatā) permeates both the gradual and the sudden, the "true emptiness beyond characteristics" (zhēn-kōng jué-xiàng) is subsumed within the Sudden Teaching.

Moreover, because the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence penetrates the Common Teaching, it is said that "the former is shallow and the latter is deep. If both emptiness and existence are simultaneously transcended, then...

Furthermore, regarding the collection and arrangement of the teachings, the masters of the seven, eight, nine, and three schools each established their own positions in order to judge the relative depth and determine the provisional and the real.
Therefore, the preface by Qingliang and the present chapter’s *Tanyuan* differ. That text states:
"Moreover, because the masters of the three preceding schools each established their own systems, they are now recounted. The eleventh school is not among those [previously mentioned]."
It is simply that they do not speak [of this] because of their mutual competition.
Regarding the third point, the opening and closing of the teachings on the vehicles (*yāna*), there are three parts.
As for the opening and closing of the teachings on the vehicles: it is truly because each school’s established judgments have their own sacred teachings (*āgama*) as a basis of reliance.
It cannot be entirely discarded. Furthermore, the opening and closing [of teachings] in the sacred doctrine fundamentally arise from differences in the capacities of sentient beings.

Even if one speaks of a "level path," it is still for the sake of transforming living beings. While there may be many faults in closing [the teaching], there is likewise no way to be entirely free from error in opening it.
Therefore, the present school’s approach of both opening and closing encompasses everything without fault and remains inseparable; thus, this section exists.
First, the opening and closing according to the teachings; second, subsuming the vehicles by means of the teachings; third, the mutual inclusion of the various teachings.
Regarding the first—opening according to the teachings—there are five meanings concerning how these five teachings mutually include and harmonize one another.

This is the general reconciliation following the doctrinal classifications found in various texts. While the phrasing differs slightly, the essential meaning is largely the same as that in the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities), with which it is entirely consistent.
That work, however, opens up four categories and presents two theories; this text lacks one of those sections.
Since it speaks of the mutual inclusion of the five teachings, the *Zhong* (Middle) and *Dun* (Sudden) teachings are naturally contained therein.
First: Alternatively, they may be taken as one in total, meaning that the fundamental and the derivative are fused into a single Great Skillful Dharma.
The two aspects of the fundamental and the derivative are like five metals smelted together in a great furnace until they become one;

thus it is said that the fusion of the fundamental and the derivative is solely the Tathāgata’s one great skillful means for gathering and delivering sentient beings. Guifeng says: "The Perfect Teaching gathers [all]."
Regarding the first four [categories], each is identical within the ocean of perfect roundness; the hundred rivers are none other than the ocean itself.

It is sometimes called the "Teaching of the Single Perfect Sound," sometimes called the "Fulfillment of the Treasury," and sometimes called the "School of Inexhaustible Perfect Penetration and Sovereignty. This is briefly as set forth in the *Tongjiao ce* (Exhortation on the Common Teaching).
Second, it may be divided into two: first, the Root Teaching, which refers to the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as it is the foundation of all teachings;
second, the Branch Teaching, which refers to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), as they flow forth from that [Root].
It is also termed the "Ultimate" and the "Provisional," because both the Three Vehicles and the Small Vehicle are considered provisional in relation to the One Vehicle.

This means that within the previous "one," two categories are established by distinguishing between the fundamental and the derivative. First, regarding "the fundamental teaching" (*mūla-śāsana*) and so forth:

it is first stated that the *Avataṃsaka* is the foundation of all teachings. Qingliang says: "Desiring to gradually bestow derivative teachings according to the capacities of beings, one first reveals the fundamental dharma by suddenly expounding this sūtra.
Second, regarding "the derivative teachings" (*anta-śāsana*) and so forth: these refer to the preceding four [teachings]. Since they flow from that [fundamental], they are called derivative.
It is called "the ultimate" (*anta*). Furthermore, regarding the terms "ultimate" and so forth, these are distinguished based on whether they possess a fruit or lack a fruit.

They are also called the "Teaching of the Fundamental Dharma" (*mūla-dharma-deśanā*) and the "Teaching that Follows the Extremes of Capacities" (*yathā-vineya-anta-deśanā*); they are also termed the "True Vehicle" (*samyak-yāna*) and the "Skillful Means Vehicle" (*upāya-yāna*). The *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundity) states:

"Alternatively, it may be divided into two, namely the teachings of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). Although within the aforementioned various teachings there exists the preservation of three [vehicles] and the merging [of them], [the former]...
The two are not the same; however, because both provide access to the three vehicles, they are termed "teachings of the three vehicles.

They are also termed "common teachings" and "uncommon teachings," as cited above from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. These distinctions may be made based on commonality and difference, or based on the Great and Small Vehicles, or based on the provisional and the real, or based on the circuitous and the direct, or based on the gradual and the sudden, and so forth.

Third: Alternatively, it is opened into three, namely the teachings of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), the Three Vehicles (triyāna), and the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna). This is because within the provisional [teachings], the Two Vehicles of those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant are distinguished.

Regarding the "One Vehicle and so forth," the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundities) states: "Alternatively, it is opened into three, namely the Lesser Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the One Vehicle."

Regarding the teaching: since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this sutra is not shared with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is termed "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). This refers to the *Mahāvaipulya* (Large) Prajñāpāramitā and other such texts.
Because they allow for the common observation and attainment of benefit by all three vehicles (*triyāna*), they are termed "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).
This refers to the three vehicles and the four *Āgamas*, which constitute the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Qingliang said: "Alternatively, the latter one is unshared; these three..."

It also accords with the four vehicles. In these two preceding gates, all three vehicles are fully encompassed, yet they are all provisional means for the attainment of the three types of persons and are not ultimate.

This differs from the system of Qingliang and Guifeng, who, within their division of the three teachings and five doctrines, place the first as Hinayana, the second as the Three Vehicles, and the third as the One Vehicle.

Fourth, it may be divided into four: namely, the Small (Hīnayāna), the Gradual, the Sudden, and the Perfect. This is because both the initial and final teachings are included within the "equal" [teachings].
Regarding the "Small" and so forth: this refers to the second sense of the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundities). In that division into four, there are two senses.

First, within the aforementioned common teaching (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*), by preserving the three and merging the two, two teachings are opened up, thus making four: first, the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).
1. The Hīnayāna; 2. The Common Teaching of the Three Vehicles (sāmānya-triyāna), such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others, which maintains the three vehicles; 3.

The Common Teaching of the One Vehicle (sāmānya-ekayāna), such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others, which subsumes the two [vehicles]; and 4. the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle (viśeṣa-ekayāna), such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Since the *Saṃdhinirmocana*—as a teaching of the second and third periods—universally admits that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and so forth will not all attain Buddhahood, it acknowledges...
Entering quiescence without arising is the initial teaching (śāstra) that maintains the three [vehicles].

If the final and sudden teachings both discuss the single nature (ekaprakṛti) and maintain that there are no five natures, then the entry into quiescence by the two vehicles is not true extinction; this is the merging of the two.
For this reason, within the school of the One Vehicle, it is opened up as the "One Vehicle of the Same Teaching" (tongjiao yicheng). Qingliang said: "The final and sudden two teachings..."
Although it is taught that there is a single nature and a single characteristic, without duality or triad, this is the sublation of duality.

Furthermore, it is said that both the Real Teaching (shijiao) and the Sudden Teaching (dunjiao) are not integrated and are thus categorized as the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao yicheng). The *Yanyi* states:

"Because they do not discern the perfect integration of all virtues, they are not the Distinct Teaching (biejiao). The principle is the same in the *Zhenyuan Da Shu*. If this is so, then regarding the former two gates:
Because all three [teachings] are for the sake of these three types of people, they are ultimately and collectively subsumed within the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
As for the fourth gate, because it takes the merging of duality as its basis, it is ultimately and directly subsumed within the One Vehicle; both the principle and the phrasing are very clear.
Furthermore, there are many passages indicating that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is considered the "same-teaching" (tongjiao) One Vehicle.
Five. Or, they may be divided into five, as explained above.
Second, regarding the inclusion of vehicles (*yāna*) by means of the teaching (*śāsana*): there are two aspects.

The teaching is that which expresses (*abhidhāna*), while the vehicle refers to that which is expressed (*abhidheya*). Since the vehicles and the teachings are not identical, this section is established to distinguish them.
First, regarding the One Vehicle according to the teachings, there are five types: (1) the Separate Teaching One Vehicle; (2) the Common Teaching One Vehicle, and so forth;

(3) the One Vehicle beyond conceptual thought, such as in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, which pertains to the Sudden Teaching; (4) the One Vehicle based on the equality of Buddha-nature, which pertains to the Final Teaching;
and (5) the One Vehicle of the esoteric meaning and intent, such as the eight meanings, which pertains to the Initial Teaching. Thus it is said.

Regarding the statements "the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle" and "the common teaching of the One Vehicle," etc., these extensively clarify the common and distinct [teachings] within the establishment of the One Vehicle;
they do not further transcribe the "One Vehicle of the Three Cuts of Thought. The *Kongmu* states: "The five vehicles are integrated to form the Non-..."

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* distinguishes the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) as being free from [dualistic] characteristics. Regarding the meaning and intent of the five secrets visible in the fourth [chapter], there are eight essential points for inquiry;

therefore, the single vehicle is taught. That single vehicle is a teaching of concealed implication (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) intended to lead those of the two vehicles, not a direct, explicit (*nītārtha*) teaching.

Second, it is explained that the Three Vehicles likewise possess five aspects: 1. Within the Hīnayāna, the three [vehicles] differ at the beginning but are identical at the end, as they all culminate in the state of an Arhat.
2. Within the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s provisional teaching), the three differ both at the beginning and the end, because there is entry into quiescence.

3. Within the Final Teaching, the three are identical both at the beginning and the end, as all equally attain Buddhahood. 4. Within the Sudden Teaching, the three are entirely devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and so forth. 5. The Perfect [Teaching].
In the teachings, the three [vehicles] are identical in both their beginning and their end, because that which you practice is the bodhisattva path, and so forth.

Regarding the three [vehicles] in the Hīnayāna, where the beginning differs but the end is the same, the *Tanyuan* states: "The beginning refers to the differences in the cultivation of the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, the Six Pāramitās, and so on;
the end refers to the attainment of the fruit, wherein the bodies and wisdoms of those of the Three Vehicles are equally extinguished. Thus it is said.
This refers to those such as the Arhats. Regarding the "Two Initial Teachings" and so forth, the *Tanxuan ji* contains two interpretive points. It states:
"If one relies on the distinctions in the practice of the Noble Truths, Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections, they may also be termed 'the beginning and end being distinct.

This is the teaching of the second and third periods; this is precisely the meaning [of our current position]. Furthermore, it says: "The two [teachings] are identical in their beginning and [identical] in their end."

There are three distinctions. This refers to those who hear the Prajñāpāramitā together and contemplate the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) together, yet as people of the three vehicles (triyāna), each attains their own respective fruit.
As previously cited, those aforementioned individuals also belong to the "shared teaching" of the three vehicles found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other such texts.

If this is the case, since the Initial Teaching (śāstra) consists entirely of the shared teaching for the three vehicles, there is also the principle that "the beginning is the same but the end is different," wherein one likewise contemplates the absence of intrinsic nature and each attains their own respective fruit. Regarding the phrase "the three ends are equal":

"the beginning is the same" means they equally hear the *Prajñāpāramitā* and equally contemplate the emptiness of nature; "the end is the same" means they all together attain Buddhahood. Furthermore, the *Tanyuan* states:
"Nearby differences and distant sameness" refers to three [aspects]: first, leading them by means of the three vehicles as skillful expedients;
later, delivering them all equally through the Great Vehicle. This is taught in such Mahāyāna sūtras as the *Baladeva-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Although within these there are differences between provisional and ultimate [teachings], they all possess the three vehicles. This is because, from beginning to end, they are of one category and are fixed for this world.
Therefore, according to this explanation, the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya) itself possesses four propositions: First, "the beginning is the same, but the end is different.
Because [all] hear the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, the beginning is the same; because they are all attained by three types of persons, the end is different.

Since the Final Teaching is also included within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-naya*) of the Three Vehicles, the second proposition is that both the beginning and the end are different. Third, as for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*...

The "Equal" (Samatā) teaching is explained as the three vehicles of the Dharma, which universally benefit the three types of persons. Thus, while the distinctions between the Truths (*satya*), the Objects of Contemplation (*ālambana*), and the Perfections (*pāramitā*) constitute the distinction at the beginning of these three Dharmas, the fact that they universally benefit the three types of persons constitutes the distinction at the end.

Although both the provisional and the ultimate teachings possess all three vehicles, because the faculties and natures of beings in this world are fixed, and because those who have not yet passed eighty thousand *kalpas* have not yet turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna], the three are distinct at the beginning, though they converge at the end.

The same. Third, regarding the differences in the faculties and dispositions (*indriya-gotra*) within this world: those in the stage of "not yet reached" (*anāgamya*) and those in the stage of "no remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) do not give rise to the resolve [for enlightenment].
One must speak of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); it is only when they are led to enter the Path that their conditions, practices, and attainments differ.

Furthermore, they differ at the outset because they remain intoxicated by the wine of *samādhi* for eighty, sixty, forty, twenty, ten, or one thousand kalpas; only after the wine has dissipated do they awaken, at which point they are ultimately the same. Fourth, the beginning...

In the end, all three are identical. At the beginning, they are identical in their hearing and contemplation. They are identical in the end because it is permitted that those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] shall become Buddhas.
Fourth, in the Sudden Teaching (Tonjiao), both beginning and end are identical in being beyond verbal expression. Fifth, within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there are three aspects:
"That which you practice" explains the identity at the beginning; "all receive the prediction of Buddhahood" explains the identity at the end.

Third, regarding the mutual inclusion of the various teachings, there are two gates: first, the gate of subsuming the derivative within the fundamental; second, the gate of returning the derivative to the fundamental.

The reason for distinguishing these modes of inclusion is to reveal that when the provisional and the real, or the upper and lower vehicles of skillful means, are viewed in relation to one another, they do not conflict.

The same applies here; it is merely intended to make known that there is no ultimate point of return. Nevertheless, there are two gates, both of which are distinguished according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The "root" (*mūla*) is the One Vehicle itself, while the "branches" (*anta*) are the various teachings. This is because, although the various teachings possess the sense of being subsumed within the root, the meaning of the root is not established [within them], as they are ultimately expedient means (*upāya*).
It is just as within the Shared Teachings (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), where there is likewise a mutual inclusion of higher and lower levels.
It is expected that among both the shared and unshared [teachings], all are included within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-deśanā*).
Within the Initial [Teaching], there may be only the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), because all other characteristics are therein exhausted;

or it may possess all five teachings, because it encompasses the provisional means (*upāya*). Within the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*), there may be only the Sudden Teaching itself, likewise because all other characteristics are therein exhausted; or...

Because the four teachings are employed to encompass the provisional means, there may be one or three within the Mature Teaching, one or two within the Initial Teaching, and only one within the Hīnayāna;
all of these should be understood according to the above principle.
Regarding "the remaining characteristics being exhausted within the Perfect [Teaching]," this is because it is originally the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Alternatively, it possesses five because it includes the previous four as skillful means (*upāya*), thus making five. This "pervasion" (*sāmānya*) carries both the meanings of "identity" and "non-identity," as will be clarified in the two gates below, numbers seven and eight.
Within the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*), "the remaining characteristics being exhausted" also refers to the fact that nothing can be spoken of, because one does not know the One. Alternatively...

Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) as being preliminary expedients: because one enters the sudden [teaching] from the gradual, the Mature Teaching (*pakvadeśanā*) is also called the Real Teaching (*tattvadeśanā*), or the Final Teaching (*antadeśanā*).
Alternatively, it may be considered as one, because other characteristics are exhausted; or as three, because the former two serve as expedients.
In the initial teaching, the faculties are indeterminate and capable of entering the mature teachings and so forth;

therefore, the initial teaching is sometimes called "beginning" (*ādi*) or "partial" (*prādeśika*), as both the Madhyamaka and Yogācāra schools have not yet exhausted the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, and thus it is collectively termed the "initial teaching.

Alternatively, one [classification] is based on its own school, while the other two subsume the Hīnayāna as a skillful means (*upāya*). For those of small faculties who are indeterminate and capable of entering the initial teaching, they immediately—
Because [the teachings] such as meditative concentration are identical, the Hīnayāna is only one.
Second, because they return to the root within the Hīnayāna, it is one; alternatively, it is five because all four subsequent teachings serve as skillful means.
Within the first teaching, it is either one because it is its own specific school, or four, meaning...

Because all three subsequent teachings involve the application of expedient means (*upāya*), in the Teaching of Maturity there is either one or three; in the Sudden Teaching, there is either one or two;
and in the Perfect Teaching, there is only one. All of these should be understood according to the above principles.

The first four [teachings] all possess the quality of leading toward a destination; thus, one knows that their own respective systems are not ultimate, and are therefore termed "expedient means" (*upāya*)—provisional designations established through skillful means according to what is appropriate.
As for the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), it is either because its own system does not know the Great Vehicle, or because all five [vehicles] are expedient means of the conditioned.
Regarding the Initial Teaching (*Ādikarmika-yāna*), it is either because its own system is singular, or because there are three.

Because both of the latter two teachings serve as skillful means (*upāya*), within the Sudden Teaching (*tun jiao*), either one [of the two] is designated according to its own school, or both are included because they both function as skillful means for the subsequent one.
One should know that this chapter concludes that the Sudden and Complete teachings belong only to the Three Vehicles;
all must enter into one [vehicle] to be called ultimate. In relation to the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*yuan jiao*), they are all termed skillful means.

If one were to categorize the "submerging of two to reveal one" as belonging to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), it would not be termed a "provisional means" (*upāya*), because the latter three teachings are all designated as the One Vehicle.
However, this is not the intended meaning here; for in the Perfect Teaching (*Vendantika-yāna*), there is only the One, because it is ultimate.
The boundaries and interconnections of the doctrines and principles elucidated in these various teachings should be understood by analogy with this.
"Interconnection" refers, for example, to the mutual relationship between the five teachings in terms of their respective boundaries.

This constitutes the web of teachings formed by the numerical categories of the beginning and end of all doctrines. The Great Sage’s skillful means nurture the capacities and conditions of beings without exception.
As for the "numerical categories of the beginning and end," these refer to the various phrases from the preceding teachings that mutually encompass one another, thereby forming the web of teachings.

Thus, it is melted and fused into the inexhaustible, perfect school (*yuanzong*). This means that the preceding teachings are integrated to form the ultimate perfection, so that many capacities and conditions are thoroughly extracted without a single one remaining behind.
One should know, therefore, that the roots of goodness of humans and devas are all subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

As for those who claim that one need only integrate the four noble truths and other dharmas that exist inherently within the Perfect Teaching itself, and not adopt the preceding teachings—how could this be so?
This is sufficient to speak of the Way.
Therefore, this sutra says: "He spreads the great net of the Teaching across the sea of birth and death, delivering the fish of devas and humans and placing them upon the shore of Nirvana.
This is precisely what that means.
Sixth, regarding the sequence of the arising of the teachings:
to briefly explain the sequence of the arising of the teachings is to discern what was spoken by the Tathāgata throughout his entire life.

By situating the teachings according to time, one reveals how the fundamental and the derivative illuminate one another and how mutual support and withdrawal constitute skillful means for the gathering and nurturing of sentient beings.

Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the primary teaching that accords with the Dharma-nature; second, clarifying the secondary teaching that follows according to the capacities of beings.
Regarding the first, this refers to the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Specifically, when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment, on the second week, while beneath the Bodhi tree—just as the rising sun first illuminates the high mountains—he simultaneously expounded the "ten tens" within the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

The Dharma-gate is complete with its primary and attendant elements, perfect and all-pervading in its sovereign mastery. It encompasses the nine and ten periods of time, exhausting the subtle realms of Indra.

Thus, at this very moment, all causes and effects, principles and phenomena, and all preceding and succeeding Dharma-gates—even down to the circulation of relics and the acts of seeing and hearing in the final age—manifest simultaneously.

The title "Attaining the Dharma for Oneself" directly explains the fundamental One Vehicle (Ekayāna) Dharma. Within this, there are four parts: first, the formal presentation of the fundamental Dharma;
second, the "seven days," which refers to the assembly in accordance with the discourse, as the time factor *Indra* encompasses both the preceding and succeeding sections.
The *Zhoushu* contains a comprehensive commentary and interpretation. The "ten-tens" dharma-gates refer to the ten-tens such as "simultaneous perfection" and so forth.

This refers to the "gate. Regarding the phrase "phenomena such as principle and phenomena" (*li-shi deng*), the "etc. includes other matters such as the stages of practice, persons, and the phenomena of dharmas.

As for "before and after," "before" refers to the initial establishment [of the teaching], while "after" refers to the final age; even up to the present and hereafter, all instances of seeing and hearing [the Dharma] manifest within this period.
Why is this? Because they possess mastery over contraction and expansion. When expanded, they encompass the nine periods of time; when contracted, they reside within a single moment.
This very contraction is expansion, and this very expansion is contraction. Why is this? Because they share the same dependent origination and are devoid of dualistic characteristics.
First, what is the basis for this inquiry? Are the prior and posterior simultaneous, and are the simultaneous also prior and posterior?
Because [in this school] the rolling up and unfolding are sovereign, they differ from the final teaching (*anta-śāsana*), where the gates of rolling up and unfolding are not sovereign.

In this school, since the sprout itself is the rolling up and unfolding, it encompasses the nine periods of time within a single moment, being fused and unimpeded. Furthermore, what is the basis for this inquiry?
