Is it because of this unrolling and rolling that such is the case? Since they share the same dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), where there is no unrolling, there is no rolling;
only when there is rolling does unrolling come to be. That which lacks these two characteristics is like the luster of a pearl, the clarity of a mirror, or the marks on a tusk.
The root sūtra states: "Within a single atom, one establishes all the Buddha-activities of the three periods of time," and further says:
"Within a single thought-moment, one accomplishes the eight phases of enlightenment, up to the nirvāṇa and the circulation of the śarīra relics," as explained at length in the sūtra.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) and other sections.
Therefore, based upon this universal Dharma (*samantabhadra-dharma*), all Buddha-teachings are expounded simultaneously—both preceding and following—at the second seven-day period.

This simultaneous exposition of what precedes and follows is like the worldly method of sealing: when one reads the text, the phrases and meanings are sealed by the preceding and following characters.
Then they manifest simultaneously. There is no logical contradiction between simultaneous and sequential [occurrence]. One should know that the principle herein is likewise;
reflect upon it accordingly. The *Kongmu* (General Overview) asks:
"The Great Wisdom Śāriputra and others were already in other lands when the Buddha appeared in the world, at a different time."
[Question: At another location, it is stated that [Śāriputra] entered the Buddha's Dharma together with Maudgalyāyana and others.
Why is it that on the second week of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* assembly, while the Buddha had not yet moved, Śāriputra and five hundred other śrāvakas were already present?
Furthermore, since neither the Jeta Grove nor the Hall of Universal Radiance had yet been established, why is this fully described in the sūtra? [Answer: It is because the Tathāgata...

The One Vehicle is established based on the virtue of liberation. Therefore, a sutra states: "Within a single atom, one establishes all Buddhas of the three periods of time turning the wheel of Dharma.
One should know that the teaching of the One Vehicle currently being established is precisely this matter.
Based on the wisdom that enters the nine periods of time, one integrates the dharmas of the nine periods to establish the tenth period; that is, for each of the past, present, and future...

There are the characteristics of the past, present, and future; these further interpenetrate one another to form the ten periods of time (*daśakāla*). During the second seven-day period, all such dharmas as these manifest before one.

Furthermore, it is said: "If one wishes to recognize the inexhaustible teachings and meanings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one should rely upon the subtle wisdom of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) and the Indra-net, as well as the sovereign dharma-wisdom of the *dhāraṇī*."

It should be understood that this present chapter employs that very text. As the subsequent passage states, "In detail, as in the *Kongmuk mundap* (Questions and Answers on the Catalogue)," one knows that his own statement—recording the subtle words of the Master and forming them into commentaries—is indeed not in vain.
Those who are not well-versed in the *Kongmuk mundap* will not understand the original source of this chapter; thus, later scholars must not fail to examine it.

Second, regarding the teachings that follow the capacities of sentient beings (*jī-mo-jiao*), this refers to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and so forth having two meanings: first, they are taught simultaneously with the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) but in different locations;

second, they are taught at different times and in different locations. As for the first meaning, it constitutes the "teaching of commonality" (*tóngjiào*), because the derivative does not depart from the fundamental.
Because it is established based on the fundamental; because, regarding the latter meaning, the fundamental and the derivative are distinct; and because it is not identical with the fundamental.
Each of these two has two meanings: first, the Three Vehicles; second, the Small Vehicle.
The phrase "the three vehicles, etc. includes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The first meaning refers to different locations at the same time.

As for the "teaching of identity," it signifies that the three and the one are in harmony and are taught simultaneously. This is because, as indicated in the subsequent chapter, the "end not departing from the beginning" and so forth all share the same initial time;
thus, the three instances of the word "therefore" (*gu*) in the text all indicate the reason why they are simultaneous.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent distinction between the fundamental and the derivative: the two characteristics of the fundamental teaching and the derivative teaching are each different.
That they are not identical with the fundamental is because they do not coincide [with it].

Regarding the "initial" [turning of the wheel]: the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* (*Miji Lishi Jing*) states that after the Buddha had first attained enlightenment and completed seven days of contemplation, he prepared a Dharma-seat adorned with various jewels and other ornaments within the Deer Park. He extensively assembled the multitudes of the Three Vehicles.

Brahmā King invited the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma, whereby the multitudes of the Three Vehicles were extensively benefited, attaining fruits ranging from the Great and Small Vehicles. This is explained at length as in that same text.

In the sūtras, and furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that when the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the stage of a śrāvaka;
immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the stage of a pratyekabuddha;
and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practiced the six pāramitās, whereby immeasurable bodhisattvas attained [the stage of non-retrogression].

They attain the patience regarding the arising of phenomena (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*) and dwell in the first, second, and even up to the tenth stages (*bhūmi*). At one time, immeasurable bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*) all attain Buddhahood simultaneously.

The commentary explains that based on this teaching as proof, one should know that during the very first and second seven-day periods, the Dharma of the Three Vehicles was preached. This is in accord with...
The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught as being simultaneous.

When the Sūtra speaks of "contemplating for seven days," this refers precisely to contemplating causal practice (*hetu-pratipatti*) and conditional practice (*pratyaya-pratipatti*). This can be seen in the relevant passages;

the meaning should be explored through the *Xuanben* (Profound Origin), wherein the distinctions between the beginning and the end, as well as the simultaneous inclusion of the Small Vehicle and the One Vehicle, constitute three categories that are simultaneous.

Regarding the second point, concerning the Hīnayāna: the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya states that after the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he entered into samādhi, and only seven days later did he turn the wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park.
Thus, we know that the Hīnayāna was also taught simultaneously with the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states that during the second seven-day period, the five hundred merchants, including Trapusa and Bhallika, offered the Buddha parched grain flour and honey.

The Buddha then bestowed upon them the prediction that they would attain Buddhahood, and so forth. Although the teachings set forth in this sūtra generally pertain to the three vehicles (*triyāna*), there is a sense in which they also encompass the dharmas of humans and devas; thus, they were taught simultaneously with the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Within each of these, there are respective citations of sutras that demonstrate the meaning.
One might ask: "Since the time of the teaching is the same in both cases, why are the locations of the teaching different?
This is a direct question, not a rhetorical objection.
Answer: It is necessary to distinguish between identity and difference because the Dharma is manifested by relying upon time and place;
that is, the manifestation of the Dharma through time and place requires both identity and difference.

Thus, the *Dilun* states: "Because it is displayed as superior through comparisons of time, place, and so forth. Furthermore, "simultaneity" indicates that this is the teaching of commonality (*tongjiao*).

Therefore, the difference in location indicates that this is not the Separate Teaching (*prthaktva-yāna*). For example, if the One Vehicle of the Separate Teaching were taught beneath the Bodhi tree, it would be intended to clarify that this is the place where enlightenment (*bodhi*) was attained;
thus, it reveals that the Tathāgata is teaching the Dharma he himself realized in accordance with its original nature, and for this reason, he does not move from that location to teach.

As for the teachings of the other three vehicles and so forth, it is intended to clarify that they are modified according to the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, [the teacher] moves [to different locations].

Regarding the statement that "at the Deer Park, he spoke according to the capacities [of beings] to reveal that [the teaching] was not the original," the term "time" refers to the initial period, and the "place" is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). As for "other places," such as the Deer Park and so forth, this reveals that it is not a separate teaching;

rather, it indicates that [the Buddha] shifted from one location to another according to the capacities of beings. It does not mean that there is a distinct One Vehicle (ekayāna) separate teaching corresponding to what he himself attained.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the second case where both time and place differ: because it does not coincide with the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in meaning, the time and place are distinct.
Alternatively, it was taught after three or seven days, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; or it was taught after six or seven days, as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that it may be preached after seven weeks, as described in the *Udayana-sūtra*;
or after eight weeks, as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; or after fifty-seven days, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Alternatively, he did not preach the Dharma for one year, and it was only after twelve years that he converted the five men, as stated in the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra*.
Some commentators explain that the "fifty-seven days" mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to fifty periods of seven days,
which is identical to the one-year period in the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra*.

Regarding the second point, "not identical in meaning," this refers to the distinctions between the fundamental and the derivative. The *Tanyuan Dashi* (Great Commentary on the *Tanxuan ji*) states that the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) contains [the relevant passage], while the others all agree with this.
As for the derivative teachings, because the capacities of the recipients differ, what they hear is distinct for each.
Therefore, they are not the same. Based on these scriptural proofs, one should know that the three vehicles and the small vehicle were not taught during the second seven-day period.

This is because they differ from the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and because they were taught according to the specific capacities of sentient beings. Other points may be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, one can understand that within these meanings there are principles such as "the root giving rise to the branches" and "the branches being subsumed back into the root," all of which have been abbreviated here.
Seventh, regarding the determination of their intent:

However, the differences between the preceding and succeeding teachings are difficult to discern. I shall briefly analyze their intent by means of ten gates. Regarding the difficulty in discerning the sequence of the various teachings:

after the two masters from the Western Regions (Xīyù) in the *Tàn xuán* [Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra], my own Patriarch [Fazang] posed questions concerning two interpretations regarding the three teachings—namely, the claim that each first taught the Hīnayāna and the claim that the *Avataṃsaka* was taught first. How should these be reconciled with the previous chapter’s three [interpretations]?
The Master [Zongmi] explains both [theories] simultaneously; therefore, this section is established to resolve their underlying intent.

Regarding the statement that "the distinctions are difficult to discern," various masters of antiquity have each offered explanations for this question, yet their many assertions differ. Some base their views on the capacities for sudden versus gradual enlightenment;

others on the two gates of the manifest and the secret; and still others on the diverse interpretations arising from a single sound. However, all of these positions encounter difficulties and contradictions.

He is able to resolve and clarify [the matter]. Fourth, the Venerable Bhadramukha provides an exegesis that clarifies the direction and resolves this difficulty, while simultaneously reconciling the two views.
There are generally two categories: first, those taught for those whose faculties are fixed in this life; second, those taught for those whose faculties are not fixed in this life.
This present chapter summarizes these two examples into ten sections.
First: there are some sentient beings whose *śrāvaka* (Hīnayāna) faculties are fixed from beginning to end within this world;
they see the Tathāgata from his initial attainment of the Way until his parinirvāṇa as teaching only the Hīnayāna, and have never seen him turn the wheel of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The wheel: those who hold to the various Śāstra schools and do not believe in the Mahāyāna are like small [wheels].
In that text, there are three types of faculties fixed for this world; this is one of them.
Second: There may be sentient beings in this world whose faculties for the Hīnayāna are indeterminate; thus, they are capable of entering the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna.
If they are already fixed [in their inclination], they perceive that at the beginning, the Tathāgata turned the wheel of the Hīnayāna to overturn the various non-Buddhist paths.
Later, they perceive him turning the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna—the wheel of the Dharma of emptiness—to lead back those of the Hīnayāna. This is as described in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
That which was stated at the beginning of the treatise is precisely this:
the gateway of the indeterminate faculties (*indriya*) in this present life. Nevertheless, this chapter is divided into multiple meanings in order to accord with the various preceding teachings;
those [teachings] merely presented the two gateways of entering three or entering one. Now, we shall proceed from the small to enter the initial [gateway].
This is the teaching. As for the term "the Dharma-wheel of Emptiness," works such as the *Kongmu* (Outline) take emptiness as their primary starting point;
this chapter records them to complete the textual structure, hence it is called "the Dharma-wheel of Emptiness. Subsequently, the School of Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇayāna*) gradually flourished.
In the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities) and other texts, Fangbian states that three and a half categories of persons cannot attain Buddhahood;

therefore, he also classifies this as belonging to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), referring to it by the name "Addition. This is not contradictory. Furthermore, the opening of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Of those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I say they are empty."

Third: There may be sentient beings who, within this world, possess indeterminate faculties regarding the Small Vehicle and the Initial Teaching, such that they are capable of entering the Final Teaching.
If they are indeed so determined, then at the initial stage they see the turning of the wheel of the Small Vehicle; at the middle stage they see the turning of the wheel of the teaching on emptiness;
and at the final stage they see the turning of the wheel of non-emptiness. This is as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other such texts.
That is to say, within the three wheels of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, first one hears only the Small [Vehicle], next one hears only the Great [Vehicle], and finally one hears all three.
This description of "empty" and "not empty" is spoken in terms of the principle that is revealed.
Fourth: There are some sentient beings whose faculties are not fixed within the gradual teaching and thus are capable of entering the sudden teaching.

As soon as they become fixed [in that capacity], they perceive that the initial teachings of verbal expression are still not ultimate; it is only when the later teaching that transcends words is revealed that it is finally considered ultimate.
This is as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* by the first thirty-two bodhisattvas and Mañjuśrī.
The non-dual [reality] is present within all verbal discourse; however, that which Vimalakīrti later reveals as the teaching that transcends words is taken as the ultimate.
This refers to the fact that the essence of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* lies in the transcendence of words, which is very clearly evident in the text.

Fifth: There may be sentient beings whose faculties for sudden awakening are matured in this world such that they immediately attain concentration and see that from the time the Buddha first attained the Way until his parinirvāṇa, he did not speak a single word. As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"If one knows that the Tathāgata constantly does not preach the Dharma, this is called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning (*bahuśruta*)."
This is also extracted from the "Probing the Profundities" (*Tanchuan*) section on the fundamental meditative concentration (*mūla-samādhi*). All that is cited therein is beyond words.

Six. There may be sentient beings in this world whose capacities for the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are fixed, who see the Buddha teaching the doctrines of the three vehicles from the very beginning until his *nirvāṇa*, with no further teachings beyond them. As stated in the *Guhyapada-malla-sūtra* (Miji Lishi jing).
This refers to what is taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Specifically, within that section on the determination of faculties (*indriya-niyama*), it states: "There may be sentient beings whose faculties for the three vehicles have matured in this life;
they see the Buddha from his beginning to his end, yet he speaks only of the three vehicles. As the *Guhyakapuruṣa-sūtra* says: "At the Deer Park, the Buddha first preached..."
At that time, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship and so forth;
this is explained at length, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the Great Chapter) likewise speaks in the same way. Furthermore, it says:

"By analogy with this principle, all that is taught in subsequent times universally encompasses these three vehicles, just as it is stated in various Mahāyāna sūtras. It further states: "Within this, although there are both provisional and ultimate [teachings]..."

All [beings] without exception possess the three vehicles. Therefore, one should know that while these preceding gates differ in terms of provisional and real, sudden and gradual, the distinctions here—such as whether the faculties and natures of beings in this world are fixed or unfixed—all belong to the three vehicles. It is only from the seventh stage [of the Bodhisattva path] onward that one discusses entering the One from the Three.
Seventh: There may be sentient beings in this world whose faculties regarding the three vehicles (triyāna) are indeterminate.
Thus, those who are capable of entering the Sameness Teaching of the One Vehicle perceive that all the dharmas of the three vehicles they have attained are based upon the One Vehicle.
The arising of the inexhaustible teaching is its skillful means (upāya) and provisional designation (prajñapti). Therefore, whatever they practice, they dedicate it all toward the One Vehicle. As...
The convergence of the three refuges into one, and so forth; likewise, as cited above regarding the simultaneous teaching of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle, and so forth.

Regarding "in this world" and so forth: those whose three faculties are indeterminate who enter into the One [Vehicle]—the turning away from the three to enter the one is the "teaching of commonality.
Seeing that one’s own dharma is the skillful means for that [One Vehicle], one abandons the skillful means to enter the True Vehicle. [This applies to] the Three Vehicles.
The teaching is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), which is its meaning. The triad [of the three vehicles] is in harmony with this; it is precisely the aforementioned Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Alternatively, because the first four of the five [teachings] serve as skillful means (upāya), although they are not the primary vehicle, they are all subsumed within the Perfect Teaching, as they are its expedients—just as a slave belongs to his master.
The *Kongmu* states: "If one relies horizontally upon the dharma-gates of skillful means, there are two meanings; now we speak of the One Vehicle."
The meaning of the middle and later [teachings] is that they are taught as the One Vehicle (ekayāna) because they serve as skillful means (*upāya*) for that ultimate, perfect One Vehicle;

it does not mean that they are themselves the meaning of perfect, all-pervading, and sovereign mastery. The intent is that they are merely called the "One Vehicle" by virtue of acting as a skillful means toward that [ultimate state], but they are not themselves that perfect, all-pervading, and inexhaustible Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "Arising based upon those teachings, they are that..."
[The term] *āgama* is translated here as "Pure Teaching" (*jingjiao*). Its meaning is that it is merely verbal expression.

Eight: There may be sentient beings within this world whose faculties for the Three Vehicles are not yet fixed, such that they are capable of entering the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) of the One Vehicle.
One should then know that those dharmas of the Three Vehicles and so forth are fundamentally no different from the Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle. Why?
For this reason, because it is that which is being referred to, and because there is no other distinct matter, it is as explained in the "Shared Teaching" section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The text says:
"There may be sentient beings in this world whose faculties for the Three Vehicles are indeterminate and who are capable of entering the Distinct Teaching."

As for these beings: when they first see the Buddha and hear the teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), after long cultivation their faculties mature and the wisdom of the universal eye (*samantacakṣus*) opens.
They then realize that what they have attained is the Dharma itself, and that it was the Buddha who, within the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), differentiated and taught three.

There is no difference in reality; there is only the single vehicle. Thus it is said they "enter the distinct. This is still to enter the one from the three; however, because their faculties are sharp, they do not perceive the [intermediate stages].
One may set aside the provisional means. Since each and every designation for that One Vehicle is perfectly interfused, there is no further distinct matter.
The *Kongmu* states: "It is established by relying on the teaching of the ultimate One Vehicle. Why?

Because it flows from the One Vehicle, and because it is designated by the One Vehicle. This is as explained in the *Lotus Sūtra* according to the theory of the "teaching of commonality" (*tóngjiào*).

The core principle of this sutra is the convergence of the three vehicles into one. Therefore, although the two preceding gates both involve entry—whether into the common or the distinct, and whether the faculties are sharp or dull—they all effect this convergence by responding to the capacities of sentient beings.
This differs from the *Avataṃsaka*, which at its initial formation was taught as a sudden revelation without provisional means to be converged;

it does not accommodate the two vehicles, but speaks solely of the uncommon One Vehicle. As previously noted in the context of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), this [One Vehicle] encompasses all within itself.
All things, from root to branch, are solely the One Vehicle; this is precisely the perfect, distinct, and ultimate Dharma expounded by this sutra.
Ninth: there may be sentient beings who, within this very life, possess the capacity for Samantabhadra;
they shall see the Tathāgata from his initial attainment of enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, and how he universally [manifests] all Buddha-dharmas during the first and second seven-day periods.
Sealed within meditative absorption, one freely expounds the inexhaustible and perfect array of primary and attendant teachings, exhausting the subtle realm of Indra’s net.
From the beginning, there has been no teaching of the three vehicles or the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as described in the distinct teachings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This refers to the stage of seeing, hearing, understanding, and practice according to the division of the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) teachings.
The following two sections both pertain to the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle.

This refers to the opening of these two gates for those whose spiritual faculties are matured in this world, as described in the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundities). That is to say, from the very beginning, the fundamental teaching is expounded.

Because those who do not perceive the three [vehicles] or the small [vehicles] directly manifest the One by means of its essential substance, it is taught as such for the sake of great bodhisattvas, directly demonstrating the ritual of attaining Buddhahood within the Dharma-realm; thus, it is not contrasted [with other teachings].
Because the Two Vehicles have nothing to be sublated, there is no provisional teaching with which they can be reconciled; this is unlike the *Lotus Sūtra*, which sublates diversity to clarify unity.

This [distinction] is made according to the classification of the teachings of Samantabhadra. Within the gateway of Samantabhadra, if one were to distinguish two divisions based solely on the categories of teaching and realization, [it would be as follows].

Thus, within the division of teaching (*śāsana-bhāga*), there are the stages of seeing, hearing, understanding, and practice; the stage of entering realization is termed the "division of realization" (*sākṣātkriyā-bhāga*).
The *Kongmu* states: "This is explained according to the division of teaching," and further: "This is based on realization. Alternatively, three divisions are established:

namely, the division of seeing and hearing, the division of understanding and practice, and the division of entering realization. These may also be called the "three positions" or the "three births. The *Kongmu* says: "In this regard..."

This refers to the stage from the "Section on Realization" (*praveśa-bhāga*) onwards in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). Furthermore, it is said that this should be explained in the context of seeing and hearing within the stages of the Perfect Teaching.

It is also stated that this is the meaning of the "Section on Samantabhadra’s Practice and Understanding" (*samantabhadra-caryā-pratipatti-bhāga*). These three sections are all subsumed under the gateway of Samantabhadra.
In the present text, the two sections of Teaching and Realization are organized into ninety-two gates; thus, within the section on Teaching, there are the aspects of seeing and hearing, and...

This is explained from the perspective of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). Tenth: there may be sentient beings who, having fulfilled their practice through understanding within the distinct teachings of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), have already entered the ocean of fruition.

Such individuals perceive all the aforementioned teachings as being nothing other than the inexhaustible ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) formed according to conditions, without any further distinction.
Therefore, all teachings are themselves the perfectly luminous and inexhaustible ocean of fruition. They possess inconceivable virtues, being unspeakable upon unspeakable [numbers].
This is explained according to the stages of entry and realization within the One Vehicle; other matters may be understood by analogy.
This is precisely the definitive analysis of the single-vehicle (ekayāna) lineage that establishes this gate.

When the sentient beings’ understanding and practice are fulfilled and they enter the ocean of fruition (*phala-samudra*), one then knows that it is not merely a fruit of quiescent extinction, perfect culmination, or sovereign mastery.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "one immediately perceives all the aforementioned teachings," one should know that the "ocean of fruition" herein refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta at the beginning of the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind."
At that time, one merely attains the fruit; it is also the fruit manifested by the inconceivable and so forth. What is stated here reveals that the ocean of fruits is ineffable.
When this text says "ineffable-in-effable," it refers to the possession of virtue and the inconceivable that transcends all numerical categories;
it does not mean that the aspect of the fruit is so remote and transcendent as to be utterly unspeakable. This is so.

Therefore, the conclusion states: "This is according to the stage of entry and realization in the One Vehicle. Since it says that this is explained from this specific standpoint, it is clear that this does not refer to the ocean of fruition.
Eighth, regarding the establishment of distinct characteristics:
However, these differences are numerous; they will be briefly summarized under ten categories to demonstrate their inexhaustibility. What are the ten differences? First is the difference in time.
This means that this One Vehicle must necessarily be taught during the first period, specifically the second week [after enlightenment], just as the rising sun first illuminates the high mountains.
Thus, the Treatise says: "Because this Dharma is supreme, it is taught at the initial time and in a supreme location."
Furthermore,
regarding the phrase "at different times" and so forth, it is as explained in the teaching concerning the sequence of the arising [of the path].
If that is so, why is it not taught during the first seven days that one contemplates the causal conditions for the formations (*saṃskāra*), as explained in the treatise?
Why is the "first seven" not mentioned in the *Mahāvaipulya*? It is because it contemplates the practice of causes and the practice of conditions; therefore, the "first seven" are not mentioned.
This treatise is the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. A detailed explanation may be found in various commentaries and records.
Furthermore, because this very moment is like Indra’s net, it encompasses all time. Whether prior or subsequent, neither can be said to exist independently;
thus, the kalpas of both the past and future limits are simultaneously subsumed within this single moment.
This is also as explained above. "Indra" refers to number; it is used to manifest the inexhaustibility of time.

The three vehicles and so forth are not like this, for they follow the capacities and suitability of beings; since their timing is not fixed, they may occur before or after, and do not necessarily encompass all kalpas at one and the same time.
This is also as previously explained.
Second, there is a difference in location. That is to say, this One Vehicle must reside beneath the Bodhi tree adorned with various jewels within the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean;
it encompasses the seven locations and eight assemblies, as well as other [assemblies] that are unspeakably unspeakable in number.
The oceans of worlds are all contained within this [world-realm], because one location subsumes all locations.

Therefore, the statement that the immovable Bodhi tree ascends universally to the six heavens and so forth refers to this meaning. Furthermore, because this Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) pervades the Indra-net of worlds, it encompasses all peripheral atoms;
thus, in this place which accords with the Dharma-realm, that One Vehicle which accords with the Dharma-realm is taught.
This is a Dharma-gate.

As for "the essential point in the lower world-oceans," this refers to the twenty tiers of Buddha-fields contained within the Lotus Treasury Fragrant Water Ocean, in which worlds numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields are arrayed. All of these...
It is purified by the causes cultivated by the Tathāgata; he constantly dwells within it and expounds the Dharma.
According to the Jin dynasty translations of the sutras, there are seven locations and eight assemblies.

Furthermore, all lands throughout the ten directions without interval, exhausting the entire dharma-realm—beyond this *Avataṃsaka* collection—are likewise contained therein. That which is "immovable" means that it is omnipresent without being divided. Moreover,
This world-system pervades the Indra-net in infinite, layered succession; its dimensions cannot be described.
Regarding the various particles on its periphery, a sutra states: "Within every single particle of all the Flower Treasury worlds, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm."
Qingliang says: This is still explained in terms of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

If one speaks in terms of the world of the Perfectly Awakened Wisdom and the world of sentient beings, then every single Buddha-body—down to its limbs, joints, and pores—encompasses infinite, multi-layered lands.
It is the same for each and every sentient being of Samantabhadra; all are places where Vairocana preaches the sutras, progressing from the narrow to the vast.
This briefly indicates ten points, as analyzed in the commentary.
The three vehicles and so forth are not like this; even in places such as wooden trees within the Sahā world, there is no single location that is identical to all locations.
This can be seen in the text.
Question: If that is so, why are the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other scriptures also said to have been taught within a pure land? Answer:
Those sūtras merely state that [the teaching occurred] in palaces of radiant light and so forth, which possess eighteen kinds of perfection; they do not specifically designate the kingdom of Magadha.

And so forth. Because these are taught as the merits of the Buddha-ground for the sake of bodhisattvas on the stages, they are spoken within the enjoyment lands (saṃbhogakāya-kṣetra) outside the triple world.
This is explained according to the Final Teaching of the Three Vehicles and the Common Teaching of the One Vehicle.

The answer below indicates the characteristics of that sūtra; it does not distinguish it as being different because the *Avataṃsaka* encompasses the entire land of Magadha within the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*). The passage beginning with "Because of that" clarifies the intent of that sūtra:

since it explains the virtues of the Buddha-ground for those on the stages (*bhūmi*), it specifically reveals the distinction between defilement and purity within the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) outside the realms, rather than teaching through the principle of total interpenetration.
This concludes the section on the scope of the teachings. The final teaching of the Three Vehicles and the common teaching of the One Vehicle both expound this meaning;
thus, one should know that the final teaching of the Three Vehicles is not a distinct teaching.

If these [teachings of] the Avataṃsaka all state that they are within the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpasaṃbhava-kṣetra), such as in the kingdom of Magadha and so forth, yet do not say they are within the Sahā world nor outside the triple world, one should know that they are distinct. Other meanings may be understood by analogy.
It is the melting and fusing of defilement and purity.
Third is the difference in the principal speakers. This means that this One Vehicle must be taught by the ten-fold body of Vairocana Buddha and by all those throughout the three periods of time.
As the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" states: "The Buddha speaks, the Bodhisattvas speak, the lands speak, sentient beings speak, and the three periods of time [speak]."
"All-encompassing explanations," etc.,
refers to these ten bodies of two kinds, which are listed in full detail in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text). Furthermore, it explains the tenfold non-obstruction of pervasive function and so forth,
extensively revealing the inexhaustible characteristics of the clouds of bodies of the Dharma-realm that pervade the three worlds throughout time.
It is taught constantly and taught universally; the scriptural passages cited here refer to the teachings of the three worlds.

This is not the same as the teachings of the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya), the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya), and so forth, which pertain to the Three Vehicles. Other meanings should be understood by analogy.
Regarding "enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga*), among the three bodies, it refers to the *parasaṃbhogakāya*, named Vairocana. The *Kongmu* states: "This refers to Vairocana according to the Three Vehicles;
he corresponds to that *saṃbhogakāya*. Furthermore, it is said that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is also the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The thousand Buddhas who are transformed, as well as the thousand-billion Śākyamunis, also correspond to the *saṃbhogakāya* when they descend to Jambudvīpa and leave home at the age of seven."
These should be understood as transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). If one follows the *Avataṃsaka*, it is not like this, because there are ten distinct Buddhas.
Therefore, Vairocana and the transformed Śākyamuni are both the transformative functions of these ten Buddhas; this should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, when Samantabhadra rides an elephant and appears before the practitioner, he is the Samantabhadra of the Three Vehicles; that is to say, the fourth.

The fifteen types of knowledge are the One Vehicle Samantabhadra. One should know that there is a vast difference between the virtues and meanings of the three-body Vairocana and the ten-body Vairocana.
As it is with Samantabhadra, so it is with Mañjuśrī; each and every one is complete with both principal and attendant aspects.
Fourth is the diversity of the assembly.

This refers to the fact that at the beginning of this One Vehicle sutra, there is listed only the Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and the various hosts of spirit-kings within the realm of the Buddhas.
This means that these [assemblies] are as listed in the "Chapter on Wondrous Adornments" (Gandavyūha-parivarta), differing from those of the three vehicles;
they may consist solely of the assembly of śrāvakas, or both the great and small assemblies, and so forth.
Alternatively, it may simply be as stated in other sūtras.
Question: If that is so, why is there an assembly of śrāvakas in the ninth chapter?
Answer: There are two intended meanings for listing the śrāvakas therein.
There being two intentions, the two śrāvakas each correspond to one intention. First:
because the Dharma is manifested by way of contrast, they are described as being like the deaf and the blind in order to manifest the profound superiority of the Dharma.
By contrasting them with those Śrāvakas, the supreme excellence of the *Avataṃsaka* is revealed. Even while seated together and making the same request, the Arhats remain as if deaf and blind;
thus, the profound and mysterious nature of that Dharma can certainly be known. Therefore, it is said to "reveal the profound and the supreme.
These are none other than the ten great Śrāvakas who were disciples of Śākyamuni, namely Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Second, regarding the six thousand bhikṣus and others mentioned as being gathered outside the assembly where Mañjuśrī appears: these are not the same group listed previously.
All of them were already established within the three vehicles; it was in order to cause them to turn toward the One Vehicle that this statement was made.
These six thousand bhikṣus, including Śāriputra’s disciple Samudrabuddhi and others, differ in their conduct from the five hundred śrāvakas who were cousins.
Therefore, the *Kongmu* states: "There were the great wise Śāriputra and the other five hundred śrāvakas."
There were also six thousand bhikṣus who were disciples of Śāriputra. The word "also" (bing) implies inclusion. There are two distinct types [of disciples] to be distinguished.
Regarding Mañjuśrī and others: since Mañjuśrī heard the teachings in this assembly and subsequently took leave of the Buddha to travel south, he is said to be "excluded from the assembly.
This means that Śāriputra likewise took leave of the Buddha to follow Mañjuśrī on his journey.
Human beings serve as assistants in the transformation [of others]. Indrasena and five hundred other bhikṣus, whom he had brought with him, emerged from their own quarters and arrived at the road.
There, Śāriputra exhorted the bhikṣus to contemplate the ten kinds of superior virtues of Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī turned his gaze toward the bhikṣus like an elephant king. All the bhikṣus attained the ten eyes, the ten ears, and so forth;
thus it is said that the "six thousand [bhikṣus] and others" who were gathered therein represent the purification of the six sense faculties. Therefore, he manifested them as six thousand.
This is not a selection of the five hundred śrāvakas; rather, it refers to the assembly of śrāvakas listed at the beginning of this sutra.
These six thousand were not listed at the beginning of the sutra, and thus these two groups are distinct. The character "列" (liè, to list) has been erroneously written as "引" (yǐn, to lead).

As for the phrase "these [monks]," these bhikṣus belong to the category of those within the Three Vehicles who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; they are not śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding those in the stage of hearing: it is precisely because, in the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī has already transformed them through his teachings, causing them to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna, that it is said they "are already within the Three Vehicles. Now, he causes them to turn their minds toward the One Vehicle;

thus the sūtra speaks in this manner. Kongzang himself says: "The second [point], which distinguishes the turning of the mind according to the ultimate meaning, is as follows in the scriptural text: 'Great...'"
The wise Śāriputra, together with five hundred bhikṣus, turned their minds toward Mañjuśrī. They spoke of having planted roots of goodness in past lives.
The appearance of six thousand bhikṣus manifested that they were long-standing companions in practice who had achieved a true retinue.
Śāriputra, while remaining within the Buddha-dharma, was by right in the rank of the intelligent; it was further said that now he had again turned his mind, he should indeed turn [toward Mañjuśrī].
At that time, one immediately attains the ten kinds of great dharmas and so forth. Furthermore, it is said that its position lies within the teachings of sudden enlightenment and matured instruction.
Moreover, regarding the practice and vows for the future, these constitute the assembly of Bodhisattvas, whereas Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and others constitute the assembly of Śrāvakas.
When one is about to turn the mind [toward the Mahāyāna], one must first laboriously and exhaustively instruct those at the stage of the Hīnayāna.
The *Kongmu* (Compendium) further states that this is like the parable of the poor son, where the elder sends a messenger to employ skillful means to provide him with wealth and other such matters.

This corresponds to the meaning of the teachings for humans, devas, and the Mahāsāṃghika school and beyond, up to the Initial Teaching (*Ādikarmika-yāna*), such as the case of Śāriputra turning his mind [toward the Mahāyāna]. This applies from the point of the Initial Teaching onward, up to...

Regarding the "Transformation of Six Thousand" mentioned in the *Kongmu* (Outline) concerning the Sudden Teaching and those below the Final Teaching: the "five hundred bhikṣus" refers to a transformation that is not [limited to] śrāvakas.

Fifth is the difference in what is relied upon; that is to say, the arising of this One Vehicle teaching necessarily relies on its emergence from within the Buddha’s Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
Regarding the phrase "must rely on the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) and so forth":

it was stated above that we are now about to expound the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) teachings of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s Sea-Seal Samādhi, which has two gates: the identical (*samāna*) and the distinct (*bhinna*).

If, as previously explained, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and so on are all within the identical teaching, how could they also emerge from the Sea-Seal [Samādhi]? The *Kongmu* states: "The identical and the distinct arise together from within the Sea-Seal Samādhi."

It is accomplished within [the state of concentration]. Therefore, it does not exist within meditative absorption. Those who speak of the "teaching of sameness" do so because they enter the distant preparatory stage (*pūrvayoga*) of the One Vehicle;
they are not like those of the three vehicles and others, who emerge from the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

This is precisely the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*). Sixth is the distinction of exposition: this refers to how this One Vehicle is taught here as a single matter, a single meaning, a single chapter, or a single assembly;

yet at that time, it must necessarily be understood as being universally communicated throughout all worlds of the ten directions, with the principal and the associates together forming a single division of the canon.
Therefore, every single word and phrase of this sutra pervades the ten directions; even many words and many phrases likewise pervade the ten directions.
This means that what follows below is identical to the previously cited *Tongshuo jing* (Sutra of Uniform Exposition), which is also the *Zhuban jing* (Sutra of Principal and Retinue).

The three vehicles and so forth are not like this; they merely follow a single direction and a single aspect in their teaching, lacking this [teaching] of the primary and its retinue, or that which is universally pervasive.
"A single direction" refers to the transformative ritual adapted to a specific region. "A single aspect" refers to a solitary gate of a single characteristic. It lacks this.
This refers to the perfect interfusion of the principal and the attendant, which extends throughout the ten directions and so forth.
Seventh is the distinction of stages (*avasthā*). This means that all the characteristics of the stages within this One Vehicle are equal from top to bottom;

furthermore, within each individual stage, all stages are subsumed. Therefore, even stages such as those of Buddhahood and so forth are contained within the stages of faith and so on. As for the other stages...
It is likewise.

That is to say, the mutual inclusion of these six stages—such as their entry into one another—is explained extensively in the commentary; a brief account is provided here as analyzed within the section on the "referent" (*vācya*).
Within the Three Vehicles, it is not so; rather, according to their respective stages, whether higher or lower, they are never separated from one another.
The rest is as explained below.

[The phrase] "not so" (*buer*) is used because those [teachings] merely concern the distinctions of sequential progression (*xingbu*), where the upper and lower levels differ. The character "separated" (*li*) is an error and should be corrected.
They form a composite term; they are not intermingled.
Eighth is the difference in practice: a single bodhisattva simultaneously possesses all six stages, such as faith and so forth.
Within each stage, all distinct modes of practice—such as those that are concentrated or non-concentrated—are cultivated at once, just as [it is] in all worlds of the eastern direction.

Entering meditative absorption and so forth, constantly making offerings to the Buddhas in the Western World and other realms—in this way, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, exhausting the entire Dharma-realm, one acts without dividing the body, yet at once pervades them all; in a single thought-moment, one universally cultivates them all.
Within each and every thought-moment, it is likewise so. From the fulfillment of the mind in the stage of faith onward, one cultivates in this manner in each and every stage. Furthermore...
There is no distinction of superior or inferior. Furthermore, a single practice is identical to all practices, as they universally interpenetrate like Indra’s net.

Thus, one who possesses faith and the other virtues attains "one" which is simultaneously "all"; therefore, by attaining a *sheng* (升), one attains a *dou* (斗). If one is not established, then all are not established together;
this is truly because they share the same dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is the wisdom of the six aspects (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa-jñāna*).

Because they are fused; because they interpenetrate; because they are mutually identical. "In each and every stage" means that "concentration" refers to being truly in samādhi, while "dispersion" refers to the time of emerging from samādhi.
"Cultivating them simultaneously" means that in a single thought-moment, all practices are universally accomplished.
"The East, etc. refers to mutual pervasion at the same time. "Exhausting the entire Dharma-realm" reveals the profound, layered pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm.
Because the meaning is established as a whole, there is no further differentiation, for the single body is itself the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*).
The passage "at once" below reveals the perfect fusion of thought-instants and eons (*kalpa*), because each individual gate exhaustively encompasses [all others].

From the stage of the fulfillment of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) onward, one distinguishes the stages based on practice, because the One Vehicle is the Buddha of Practice. As it says in the Question and Answer: "If one possesses the five stages..."

And as for the nine stages, the Buddha is subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), because there is no longer any distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority;

all are fused into one. Furthermore, from the perspective of the One Vehicle, all phenomena (dharmas) together constitute dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), wherein both the identity and difference of their essence are mutually interpenetrating.
The three vehicles are not like this; even Bodhisattvas on the stages each have their own limits, let alone those prior to the stages.
The rest is as explained below and can be seen in the text.
Ninth, the difference in the dharma-gates: this refers to briefly citing ten major points to clarify it. First, they have three Buddhas while these have ten Buddhas.

Second, they have six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) while these have ten supernormal powers. Third, they have three types of clear knowledge (traividyā) while these have ten types of clear knowledge.
4. They have eight liberations; these have ten liberations. 5. They have four fearlessnesses; these have ten fearlessnesses.
6. They have five eyes; these have ten eyes. 7. They speak of three periods of time; these speak of ten periods of time.
8. They speak of four truths, whereas here there are ten truths. 9. They have four analytical knowledges, whereas here there are ten analytical knowledges. 10.
They possess eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), whereas here there are ten unique qualities. Other categories are immeasurable and extensive, as explained in the sūtras.

The ten [aspects] that are distinguished and revealed through contrast—such as those in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) and others—are as explained in their respective chapters. The ten [aspects] common to all, as well as the ten clarifications (*daśa-vyākhyāna*), are likewise as found in their respective chapters.
The remainder are as in the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) and others.

As for the "ten," they refer to the diversity of phenomena; that is to say, whatever phenomena exist—whether houses, forests, ponds, lands, mountains, and so forth—all are *dharmamukhas* (gateways to the Dharma), or they are...
Whether it be practice, stages, or doctrinal meanings, they do not impair their respective functions;

yet within each and every atom, all the diverse phenomena of the dharma-realm are fully present. Just as with the subtle accomplishment of Indra, it is exactly the same for the arising of each individual phenomenon.
This means that, for example, as Sudhana encountered greed, anger, and delusion, he attained dharma-gates from them all; encountering mountains, he entered the dharma-realm of mountains;
encountering water, he entered the dharma-realm of water, and so forth—all such phenomena are themselves the reality. Furthermore, every single atom contains the entire dharma-realm.
Just as a single atom is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), so too are persons, dharmas, principle and phenomena, cause and effect, practices, and stages.
The ten pairs of twenty matters constitute the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth; each and every atom is likewise in this manner, and thus the term "Indra" and so on are obtained.
The three vehicles and others are not like this;
they can only be described as being "identical to emptiness," "identical to true suchness" (*tathatā*), and so forth. Therefore, they are not the same as this.

Furthermore, if one were to manifest [these states] momentarily through the inconceivable power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), it would not be because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those dharmas is such;
other cases may be understood by analogy. The *Kongmu* states:

"In the Initial Teaching, there is emptiness; in the Final Teaching, there is suchness (*tathatā*); in the Sudden Teaching, there is total cessation. Moreover, this serves to distinguish [the teachings] below.
[This refers to] the pressing of the earth with the toes, as well as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Acintya-viniścaya-prabhāsa-sūtra*, and so forth.

Ninth, clarifying the distinctions among the meanings elucidated by the various teachings: because ten categories of differences in meaning are briefly set forth, the non-uniformity of the distinctions among those expressive teachings is revealed. The remainder is as explained elsewhere.
Regarding "all teachings," this refers to the five categories of the expressive teachings (*vācaka*).

Regarding "the expressed," this refers to the three—principle, practice, and fruit—which are the meanings designated by those teachings. As for "distinctions," within each of these expressed meanings there are five gates.

For example, in the case of the profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the single mind (*ekacitta*) possesses five gates of meaning. From this, one can understand those expressive teachings.

The Dharma consists of five distinct categories; thus, it is said that these reveal its non-unity. Our Patriarch stated: "This is a classification according to meaning, not based on temporal events," referring to the ten gates.
Of these, the first two are principle (*li*), the latter three are fruition (*guo*), and those in between are practice (*xing*). The aforementioned passage states:
"If classified according to the meaning of the Dharma, as distinguished below"—this refers precisely to this point. The above constitutes the Dharma as the signifier (*neng-quan*).
This is the meaning of the "lower dharma. By upholding this meaning, one distinguishes that dharma and clarifies the truth.
1. The mind-consciousness as the single basis; 2. Clarifying the Buddha-nature (*gotra*); 3. The demarcation of stages and positions in practice;
4. The duration of the period of cultivation; 5. The physical basis for cultivation; 6. The demarcation of the abandonment of afflictions.
7. The turning of the mind of the two vehicles; 8. The characteristics of the meaning of the Buddha-fruit; 9. The sphere of conversion and guidance; 10.
The opening and closing of the Buddha-bodies.
First, regarding the distinctions of mind and consciousness:
Mind, mentation, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) serve as the basis for all phenomena; various teachings delineate their respective distinctions.
For instance, in the Hīnayāna there are only the six consciousnesses, and the conceptual differentiation of mind, mentation, and consciousness is as explained in the Hīnayāna treatises.
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*, one merely encounters its name, as stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
It is said that there are only six consciousnesses and no seventh or eighth. Regarding this meaning, the *Yanyi* (Exposition of Meaning) in the lower section states:

"The Hīnayāna school asserts that the future is called 'mind' (*citta*), the past is called 'intellect' (*manas*), and the present is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*). Although they make such various distinctions, these have no separate substantial entities.
These names—mind, intellect, and consciousness—are spoken of according to the different meanings of these three time periods; their substance, however, is simply the sixth consciousness."
The *Abhidharma-kośa* is precisely the *Vibhāṣā*. Regarding the Ālayavijñāna, it receives only the name "the eighth" [consciousness] and lacks a separate self-substance;
this is because the Hīnayāna merely posits the sixth consciousness as spanning the three periods of time, as indicated by the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
If one relies on the Initial Teaching (Śāstra), one only attains a partial understanding of the meaning of arising and ceasing regarding the *ālayavijñāna*.
This is because one has not yet been able to harmonize it with ultimate truth; thus, it is taught that [the *ālayavijñāna*] is immutably quiescent and does not produce any phenomena.

This refers to the clarification of the meaning of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) within the context of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Because the causes and conditions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because they were not produced from the beginning, they are not "accomplished"; yet because they are formed through conditions, they are not "unaccomplished. Because they are formed through conditions, they are not "accomplished" [in an absolute sense].

This applies to all gateways of consciousness (*vijñāna-mukha*). The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (*Qixinlun shu*) states: "Because the School of Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇa-vāda*) in the Initial Teaching..."
Knowing that the Buddha taught the *tathāgatagarbha* as the *ālayavijñāna*, it is said that [the opponent] has attained only one portion [of its meaning].

They take the "aspect of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*) as the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the *ālaya*, the "aspect of transformation" (*pariṇāmalakṣaṇa*) as the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*), and the "manifest aspect" (*nimittalakṣaṇa*) as the object portion (*nimittabhāga*).
Thus, according to the Yogācāra school, this "aspect of karma" is the basis for the arising of all phenomena; however, this is merely [the realm of] birth and cessation.

Regarding this, the *Commentary on the Treatise* (*Lun shu*) further states: "Because that school does not clarify that consciousness and so forth, together with True Suchness (*tathatā*), share a single mind as their source, it asserts that True Suchness is without cognition or awareness, being quiescent and unchanging.

It does not admit that [True Suchness] accords with conditions; rather, it holds that the eight consciousnesses alone serve as the basis for all phenomena. Therefore, the ultimate truth does not produce all phenomena."

Therefore, based on the phenomena of dependent origination involving arising and ceasing, the ālayavijñāna is established. Its essence is discerned from seeds such as karma, and it arises as the retributive maturation consciousness (*vipākavipāka-vijñāna*) which serves as the support for all dharmas.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle four, states: "All minds and mental factors have three supports (*āśraya*). First is the causal support (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*), which refers to their own seeds;
all conditioned phenomena depend upon this support, for they would necessarily not arise were they separated from their own causal conditions.

Second is the dominant support (*adhipati-āśraya*), which refers to the six internal bases (*āyatana*); all minds and mental factors depend upon this support, [for they would not arise] were they separated from their simultaneous faculties (*sahabhū-indriya*)."

Because it certainly does not undergo transformation. Third is the "immediately preceding basis" (*samanantarāśraya*). This refers to all minds and mental factors that take the consciousness which has just ceased as their object;

they must rely upon this basis, for they would necessarily not arise apart from the "opening and guiding" faculty (*vivṛtti-nayanāśraya*). The commentary states: when a faculty and consciousness are simultaneous, they are called "coexistent" (*sahabhū*).
Because the consciousness that has just ceased and so forth are still able to open up and guide what arises subsequently, they are called "opening and guiding. However...

Regarding these three—*āśraya*, *pravṛtti*, and *utpatti*—what are their distinct characteristics? *Āśraya* (basis) refers to the generation [of the body] by way of distinguishing its substance (*svabhāva*) based on the seeds.

*Pravṛtti* (evolution) refers to the conforming [of the body] to [karma], providing the power for it to evolve. *Utpatti* (arising) refers to the opening of a path by what precedes, allowing what follows to arise. Furthermore, it is said:

"If there is karma but no seeds of consciousness, the substance [of experience] cannot be directly distinguished; if there is consciousness but no seeds of karma, suffering and pleasure cannot be summoned. Since this is so...
Because it relies upon these, it is said that [birth] arises from karma and so forth. "Karma" refers to the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*):

the habitual tendency of the *bhava-aṅga* (the link of existence), the habitual tendency of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), and the dual habitual tendencies of names-and-words (*nāma-kāya*) and conventional designations (*prajñapti*). The continuity of birth and death proceeds by means of these various habitual tendencies.

Furthermore, there are generally three types of such habitual tendencies: first, the habitual tendency of names-and-words; second, the habitual tendency of the grasping at a self; and third, the habitual tendency of the *bhava-aṅga*. These are called...
Regarding the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): it refers to the specific, individual seeds of conditioned phenomena. There are two types of "expressive terminology" (*nāma-vyavahāra*):

first, the terminology that expresses meaning, which consists of the distinct vocal sounds capable of denoting an object; second, the terminology that manifests objects, which consists of the cognitive faculty capable of apprehending an object.
The seeds perfumed by the two types of linguistic expression within the mind and mental factors act as the specific causes and conditions for each conditioned phenomenon.
Regarding the "habitual tendencies of the two forms of self-grasping," this refers to the seeds of the false attachment to a self and what belongs to a self. There are two types of self-grasping.
1. Innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*), which is the grasping of "self" and "mine" to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

2. Conceptual self-grasping (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*), which is the grasping of "self" and "mine" to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*). These two types of self-grasping perfume the seeds that bring about the distinctions between self and others among sentient beings. 3.
The habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*), which refers to the seeds of karma that project the maturation (*vipāka*) of the three realms; these are the links of existence.
There are two types: first, contaminated wholesome karma, which is that which can summon desirable fruits; second, all unwholesome karma, which is that which can summon undesirable fruits.
Because karma perfumes the seeds within the two branches of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), it causes the distinction between the ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of the good and evil destinies.
As the verse of the treatise says: "By the habitual tendencies of various karmas, together with the habitual tendencies of the two graspings... [The preceding...]
Once the maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises again. This karma capable of projecting [a new existence] is precisely the karmic habit-energies (*vāsanā*).
If there were no karmic seeds, suffering and pleasure would not be summoned; it is like how a sprout will never grow if there is a seed but no field.

Therefore, these nominal designations (*nāma-kāya*) are induced by karma so that one subsequently experiences the fruit of maturation in the future. Regarding "maturation and so forth," the *Kongmu* states:
The ālayavijñāna, which contains all seeds that are perfumed, is also called the vipākavijñāna and the ādānavijñāna, because it is able to accumulate all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Habitual tendencies refer to the fact that through the activity of the manifest aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, those seeds are all caused to increase.
The "consciousness containing all seeds" refers to that which is capable of producing the aggregates and so forth.
Because it is the accumulation of the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*), the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is so called because it can contain and store the seeds of all phenomena;
furthermore, it is so called because sentient beings grasp it as a self. The *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness) is so called because it is produced by prior karma.
It is the support for all phenomena because the *ālaya* is the fundamental support. All consciousnesses depend upon it universally.
There are only the seven consciousnesses, for all mental factors and other phenomena depend upon them; thus it is said that "all phenomena rely [upon them].
As a skillful means to gradually lead one toward ultimate truth, it is taught that perfuming and so forth are all immediately empty.
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva does not perceive a storehouse nature internally or externally, does not perceive perfuming, and does not perceive the ālaya..."
The ālaya does not perceive the ālayavijñāna; it does not perceive the ādāna, nor does it perceive the ādānavijñāna.

One who can know in this manner is called a bodhisattva. It is up to this point that the Tathāgata establishes the skillful means regarding the secrets of all mind, thought, and consciousness. The same is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth, the *Kongmu* states: "The principle-body is distinguished as being accomplished. It further says:
"One should know that if one wishes to establish the *ālayavijñāna*, it must necessarily be understood as the *tathāgatagarbha* in order for it to be established as a firm and solid basis."
If one merely grasps the characteristics of arising and ceasing, consciousness is identical to the seven dharmas that do not abide; it is not the ultimate refuge.

That [text] refers to the ultimate as returning to the *tathāgatagarbha*, while this is according to the initial teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), and thus it says "gradually leading toward the true principle," and even further, "all are ultimately empty.
This is as explained below regarding "if a bodhisattva," from the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty.
It is said: Because this mind-consciousness is comprised of subtle objects, it is not taught to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the two vehicles;
rather, it is taught for the sake of the Bodhisattvas. There must be a superior station for the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), and therefore the Buddha teaches it.
Why is this? It is impossible that one could attain unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttara-bodhi) apart from this wisdom. If a Bodhisattva...

Regarding the distinctness of the internal and external, those who do not perceive the *ādāna* or *ādāna-vijñāna*, nor the *ālaya* or *ālaya-vijñāna*, [fail to see that] these are all synonymous terms for the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) repeated for emphasis.
The terms *ālaya* and *ālaya-vijñāna* are used in terms of the sense of "that which is stored" (*ālaya*) and "that which stores" (*vijñāna*).
The terms *ādāna* and *ādāna-vijñāna* refer to that which repeatedly causes the production of the marks of existence.
Because it continues to maintain the faculties and so forth so that they do not perish, and because it can accumulate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all phenomena.
Qingliang says: *Ālaya* here means the "store-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*).

It is so called because it can store all factors belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) so that they are not lost, and because it is grasped and stored as one's own internal self by self-view, craving, and so forth. This name applies only to...
Ordinary beings and those in training: *ādāna* (here translated as "grasping") so called because it grasps the seeds and the material sense-faculties;
this name applies to all stages. These two are alternative names for the mind. The Master’s intention is to clarify that the mind contains both the defiled and the pure;
he cites these two names together to explain the meaning of the single mind. What is its meaning? If there is grasping at a self, then...
One achieves the state of *ālaya*. If the grasping at a self (*ātman*) ceases, then the name *ālayavijñāna* is relinquished, and it remains merely as the *ādānavijñāna*.

By sustaining the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), the deluded mind is extinguished and the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) manifests. Thus, a verse says: "If the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted"—this refers to the extinction of the deluded mind.
It does not mean the extinction of the essence of mind; rather, it refers to the Bodhisattva. "Bodhisattva" serves to distinguish [him] from those who are not [true] Śrāvakas.

It is heard that for Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as for Tathāgatas, the establishment of mind, mentation, and consciousness does not rely equally upon the wisdom of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"In this way, Bodhisattvas are skilled in the secret [of mind, mentation, and consciousness] by relying upon and establishing themselves through the wisdom of the stability of phenomena; however, all Tathāgatas do not rely equally upon this."
The detailed establishment of mind, thought, consciousness, and so forth is fully set forth in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun).

The commentary explains: since these [terms] are established as skillful means for the mind and thought at points such as "not seeing" and so on, the characteristics of the ālayavijñāna as being subject to arising and ceasing are all of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).
This is to prevent one from grasping them literally; therefore, they are to be reconciled [with the ultimate truth].
It is indeed so.
Therefore, that which follows—namely, the accomplishment of the preceding marks—is the mark of arising and ceasing produced from karma and other factors.

All of these, as indicated by the heading, merely distinguish the principle of the mutual production of cause and effect within the cycle of birth and death; they are all transformations of the principle.

The gates lack true reality; therefore, it is said that they converge upon the ultimate truth, clarifying that they are immediately empty. There are two gates in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*):
the accomplishment of characteristics corresponds to the initial gate, while the accomplishment of principle corresponds to the final gate.
If one relies on the Final Teaching (Jōgyō), within this ālayavijñāna one attains the meaning of the two aspects—the integration of principle and phenomena.

If one relies on the [Equal] Teaching, it is because this teaching explains that the Tathāgatagarbha does not maintain its own nature, but follows conditions to become the ālaya, or is called the āliya;
these are merely differences in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit sounds. And as for the ālaya...
Ignorance and the seven consciousnesses coexist together, like the waves of the great ocean, which are constantly uninterrupted;

as the Śrīmālā-sūtra says, "being unstained yet stained, and stained yet unstained," and as the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra says, "the defiled dharmas of the seven consciousnesses constitute birth and cessation."
Because the pure dharmas of the *tathāgatagarbha* are non-arising and non-ceasing, and these two are conjoined to form the *ālayavijñāna*, the principle and the phenomena are thus interfused.
Therefore, the treatise simply states that the non-arising and non-ceasing conjoin with the arising and ceasing; being neither identical nor different, it is called the *ālaya*.
The *ālaya-vijñāna*.

That which is neither arising nor ceasing is the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure mind; because its activity and its arising-and-ceasing are inseparable, they are said to be "in union" (*saṃyukta*).
That it is "neither identical nor different" means that as the entirety of *tathatā* moves, the mind and the arising-and-ceasing [are likewise inseparable].
Cessation is not different [from arising], yet because its true nature is eternally unchanging, it is not identical to arising and ceasing.

This meaning of the non-identity between arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing is such that, apart from this mind, there is nothing else. Designating these two meanings, the non-dual mind is called the *ālayavijñāna*.

Because it is admitted that True Suchness (tathatā), through the process of being perfumed and harmoniously combined, constitutes this fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna); it is not produced from seeds such as karma, as taught in previous doctrines. The *Kongmu* states:
"The ālaya-vijñāna, by virtue of being perfumed, must possess four qualities to be capable of receiving perfuming: first, firmness—meaning it is 'firm' because its principle is real;
second, the state of being indeterminate (avyākṛta)—only in this sense can it receive perfuming. Why? Because that which is indeterminate is precisely [free from]..."

Regarding the meaning of "discrimination": it is only within the *tathāgatagarbha* that this dharma exists. Third, as for being "susceptible to perfuming" (*vāsya*), only the *tathāgatagarbha* does not maintain its own nature;
because it arises in accordance with the conditions of all dharmas to manifest as semblance-objects, it is susceptible to perfuming.

Fourth, as for "being associated with the perfumer" (*vāsaka*), only the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses the capacity to correspond to the meanings of all dharmas, whereas other dharmas lack this. Why is this so?
Therefore, because it does not maintain its own nature, it can be perfumed. Furthermore, there are four meanings of "that which perfumes": first, pure phenomena are called *tathatā* (suchness);
second, all causes of defilement are called *avidyā* (ignorance); third, the deluded mind is called the *karmic consciousness*;
and fourth, deluded objects, namely the six sense-fields. As for the meaning of "perfuming," it is like clothing in the world.
In reality, there is no fragrance; yet because a person is perfumed by fragrance, the scent arises.
Similarly, the pure dharma of *tathatā* is in reality free from defilement, but because it is perfumed by ignorance, the characteristics of defilement arise. Chengguan (Qingliang) says:

"Now, in the Dharma-nature school (*Faxing zong*), the seven consciousnesses and so forth act as the perfuming agents (*nengxun*), while the eighth consciousness acts as the object perfumed (*suoxun*)."

Within the eighth consciousness, the *tathāgatagarbha* is established according to conditions; because it contains both the meanings of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing, when the eighth consciousness is perfumed, it is truly the *tathatā* (Suchness) that is perfumed.
Regarding the four characteristics of what is perfumed according to the *lakṣaṇa-vāda* school: first, the quality of stable persistence.
If a phenomenon continues as a single, uniform stream from beginning to end and is capable of sustaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is that which is perfumed. Second, non-...
The nature of being a receptacle for memory: if a phenomenon is impartial and not subject to contradiction, and is capable of receiving habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is that which is perfumed.
Third, the nature of being susceptible to perfuming: if a phenomenon is sovereign in nature and not solid or dense, and is capable of containing habitual tendencies, it is that which is perfumed.

Fourth, it possesses the nature of being in mutual conjunction with the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*). That which is simultaneous with and co-spatial to the perfuming agent, yet is neither identical to nor separate from it, is the perfumable (*bhāvyatva*).
The perfuming agent also possesses four characteristics: first, it undergoes arising and ceasing; second, it possesses superior efficacy.

Third, there is increase and decrease; fourth, it evolves in conjunction with that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*). However, according to the *lakṣaṇavāda* (Dharmalakṣaṇa) school, the ālayavijñāna is exclusively subject to arising and ceasing.
