because it is in total darkness regarding all aspects, it is called "ignorance. This refers to the delusions regarding phenomena within and outside the realms; one cultivates the eight [knowledges] to counteract them.
Regarding the "Victorious Liberations" (*vimokṣa*), the *Kongmu* (Outline) states: There are eight liberations, also called "reversal liberations" (*prātikūlya-vimokṣa*).

These are: first, possessing internal form while perceiving external forms; second, being without internal form while perceiving external forms; third, the liberation-sphere of the body-witness of purity; fourth, the sphere of infinite space;
fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the cessation of perception and feeling.

Regarding the eight stages of the realization of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-sākṣātkriyā-āyatana*): the first three are called "liberation" because they turn away from afflictions;

the next four are called "liberation" because they turn away from the lower stages; and the final one is called "liberation" because it turns away from the mind that takes conditioned existence as its object.

Furthermore, regarding these eight liberations, the interpretation here differs from that of the Hīnayāna; according to the intent of Mahāyāna sūtras, one contemplates form and realizes emptiness, and by being unimpeded, one accomplishes form—this is what is meant here.

The meaning of the text is as follows: First, liberation is the relinquishing of the characteristics of defiled form; second, the relinquishing of form and mind; third, the accomplishment of non-obstruction regarding form;
fourth, the relinquishing of the perception of emptiness; fifth, the relinquishing of the grasping of consciousness and ideation;

sixth, the removal of residual consciousness and ideation; seventh, the removal of the grasping of the ideation of meditative concentration; eighth, the removal of the attainment and relinquishing of meditative concentration.
Regarding "lack of mastery" and so forth:

furthermore, all liberations are manifested by liberation from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have attained liberation from the cognitive obstructions.

Regarding the statement that "the cognitive obstacle (jñeyāvaraṇa) is not an obstacle to what is known, yet it is an obstacle because it obstructs what is known": this obstacle is fundamental ignorance (*mūlavidyā*), which can obstruct this principle;

the essence of the principle itself is not an obstacle. When it says "liberation of mind" (*cittavimukti*) and "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñāvimukti*), it clearly explains liberation from the two obstacles.
If the term "liberation" were merely empty words, and one did not point to the mind or to wisdom, what dharma would be liberated?
If one were to speak merely of liberation from the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it would not specifically identify the nature of the phenomena being obstructed.
Now, however, it is said that these hinder the mind and hinder wisdom, thereby preventing liberation.

Although the two hindrances are distinguished as coarse and subtle based on whether they pertain to the mind or to the object, the seeds of both hindrances are only exhausted upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, each can mutually obstruct the other.
It should be understood that this Initial Teaching (śāstra) is established in order to lead those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant gradually toward the Great Vehicle;
because this teaching is profound and superior to that [Hīnayāna], it is also admitted that the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are partially severed.
However, what has been severed above differs from the "Dharma of the Ignorant" (bāla-dharma), because the latter severs only the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions, whereas this [path] does not;
rather, it severs the seeds.

This merely distinguishes between the Great and Lesser Vehicles; as for the Lesser Vehicle, it involves contemplating the eight truths in their ascending and descending order, such as the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), and so forth.

The sixteen moments of mind consist of eight patiences (*kṣānti*), which are called the "uninterrupted paths" (*ānantarya-mārga*) because they are capable of severing the delusions regarding the principles underlying the eight truths.
Because these eight patiences are not interrupted by the acquisition of delusion (*kleśaprāpti*), they are termed "uninterrupted.

This means that although the substance of the delusions no longer manifests, even though their acquisition still exists, it lacks functional power and does not constitute an obstacle. The eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are called the "paths of liberation" (*vimukti-mārga*).

The path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is able to realize the unconditioned principle (*asamskṛta-dharma*) underlying the eight truths; therefore, these eight knowledges (*jñāna*), having already become free from the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*), are called "liberation.
In the Mahāyāna, this refers specifically to the severance of the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Regarding the Bodhisattva of Direct Progress who severs delusions, both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are severed simultaneously.

The *Kongmu* states: "If, within the sūtras and śāstras, the specific ignorance (*avidyā*) is revealed according to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) without distinguishing between coarse and subtle, these all fall under the 'Direct Progress' teaching within the Initial Teaching (*śrāvaka-piṭaka*). Why? Because it accords with the sudden [realization] at the final mind of the tenth stage."
Because they sever all delusions.
Furthermore, within the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they differ from the two vehicles in their classification by realm and category;
they differ from the ignorant Hīnayāna in their distinct severance of the ignorance of the views and meditations across the three realms and nine stages.

However, regarding those [afflictions] arising from conceptual discrimination within the two obstructions, their active manifestations are suppressed prior to the stages; then, at the moment of the first stage’s true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), their seeds are severed instantaneously.

That is to say, during the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra*) and preparation (*prayoga*) prior to the stages, the active manifestations of both obstructions are suppressed, and upon ascending to the stages, [the seeds are severed].
Because the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is realized, the seeds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-bīja*) are suddenly severed.
Regarding the innate afflictive obscurations (*sahaja-kleśāvaraṇa*), from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they can be severed at will; yet why are they not severed?

It is because [the Bodhisattvas] sustain rebirth to gather and transform sentient beings, so as not to fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and in order to sever the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because one attains great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

As determined in the *Śata-śāstra*, the conceptualized view of self (*parikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*);
since [this innate view] is retained here, it is not abandoned, as its function is to abandon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) and so forth.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "By retaining the afflictions until they are exhausted, one realizes the Buddha’s omniscience.

The commentary explains that "the exhaustion of afflictions" refers to the exhaustion of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Thus, by retaining the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) while initiating superior practices, one reaches this stage and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

The *Śāstra* states: "Afflictions are suppressed so that they do not arise, like poison neutralized by a mantra; one retains these delusions until they are exhausted, thereby realizing the Buddha’s omniscience.
The *Kongmu* states: "All Bodhisattvas retain their latent propensities (*anuśaya*) as factors that assist the Path, which differs from the Two Vehicles who enter parinirvāṇa too quickly.
For this reason, when the path of cultivation is perfected, the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) are completely extinguished."
Thus one realizes perfect wisdom.

Furthermore, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states: "Since it is said that the seeds are retained, one should know that the seeds of the afflictive hindrances persist until the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi."
Because the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) have not yet been permanently severed within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), those seeds are retained in order to take birth.
Since the aspects of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are subtle, they directly obstruct the path of the bodhisattva; therefore, they must be severed stage by stage.
Only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood can they be completely exhausted.

Regarding the severance of obstacles at each stage: on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one severs the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*); on the second stage, one severs the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti*).

Because these are the primary obstacles to the wisdom that obstructs the Bodhisattva path, they are ultimately exhausted only upon reaching the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
From this, it can be understood that both obstacles—the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations—are abandoned together up until the stage of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya states: "Furthermore, throughout the path of cultivation in the ten stages, Bodhisattvas cultivate only the [removal of] the cognitive obscurations."

The path that serves as the antidote to the hindrances does not eliminate the afflictive hindrances; rather, at the moment one attains bodhi, one simultaneously eliminates both the afflictive hindrances and the cognitive hindrances, thereby suddenly becoming an arhat and a Tathāgata.
In the stage of the Bodhisattva’s path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates the antidotes to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) for the purpose of retaining the delusions;
these continue until the adamantine concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), at which point they are severed. The present explanation is made from the perspective of the exhaustion of both obscurations.
Because the mental concomitants (*ākāra*) that arise simultaneously with the manas are subtle, they likewise persist until the attainment of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).

However, the manas itself is associated with the four proclivities (*anuśaya*)— the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), self-love (*ātmasneha*), and ignorance (*avidyā*)—
and it persists until the Buddha-ground is reached before finally ceasing.

Question: Regarding the two obstacles, what are the similarities and differences between the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and their manifestation in the various consciousnesses on the stages (*bhūmi*)?
As for the "various consciousnesses," how do the similarities and differences regarding the sixth and seventh consciousnesses correspond to those on the stages?
The answer is: because the delusions of the sixth consciousness within the afflictive hindrances have already been exhausted, those [afflictions] are retained.
Therefore, both the manifest and the seeds are governed by wisdom; they are employed to accomplish supreme practice without giving rise to faults or calamities.

This is just as a venomous snake is controlled by the power of mantras so that it does not die, yet its remaining functions are not obstructed from arising. The Bodhisattva’s skillful retention of afflictions is likewise.

The *Śāstra* states: "All afflictions have already been extinguished and suppressed, as if neutralized by a poison-antidote. The commentary explains: This verse clarifies the eleventh [topic], the extinction of afflictions.
Regarding these profound afflictions—namely, the afflictions of seeing and cultivation—they have already been completely extinguished within the stages of a Bodhisattva.
Although the remaining mental afflictions have not yet been extinguished, they are suppressed by mindfulness and wisdom, rendering their functional power ineffective.
For example, just as various poisons are neutralized by the power of a mantra so that they no longer possess their original potency, so too it is with the delusions of the mind:
when guarded by wisdom and mindfulness, the two types of defiled delusions can no longer arise.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Just as poison is neutralized by a mantra," and so forth. Thus, one should know that regarding those afflictions, whether manifest...
Alternatively, all seeds attain mastery.
The treatise states: "From affliction to the exhaustion of afflictions, one realizes the Buddha’s omniscience.

If these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not eliminated, one's desire would be identical to that of the two vehicles' *nirvāṇa*; if the manifest desires (*paryavasthāna*) are not removed, one would not differ from ordinary beings."
The seventh consciousness, being of the nature of affliction, does not moisten rebirth; its objective aspect is subtle and thus is not what is retained [in the cessation of meditative attainment].
It manifests temporarily from the seventh stage onward, because the wisdom of contemplation is intermittent.

Why is it that at the initial stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the manas is immediately extinguished? It is because it obstructs the realization of the principle of selflessness (*anātman*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "By transforming the defiled manas, one attains the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*)."
The cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) all arise either in subsequent stages, or they arise in preceding stages, whether as manifest states or as seeds,

because they are severed stage by stage. Just as the obstructions severed in the tenth stage are severed in the ninth stage, and so on, down to the obstructions of the first stage being severed prior to that stage.
[This is] excluded.
Question: If that is so, why is it stated in some places that one may give rise to impure (*sāsrava*) minds and so forth from the seventh stage downward?
Since it is said that [defilements] are severed stage by stage, how can this lower objection not be contradictory?

Answer: If one considers the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the sixth consciousness to be "outflowing" (*sāsrava*), they are "as if outflowing" because those [Bodhisattvas] intentionally retain the afflictions;
if one considers the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) to be outflowing, they are "actually outflowing. These two categories both pervade the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the six consciousnesses and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—these two pervade all ten stages (*bhūmi*), differing only in being "semblance" or "actual," and both are exhausted upon reaching the tenth stage.
As for the afflictions of the *manas*, they are actual outflows (*sāsrava*); their presence or absence is indeterminate up to the seventh stage, as there are times when they exist.
Because a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) may arise for a brief moment, the remaining points should be understood by analogy.

In the seven stages, such [contaminated] insight-wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) may temporarily arise because it is weak; however, in the eighth stage, it does not arise spontaneously due to the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*).

Furthermore, regarding the limits of the cessation of afflictions and the arising of wisdom within this teaching: when the seeds of affliction are in the state of cessation, wisdom is simultaneously in the state of arising;
these two states are mutually exclusive, like "rising" being "falling" and "falling" being "rising," as explained at length in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

The treatise examines the sequence of the four characteristics regarding the question of whether the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) first arises and the defilements are subsequently extinguished, or whether the defilements are first extinguished and the path subsequently arises, or whether they occur simultaneously.

In each of these three cases involving the defilements and the wisdom, there are two faults that fail to establish the meaning of "abandonment": namely, if the wisdom were to arise first, it would entail the error of being spontaneously uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) without cause.

[If it is argued that] because delusion has already ceased, there is no fault of [the wisdom] being unable to extinguish delusion; [this is not so,] for even when wisdom arises, delusion still persists, and thus there is the fault that delusion extinguishes itself spontaneously (since the preceding moment of wisdom has arisen while delusion remains, its subsequent cessation would be a spontaneous self-extinction).

Furthermore, there is the fault of not obstructing the Noble Path (because it would cause wisdom to arise first). Wisdom—whether arising subsequently or simultaneously—is subject to these four faults in each case.
Regarding both wisdom and delusion, two faults are stated for each; the names of the faults are the same as before, though their meanings differ.
These are explained as occurring either subsequent to wisdom or simultaneously; when combined with the characteristics of what is known by the mind, they collectively constitute twelve faults.

If this is so, how are they severed? The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When the two true paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifest, the seeds of those two obstacles are necessarily no longer established.
(The "two truths" refer to the truth of the two vehicles and the truth of the Bodhisattva; hence, "two truths. This is like the relationship between light and darkness.
Concentration and [its opposite] do not arise simultaneously, just as the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale occur at different times;
this must necessarily be so according to the principle that mutually contradictory phenomena cannot coexist. Therefore, there is no fault of the two natures being established together.

This merely cites one aspect of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and does not contradict the meaning of cessation through the gathering of other conditions. Some texts read "ya" (押) for "qióng" (笻) and "qióng" for "ya," which are errors.

Furthermore, because these obstructing dharmas rely upon the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of consciousness, they are empty and non-conceptual; this constitutes their meaning as obstructions.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "To penetrate the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as empty and without arising is the meaning of suffering. One should understand that the meaning of the obstructions here is likewise based on that.

Because the Śūnyatā school of the Initial Teaching (śīkṣā) reveals that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth are empty, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The mind (*citta*) is like a stage performer; the intellect (*manas*) is like the assistant;
the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are like the companions; and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is like the audience watching the performance.

Based on this scriptural passage, although one knows these are consciousnesses, one still cannot avoid conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). To prove the point regarding the nature of suffering as an obstruction, [the text] now cites the chapter of Kātyāyana.
That emptiness is the meaning of true suffering is the final gate of the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching).
If one relies on the Final Teaching, even the various Śrāvakas cannot yet sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but can only suppress them;
how much less could they sever the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?

The Mahāyāna Final Teaching explains in a profound and subtle manner that one is not permitted to transcend the realm [of saṃsāra]; it merely suppresses the active manifestations of the afflictions (*kleśa*) without eliminating their seeds.
How much less could it eliminate the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
Therefore, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* on the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā* states: "No Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can [perceive] things as they truly are."
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states, as mentioned above, that practicing the four immeasurables cannot ultimately sever all afflictions, but can only suppress them.
This means that the practices and fruits of the two vehicles are not true; they are not practiced according to reality, and thus are not true.

They do not constitute the ultimate fruit of cessation, and thus are not true. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Those who relish the bliss of samādhi and dwell in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) are like a person who is intoxicated;
only after the wine has worn off do they awaken. It is said that those of the two vehicles who have attained nirvāṇa have not attained it ultimately."
Question: For what reason does this teaching differ from the previous one? Answer:

Because in the Initial Teaching (Śākyadeśanā), there is a specific school that asserts that those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant (bāla-dharmika) must sever all afflictions (kleśa) to transcend the realm [of existence], whereas they only partially sever the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa).

Now, since even the teachings of the *de facto* (provisional) vehicle have not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), how much less could they sever the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*)? This question arises because the two teachings differ.

The answer is: those [teachings] were intended to lead in the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and did not provide a profound exposition; therefore, it is said that the higher [truth] addresses the lower by way of the afflictions.
The obstacles are the same as those of the two vehicles; they are only exhausted upon reaching the wisdom of the Buddha-ground.

Furthermore, as mentioned above, it is also accepted that the two vehicles completely sever the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and partially sever the obstacle to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). However, according to the ultimate truth, because the two vehicles of those who follow the Dharma of ignorance lack the vast mind, they do not exhaustively sever the obstacle of afflictions.

The Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching (Shijiao) also state that afflictions must be suddenly severed at the final moment of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), and they further allow that Śrāvakas completely sever the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and so forth.

Now, this [text] speaks according to the ultimate reality in its subtle and profound sense, asserting that none of these can be called the ultimate transcendence of the triple world or the complete severance of afflictions.
Some claim that in the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), there is no perception of the mode of action for the two vehicles’ severance of afflictions; however, this is not the case.

Since the teachings have coarse and subtle aspects, because the capacities of those previously addressed were coarse, this teaching had to appear similar to the Lesser Vehicle. Yet, as this teaching is profound and superior, it does not rely on such similarity;

for is the Lotus Sūtra’s parable of the burning house, which uses the three carts to entice the children, not itself the true teaching regarding the characteristics of the practice of the Three Vehicles?

Furthermore, it may also be said that the former was based on the Śrāvaka within the context of the Three Vehicles, whereas this [latter] is based on those of "deluded dharma" (fo-fa), and thus they differ.

This is because while the previous two teachings both spoke in terms of deluded dharma, these current two teachings differ: the Initial Teaching (shi-jiao) refers to the two vehicles among the three, while this Final Teaching (zhong-jiao) refers to the two vehicles of deluded dharma;
yet if the Final Teaching were to speak in terms of the Three Vehicles, it would refer to the Śrāvaka.

This is also like the various treatises: if the Initial Teaching (śikṣā) is defined according to the meaning of the "Dharma for the Ignorant" (*mūrkha-dharma*), it is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus, these two teachings emerge interchangeably.

Regarding those who are Bodhisattvas, among the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), they do not distinguish between the innate (*sahaja*) and the discriminative (*vikalpita*), but only recognize the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*); the active afflictions (*anuśaya*) are severed at the first stage; the seeds of the active afflictions are eliminated from the second stage onward;

and the habitual tendencies are finally purified at the Buddha-stage. Regarding the term "active afflictions" (*anuśaya*): it is like a public official’s messenger who follows a person and compels them to be bound; therefore, they are called "active afflictions."
Regarding the statement that this permeates both obstacles, "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refers to the perfumed latencies; as the *Kongmu* states, there are broadly two kinds:
first, the perfuming of seeds, and second, the perfuming of manifest mental states (*udbhūta-citta*).
However, during the stage of the three types of worthy ones prior to that bhūmi, they do not initially fall into the stages of the two vehicles;

rather, they possess mastery over the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and can sever them as they wish, yet they do not sever them [immediately] because they intend to retain them for the purpose of eliminating the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Although one suppresses the active manifestations of the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), because their seeds remain, one does not fall into the level of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Therefore, the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that from the "Ten Understandings" (*daśajñāna*) onward, one attains supramundane pure mind;

it further states that those with a mind above the "Ten Understandings" are called "sages" (*ārya*) because they do not fall into the level of the two vehicles. Thus, the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing) says that before the stages, one attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, not realizing [the fruit] prematurely, as well as the passage in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* stating that one attains a partial realization of the Dharmakāya and manifests the eight signs,
are all of this same meaning;
this should be understood.

Because these Bodhisattvas fear only the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they cultivate the contemplations on consciousness-only, suchness, and so forth, to suppress and sever those obstructions.

Regarding the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), however, they not only do not fear them nor cultivate remedies for them, but intentionally retain them to assist in accomplishing superior practices.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, because a portion of the coarse cognitive obstructions has been severed, they no longer [fear] the afflictive obstructions.
Furthermore, for this reason, the two obstacles are not distinguished as being [exclusively] of the path of seeing or the path of cultivation.

The obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstructs the attainment of *bodhi*; its antidote consists of the contemplation of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the perfected nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*), which is the contemplation of principle, while the contemplation of the phenomena of consciousness is the contemplation of facts.
However, regarding the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they are retained [in the path of cultivation] in order to accomplish their superior function.
Upon reaching the first bhūmi, the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of both obstacles are completely exhausted.
As for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they gradually diminish stage by stage until, at the ultimate limit of the vajra-like samādhi,
they are finally and utterly eliminated.

Therefore, the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra* states: Question: If a śrāvaka first severs the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and subsequently gradually severs the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), why is the bodhisattva not the same as the śrāvaka? Answer:
Because for immeasurable lifetimes, the bodhisattva has performed deeds to benefit all sentient beings, and only thereafter realizes suchness (*tathatā*).
Contemplating the nectar-like Dharma-realm, one sees that the bodies of all those sentient beings are in reality no different from the locus sought by oneself;

therefore, because all afflictions that obstruct the bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting sentient beings must be abandoned simultaneously within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), this text serves as the proof.

Question: Regarding the Final Teaching (Jiǒngjiào), it states that even the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) [are exhausted]; why then does it cite afflictions such as those associated with the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) as evidence?
Answer: Although the names of the afflictive hindrances differ between these two teachings, their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the same; therefore, they may serve as mutual evidence.

As for the *Kǒngmù* (Pivot) section on the "Dense Forest of Active Afflictions" (*paryavasthāna*), passages such as these all belong to the Initial Teaching (*shǐjiào*). Now, we shall explain the Final Teaching.

Why does the *Jiao* (Teaching) cite the following passage? It states that "the meaning should be understood as applying to the matured teachings (*yì dāng shú jiào*), and these divisions may also be applied to the direct-advancement teachings (*zhí jìn jiào*) within the Initial Teaching (*chū jiào*).

Regarding the afflictions of the *manas*, they are severed in their coarse form at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), while their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are eliminated later; thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asaṅga says:

When the defiled *manas* is transformed and the Wisdom of Equality is attained, at the time of the initial clear observation (*abhisamaya*), one has already realized this during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is said that "transforming the pure" means the elimination of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), because the fundamental afflictions (*anuśaya*) have already been severed previously;
therefore, later it is only called "transforming the pure" and no longer mentioned as being "severed."

Regarding the statement "the wisdom of initial contemplation manifests at the beginning of the path of seeing for those of no-nature (niḥsvabhāva)," it must first be understood that this refers to what is realized within the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) for the purpose of eliminating habitual tendencies (vāsanā).

If one were to claim that this is merely a temporary non-arising during the entry into the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not a definitive abandonment, then one could not say [that it eliminates habitual tendencies].

Regarding the statement that [the path] becomes further purified: if it has not been completely severed as a whole, how can it be called "purified"? According to the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna), this may be as stated there;

however, even if one claims that the afflictions are suppressed by the Path of Seeing rather than being correctly severed, one must be refuted by saying that it cannot be called "purified" because they have not been completely severed as a whole.
This point is permitted according to the aforementioned teaching (the Mahāyāna).
Therefore, one should know that according to this teaching, those on the stages (bhūmi) merely eliminate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). As the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:

"The 'impure' refers to all ordinary beings who possess the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*); the 'stained' refers to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others who possess the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
and the 'cleansed' refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others who rely upon those two kinds of habitual tendencies."

Regarding the phrase "due to the obstacle of habit-energy" (*vāsanā-āvaraṇa*), the *Śāstra* commentary explains that because those on the stages (*bhūmi*) are called *mahāsattvas*, we know there is only the obstacle of habit-energy.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "The 'impure' refers to ordinary beings who possess the obstacle of delusion (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*); the 'stained' refers to..."
Because the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others possess cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they have "stains" (*mala*);

because bodhisattvas possess the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of these two obstructions, this chapter refers to them as "clever" (*jia*). It is feared that "stained" (*dian*) was a scribal error for "clever" (*jia*).
In this context, the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) arise immediately after the seeds of the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have been severed.

Why is this? Because prior to their severance, they do not exist in a subtle or attenuated state; it is only upon the immediate cessation of the seeds that they become subtle and attenuated. Therefore, the treatise describes them as "habitual tendencies arising without interval" (*anantara-utpanna-vāsanā*).

Before the stages (*bhūmi*), one abandons the seeds of those proclivities (*anuśaya*) and their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*); on the stages themselves, one eliminates the residual impressions (*vāsanā*). Regarding the categories of these residual impressions, it is said there are three types:

first, the impression of names (*nāma-vāsanā*) and the impression of consciousness (*vijñāna-vāsanā*); second, the impression of form-consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna-vāsanā*), the impression of object-consciousness (*viṣaya-vijñāna-vāsanā*), and the impression of view-consciousness (*dṛṣṭi-vijñāna-vāsanā*);
third, the impression of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*), the impression of karma (*karma-vāsanā*), and the impression of maturation (*vipāka-vāsanā*). These are as follows:
The perfuming (vāsanā) permeates all categories: the defiled, the pure, and the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Question: If the afflictions and latent tendencies (anuśaya) are exhausted on the stages (bhūmi), why does one not fall into the level of the Two Vehicles?

In the Initial Teaching (ādikarmika-yāna), it is said that because one retains the afflictions, one does not fall; but in the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-yāna), since the seeds of the afflictions are exhausted, why does one still not fall?

Answer: Because their power of wisdom is superior and because even the active afflictions (anuśaya) that obstruct wisdom have already been eliminated, they do not fall [back] now, as two reasons for this are presented in the True Teaching (*saddharma*).

For example, when a person who has attained immediate departure according to the Initial Teaching of the Hīnayāna exhausts the sixth grade of afflictions of the desire realm, regarding the upper two realms...
Since the six categories [of afflictions] are likewise severed and exhausted, one still cannot yet attain the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Now, taking the three [categories] within the Lesser Vehicle as an example, *Chai-xuan* says: "In the Mahāyāna, the two vehicles may have sudden transcendence, but in the Lesser Vehicle there is not.

Having severed the eighty-eight *kleśas* of discrimination during the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), one proceeds to sever the six [categories] of innate [afflictions] (*sahaja*) during the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
If those who cultivate the afflictions of the stages still do not realize the two fruits,

how much less so this Bodhisattva, whose power on the path is exceptionally superior, and all the more so because he has already severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
While such a fault may possibly exist for those prior to the stages or in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*), it does not exist here.
In this context, because the bodhisattva simultaneously abandons both obstacles, he does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles.

Furthermore, in this teaching, when delusions are correctly severed, wisdom arises and delusions perish; since they are not grasped as being prior, intermediate, or posterior, nor as having a prior, intermediate, or posterior sequence, how are they extinguished?
They are extinguished like space, which is originally pure. This extinction is explained in detail in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

In the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*), it is said: "Neither beginning, nor middle, nor end. Regarding this passage, the *Tanxuanji* (Probing the Profundities) provides two interpretive approaches: first, the approach of mutual exclusion based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-viparyāsa-mukha*);

second, the approach of continuity based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-saṃtati-mukha*). This means that the arising and ceasing of the wisdom of this stage continues through the preceding, middle, and [subsequent] moments.
When, then, can the final three moments definitely sever the afflictions? It is not the first moment alone that can sever them, because it has already passed away.

It is not the last moment alone that can sever them, because it has not yet arisen. Nor can the middle moment sever them, because it does not abide. Therefore, in all three times, there is no sense of severance.
If this is so, how are they severed? The treatise states: "It is like a lamp flame; it is not [severed] by [any single part] alone."
Because one grasps [the object] at the beginning, middle, and end, or at the beginning and middle, or the middle and end, this is merely the "middle" [moment];
it cannot constitute a cessation. If there were a continuous grasping of the preceding, middle, and subsequent moments, then the sense of cessation could exist. [The opponent asks:

Since grasping each of the three times individually does not result in cessation, even if these were combined, how could cessation be established? It is like a single grain of sand having no oil; even many grains of sand have none. How, then, can there be cessation?

Because the nature of offenses is empty and fundamentally pure, this definitive teaching necessarily clarifies both their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to sever delusions.

Furthermore, within this teaching, all phenomena such as afflictions (*kleśa*) are the manifestations of True Suchness (*tathatā*) through the conditioning of conditions; therefore, they are not different from it.

Suchness (*tathatā*) has the meaning of affliction (*kleśa*), as explained in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*. Furthermore, a sutra states that "all phenomena are precisely suchness," and so forth;

afflictions are to be understood according to this. Therefore, one should know that this differs from the provisional designations found in the aforementioned various teachings; this point should be properly understood.
Regarding "afflictions are themselves suchness": in the Initial Teaching (Shijiao), all karmas are empty and thus cannot be differentiated;
in the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), they are suchness, for all dharmas are likewise suchness.
Second, the clarification of the stages by means of relying on delusions refers to the eighteen categories briefly mentioned in the holy teachings.
By entrusting the delusions to reveal the stages, this is the "Kongmu" (Catalogue) which, by means of the stages, clarifies the afflictions;

through various teachings, the coarse and subtle categories of delusion are clearly elucidated, briefly listed as eighteen, as explained at length in the *Sakalasaṃprayukta-saṃyojana-gahana-vyūha* (The Thicket of Latent Tendencies).

First, by relying on the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) to reveal the two stages: that is, by distinguishing between the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one reveals these two stages of realization.

The *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Before the stages (*bhūmi*), one gradually eliminates the obstacle of afflictions; from the stages onward, one gradually eliminates the obstacle to knowledge. It further states:

"From the stage of ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward, one attains the supramundane pure mind. And it also states: "Although one attains the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) before the stages, regarding phenomena (*dharma*)," [one does not yet fully realize it].

Because the selflessness of persons has not yet been purified, the person's selflessness is likewise impure. Furthermore, it is said that the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) was already eliminated during the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-nirvedha-bhāgīya*);
now, one merely extinguishes the grasping at a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman*). The *Ratna-rāja-sūtra* states:

"The stage of the nature of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*) has already entered the position of emptiness regarding living beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), because one has attained the nature of a noble being (*ārya-gotra*). The *Mūla-karma-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* also speak in this same way.

If, within the teachings of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), the severance of delusions necessarily involves the simultaneous clarification of both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then we know that the present case—

where the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are removed by the inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are removed by the realized knowledge (*sākṣāt-kriyā-jñāna*) on the stages—

is a provisional manifestation rather than actual severance. The cited sūtras and śāstras establish that one attains the mundane mind prior to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), while those of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-vidha-satpuruṣa*) attain the supramundane mind on the stages.

Because one attains the supramundane mind at the stage of the Three Worthies (*tri-piṭaka*) within the *Śikṣā-bīja-gotra* (the lineage of the seeds of training) in the *Renwang jing*; because one attains the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) in the *Gotra-bhūmi* (the lineage stage); and because one attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) on the stages (*bhūmi*).

Second, by means of the three delusions likened to the skin and so forth, the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are manifested; as the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one severs the skin."
The afflictions of the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa are severed; the afflictions of flesh are severed in the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa; and the afflictions of the mind are severed.
Regarding the metaphor of the skin and so forth, the *Kongmu* states: "Afflictions that are innate (*sahaja*) are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This metaphorically assigns the afflictions to the categories of seeing and cultivation, corresponding to the three afflictions of skin, flesh, and mind: the afflictions of the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa sever the skin, and those of the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa sever [the flesh].
The meaning of "flesh" and so forth is analogous.
Third, by means of these three delusions, the differences among the three types of mind in each stage (*bhūmi*) are illustrated;

as stated in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, within each stage there is the "entering mind" which removes the skin, the "abiding mind" which removes the flesh, and the "emerging mind" which removes the heart.

Regarding the phrase "thirty-three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*": the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) themselves comprise three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, while the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) comprise thirty *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

A treatise states that within each stage there are three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, referring to the entry (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and emergence (*niṣkramaṇa*). This is the explanation provided in the commentary.
It is said that one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) to eliminate the afflictive hindrances of the skin; one dwells in the first stage to eliminate the afflictive hindrances of the flesh;
and one emerges from the first stage to eliminate the afflictive hindrances of the mind, and so forth.
Fourth, the coarse and subtle aspects of the two obstacles are correlated with three stages, as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "The two obstacles pertain to three locations, namely:
before the stages (*bhūmi*), on the stages, and the Buddha-stage.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* correlates the coarse and subtle aspects of the afflictive and cognitive obstacles with these three stages, assigning the abandonment of the coarse afflictions of the two obstacles to the stage prior to the [ten] stages.
Because they constitute direct obstacles to arising upon the stages (*bhūmi*), the subtle afflictions of the two obstacles are abandoned at the time of entering the stages;
because they constitute direct obstacles from the seventh stage downward, the extremely subtle afflictions of the two obstacles are abandoned at the time of entering the eighth stage;

and because they constitute direct obstacles from the Buddha-stage downward, they are abandoned at the time of entering the Buddha-stage. These three positions are thus presented for illustrative purposes.
Fifth, the coarse and subtle aspects of the defiled mind are mapped onto three stages to reveal the three bodies, as explained in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:

by relying on the path of suppression (*vibhava-mārga*), when the arising of the active mind (*pravṛtti-citta*) is exhausted, the nirmāṇakāya is revealed; by relying on the path of abandonment according to the dharma (*dharmaprahāṇa-mārga*), when the fundamental mind (*mūla-citta*) is exhausted, the saṃbhogakāya is revealed;
and by relying on the path of supreme extraction (*viśeṣoddhara-mārga*), when the fundamental mind is exhausted, the dharmakāya is revealed.
In the *Combined Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, it is stated that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet been able to eradicate the three minds;
consequently, they remain distant from the three bodies (*trikāya*) and are unable to attain them. What are these three? First, the mind that initiates activity (*pravṛtti-citta*);
second, the mind that relies on the fundamental, which is the *manas* because it takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its object; and third, the fundamental mind, which is the eighth consciousness.
The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses rely upon three stages to manifest the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Some explain it thus: the path of suppression corresponds to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), wherein the active mind is the sixth consciousness;

the path of abandonment corresponds to the stages from the first ground upward, wherein the fundamental mind is the *manas*, for it relies upon and depends on the *ālayavijñāna* as its primary mind, and is therefore superior.
The path of extraction (*uddharaṇa-mārga*) is the fundamental mind of the stage of Vajra; the mind of the *ālayavijñāna* is the object of subduing.
On the path of suppression, the sixth consciousness—which discriminates all objective phenomena—is severed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

On the path of dharma-severance, from the first stage onward, one realizes the principle and severs the afflictions that delude one regarding that principle. Because it eliminates even the most subtle afflictions, it is superior to the path of extraction.

The six [purifications] are based upon the three obstacles to directly reveal the three bodies; as that sūtra states: "The purification of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) enables the manifestation of the response body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

the purification of the karmic obstacle (*karmāvaraṇa*) enables the revelation of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); and the purification of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) enables the revelation of the dharma body (*dharmakāya*)."
That sutra—namely, the aforementioned *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*—states: "The Dharma-body is manifested because afflictions (*kleśa*) are purified;

the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is manifested because karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) are purified; and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is manifested because cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are purified.
This is like lightning emerging from space, and light emerging from lightning, which differs from the [current] chapter.
Seventh, because the afflictions arising from delusion regarding the three natures (trisvabhāva) serve as a metaphorical manifestation of the three bodies (trikāya), that sutra states:
"All ordinary beings, on account of the three characteristics, possess bondage and hindrances; they remain far removed from the three bodies and do not attain them. What are these three?

First, the characteristic of conceptualization through discursive thought (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa); second, the characteristic of dependence on others (paratantra-lakṣaṇa); and third, the characteristic of perfection (pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa). As it says:
Because these three natures cannot be understood, cannot be extinguished, and cannot be purified, one cannot attain the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Conversely, because these three natures can be understood, can be extinguished, and can be purified, the Buddhas attain the three bodies.

Regarding "can be understood," it should be known that this refers to the nature of the grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), as both [the grasper and the grasped] are to be understood. Regarding "can be extinguished," it refers to the defiled portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Because that which arises dependently (*paratantra-svabhāva*) should be abandoned and extinguished, that which can purify is suchness (*tathatā*) while in its state of entanglement, which is purified through cultivation.

Regarding the "three natures of non-existence" (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on these three natures, those three natures of non-existence are established: first, the nature of the absence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

second, the absence of self-nature (*svabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*); and lastly, the nature resulting from the removal of the previously grasped self and phenomena (*parikalpita-ātma-dharma-niḥsvabhāvatā*)."
That same sutra, as explained in the *Qingliang* commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, states:

"The 'nature of lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established based on the 'imagined nature' (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because its essential characteristics are ultimately non-existent, like a flower in the sky or a snake upon a rope.

The 'nature of lack of intrinsic nature in terms of production' (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established based on the 'dependent nature' (*paratantra-svabhāva'), which is like a magical illusion that relies upon various [conditions]."

Because one falsely clings to the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) within dependently arisen phenomena from beginningless time, the "ultimate lack of intrinsic nature" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This means that the ultimate itself is so designated because it is far removed from the previously mentioned nature of the self and phenomena as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).

Now, by being deluded regarding these three absences of intrinsic nature, one gives rise to various afflictions and fails to reach the three bodies (*trikāya*); conversely, by reversing this, one is able to reach them.

Another interpretation states that because it refutes the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) below, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has two aspects: first, its pure portion is identical to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
second, its defiled portion is identical to the imputed nature. Because it can extinguish the defiled portion of the dependent nature, it reveals the perfected nature.
The eighth section explains the four stages by relying on the four obstacles; this has two meanings.

Regarding these two meanings: they refer to the difference between the two senses of the "outstanding afflictions" (*paryavasthāna*) and their "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) prior to and upon entering the stages [of the path].
First, regarding the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), we shall illustrate the four stages, four practices, four causes, and four retributions prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*). What are these four?

The first is that once the affliction of the *icchantika*’s lack of faith has been extinguished, it is overturned to reveal the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which constitutes the practice of delighting in the Mahāyāna as a cause for pure merit, resulting in the retribution of an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
The second is that the attachment to a self by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) is used as a metaphorical basis...

The manifestation of the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) as the practice of *prajñā* is the cause for the quality of self; it is metaphorically revealed through the retribution of a copper-wheel-turning king (*tāmra-cakravartin*) and the obstacle of fear of suffering in the three types of *śrāvaka*.
The manifestation of the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-carita*) as the practice of the "space-shattering vessel" samādhi is the cause for the quality of bliss;

it is metaphorically revealed through the retribution of a silver-wheel-turning king (*rūpya-cakravartin*) and the obstacle of the solitary realizers' (*pratyekabuddha*) relinquishing great compassion. The manifestation of the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) as the perfection of great compassion...
The practice of the constant virtue [of giving] is the retribution for being a Golden Wheel-Turning King.
Regarding the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), and the four stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*)—what is the evidence?

First, regarding the specific explanation of the four obstacles and so forth, *Qingliang* states that both the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) and the *Foxing lun* (Buddhadhātu-śāstra) say that one cultivates four kinds of practices prior to the grounds. This refers to: [The text continues with the list of the four practices.]

The ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) cultivate the practice of aspiring to the Mahāyāna; the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) cultivate *prajñā*; the ten stages of practice (*caryā*) cultivate the practice of *samādhi*;
and the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) cultivate the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). These correspond respectively to the four stages.

Furthermore, because they eliminate the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of four types of beings, these same four stages are designated as follows: first, the elimination of the obstruction of lack of faith in the *icchantika*; second, the elimination of...

The first removes the obstacle of the non-Buddhists' clinging to a self; the second removes the obstacle of the śrāvakas' fear of suffering; the third removes the obstacle of the pratyekabuddhas' relinquishing great compassion.

Furthermore, faith establishes the seed for the cause of pure qualities, understanding establishes the seed for the cause of the qualities of selfhood, practice establishes the seed for the cause of the qualities of bliss, and dedication establishes the seed for the cause of eternal qualities.
Moreover, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* correlates these with the four wheel-turning kings, namely those of iron, copper, [silver, and gold].
Because there are four rewards for silver and gold, we know that the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) also constitute distinct positions.

If, in the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), the ten stages of faith were merely the preparatory means (*upāya*) for the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) and lacked separate positions of their own, then the previous nine gates—when considered according to the Final Teaching—would be speaking from a majority perspective.
Furthermore, the four practices obtained by overturning the aforementioned four obstacles constitute the four meanings of being a "Son of the Buddha.

First, overturning the initial obstacle results in the seed of faith and delight in the Mahāyāna as the cause; this is like the father. Second, prajñā serves as the condition; this is like the mother.

Third, manifesting the *ākāśa-samādhi* (space-like concentration) to depart from the attachments of the Hīnayāna and cause the *dharmakāya* to be firm and stable is like the womb. Fourth is great compassion.

Benefiting others like a wet nurse, because one possesses four conditions, one is able to transition from the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) to birth within the family of all Buddhas from the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward;
therefore, one is called a "Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*).

By overturning and destroying the four obstacles prior to the grounds, one accomplishes the four types of practice and attains entry into the first ground, where one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and succeeds to the lineage.
One who causes the lineage of the Buddha to flourish is called a son of the Buddha.

Furthermore, these four factors combined are like the wheels of a chariot, capable of transporting and turning one toward the state of liberation, just as the wheel of a noble cakravartin king is equipped with four things:
the hub, the rim, the spokes, and the axle; these four meanings should be understood according to their respective order.
Regarding the "Noble Wheel" (*ārya-cakra*): first, dwelling in a land that accords with the Dharma; second, relying upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, disciplining one's own body;

and fourth, having planted roots of goodness in the past. Just as the wheel of a noble universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is complete only when equipped with four components—namely, the hub, the rim, the spokes, and the axle—if these four wheels are absent, it cannot be formed.

The second [section] uses the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of four obstacles to manifest the four stages, four concentrations, four virtues, and four retributions of the four levels above the ground (*bhūmi*).
First, in the first three stages, the extinction of the habitual tendency toward the lack of faith of *icchantikas* manifests this stage as being identical to the mundane world;

furthermore, by attaining the Mahāyāna-āloka-samādhi (Samādhi of the Radiance of the Great Vehicle), one accomplishes pure virtue and eliminates the retribution of the transformation of birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-vaiparītya*) which shares the same conditions. Second.
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one eliminates the habitual tendencies of the non-Buddhists' grasping at a self;

this stage is shown to be identical to that of the Two Vehicles, wherein one attains the King of Accumulated Merit Samādhi (*Puṇyasaṃbhārarāja-samādhi*) and accomplishes the virtue of the self, thereby eliminating the birth-and-death of expedient means.

In the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, one eliminates the habitual tendencies of the Śrāvakas' fear of suffering; this stage is shown to be identical to that of the Mahāyāna, wherein one attains the Bhadra-pāla Samādhi (*Bhadrapāla-samādhi*) and accomplishes [the path].
The delight in virtue eliminates the cycle of birth and death within the forty stages from the stage of existence up to the stage of Buddhahood.

Having attained cessation, the Pratyekabuddha relinquishes great compassion and habitual tendencies; this stage reveals the perfection of cause and the fulfillment of fruit through the attainment of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, thereby accomplishing the virtue of permanence.
Because the four virtues are perfected and birth and death are forever exhausted, it is said that "there is no [birth and death]. This is the meaning of the above.

This is explained in detail in such works as the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, the *Karmanirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, the *Ratnagotra-vibhāga*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated during the Liang dynasty.

In the second fascicle of the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature), Qingliang provides a brief indication of its names and characteristics: first, "birth-and-death through expedient means" (*upāya-jāti-maraṇa*), which refers to the conditions for birth-and-death—namely, the afflictions of the *avidyāvāsabhūmi* (the ground of the latency of ignorance)—which are capable of producing new out-flow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*). This is analogous to the ignorance within the [lower] realms.
The arising of practice through delusion gives rise to wisdom; because they are not of the same category, this is called "expedient means.
Second, the causal condition of birth and death refers to the cause of birth and death, namely, the uncontaminated karma with conceptual differentiation produced by the aforementioned ignorance.
For example, the karmic actions produced by ignorance only receive their corresponding results and are therefore termed "causal conditions. Third, the existence of birth and death is...
Due to the aforementioned causes and conditions, one experiences the fruit of transformation and maturation (*pariṇāma-vipāka*).

Just as within the three realms, one experiences the bodies of the six destinies through contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karma*), it is said that "there is existence" because there is the further existence of future birth.
This is also called "having this fruit of existence," as in the case of the *ūrdhvasrotas* (Upstreamer) Anāgāmin who attains parinirvāṇa in the second birth.
Therefore, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). There are four [types of] existence, yet there is no birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) that undergoes alteration, change, or transition.

For example, with birth as a condition, there arise the afflictions of old age, death, and so forth; when this single period of retribution expires, there is no further "existence," and thus it is called "non-existence" (*vibhava*).

In the preceding chapter, the causes and conditions of birth-and-death were first raised out of fear that scribes might err regarding the first three stages. Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it says: "First..."

The Mahāyāna-āloka-samādhi (Samādhi of the Radiance of the Mahāyāna) is so called because it can produce the light of wisdom that illuminates and realizes the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of the Mahāyāna.

The Liang Dynasty *Śāstra* states: "This samādhi can destroy the habitual tendencies of icchantikas, which are the obstacles of 'conventional birth and death' regarding the Great Purity [of the Buddha-realm].

Regarding the second, fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* refers to it as the Samādhi of King Jambūnada-gold, while the Liang Dynasty *Śāstra* calls it the Samādhi of Accumulating Merit.

It is said that being able to destroy the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the *ātman*-view of non-Buddhists constitutes the obstacle of birth-and-death through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-janma-maraṇa*) regarding the Great Self (*mahātman*) on the third, seventh, eighth, and ninth stages (*bhūmi*).

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is called "Worthy Protector" (*Bhadrapāla*), and the *Dacheng yi zhang lun* states that being able to destroy the habitual tendencies of fear in the Śrāvakas constitutes the obstacle of birth-and-death through existence (*bhava-bhava-janma-maraṇa*) regarding Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) on the fourth and tenth stages. This is what is termed in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The *Jianxingding lianglun* (Treatise on the Bridge of Vigorous Practice and Samādhi) states: "This samādhi is that practiced by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and Buddhas;
it can destroy the habitual tendencies of solitary realizers' self-experience, which constitutes the obstacle of birth and death regarding the Great Constant."

Furthermore, among these four, the first two pertain to both obstacles, while the latter two pertain only to the obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This text also serves as proof that the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are eliminated prior to the stages [of the path of cultivation], whereas the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are purified upon reaching the stages [from the first bhūmi onward].

These four obstacles are presented to manifest the first two stages among the four; the first two are common to both afflictive and cognitive obstacles, while the latter two are exclusively cognitive obstacles.
This is pointed out by citing the aforementioned sūtras and śāstras as evidence.

Ninth, because they function as distinct characteristics within the ten stages, the two obstacles and the cultivated afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya*) are abandoned up until the final moment of mind in the third stage.
Even if all [defilements] up to the fourth stage are exhausted, there remains only subtle habituation. Why?
Because the first three stages are similar to the mundane world, whereas from the fourth stage onward is supramundane.
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are assigned to distinct characteristics: from the first stage downward, one eliminates the coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) of both the views and the path of cultivation;

from the fourth stage onward, one removes the subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the path of cultivation. Furthermore, the first three stages are assigned to the characteristics of the three realms and are thus similar to the mundane, while from the fourth stage onward, they are assigned to the meaning of the *śrāvaka* and are thus similar to the supramundane.
Therefore, the concluding passage at the end of the third stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:

"All fetters of desire (*kāma-bandhana*) become further attenuated; all fetters of form (*rūpa-bandhana*) become further attenuated; all fetters of existence (*bhava-bandhana*) become further attenuated; all fetters of ignorance (*avidyā-bandhana*) become further attenuated;
as for the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*), these have already been severed. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains this as: "All fetters of desire become further..."

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, they become thin and slight" and so forth: this means that all afflictions of the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the desire, form, and formless realms, along with their causes—the latencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance—are all rendered thin and slight because they have been abandoned;
as for the bonds of views (*dṛṣṭibandhana*), these have already been severed at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
First the sūtra is cited, followed by the exposition of the treatise.

The commentary explains: "And those causes" refers to the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*); "the habitual tendencies of ignorance" refers to the seeds of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because these seeds of the two hindrances are simultaneously abandoned, they are said to be "identical. Therefore, one should know this.
The seeds of the two obstacles and the active afflictions (*kleśa*) are all exhausted in this stage; the above has for the most part been explained according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhānaya*).

Qingliang says: "This refers to the active manifestations and seeds of the three bonds of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*); therefore it is said that their causes are extinguished simultaneously with the seeds of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of that same stage.
The present statement, "simultaneously distancing oneself [from them]," follows the previous explanation and serves as a general conclusion.
The ninth gate: Furthermore,

because the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) manifest the distinctions between the three positions of the mundane world, the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), and the bodhisattvas,

the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang jing) states that the afflictions of form (*rūpa-kleśa*) within the triple world are severed in the first three stages, while those of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are severed in the subsequent [stages].

The afflictions of the mental consciousness within the three realms are severed in the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages; the habitual tendencies of form within the three realms are severed in the tenth stage and the Buddha stage;
and the habitual tendencies of the mental consciousness within the three realms are severed [in the same].
This is stated to clarify the distinctions between the three stages: the mundane, the supramundane, and the ultra-supramundane.

Thus, the Bodhisattvas of the stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and patience (*kṣānti*)—namely, those on the stages of Joy (*pramuditā*), Purity (*vimalā*), and Radiance (*prabhākārī*)—are able to sever the three obstructions consisting of the bonds of form and afflictions.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas of the stage of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*)—namely, those on the stages of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī*), Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), and Presence (*abhimukhī*)—are able to sever the three obstructions consisting of the bonds of mental afflictions.

A Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can sever the habitual tendencies of the three obstacles regarding both form and mind on the stages of Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), Immovable (*acalā*), and Good Wisdom (*sādhumatī*);
upon reaching the tenth stage and the stage of Buddhahood, they sever the mental habitual tendencies of the three obstacles, which is ignorance (*avidyā*).

The commentary explains: Because one attains the ultimate limit of the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) at the final stage of the third ground, reaching up to the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and thereby becomes detached from the matter of the lower realms, it is said that "the delusions regarding matter are severed.
From the fourth ground onward, one attains the supramundane state of the two vehicles' outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);
thus, both the mundane matter and mind are exhausted. From the seventh ground onward is the stage of the Bodhisattva, which is progressively more subtle than what preceded it.
Therefore, the cessation [of the path] is attributed to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of form and mind in order to manifest that stage.
While the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* divides this into four stages, the present chapter attributes and manifests three stages, explaining them by combining form and mind.
Eleventh, within this stage of the bodhisattva, in order to clarify the distinction between the two states of mastery and non-mastery:

from the seventh ground downward, one metaphorically extinguishes the afflictions of form and mind within the three realms, as well as their karmic retributions; from the eighth ground upward, one metaphorically extinguishes the ignorance of the dual habits of form and mind.
Thus, the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Primary Karma) states: "From the seventh ground downward, one extinguishes the [afflictions] of the three realms."
The retributive fruits of the two habitual tendencies of form and mind are extinguished without remainder: at the eighth stage, the ignorance of the habitual tendency of form is exhausted;
at the ninth stage, the ignorance of the habitual tendency of mind has already been eliminated; and at the tenth stage, the ignorance of both habitual tendencies is completely extinguished.
Because one has not yet attained mastery prior to this seventh stage, whereas from the eighth stage onward mastery is manifested,
what are termed "afflictions," "habitual tendencies," or "ignorance" are all general designations for delusion and karma, cited interchangeably across the sūtras and śāstras.

In the *Treatise on the Three Natures* (*Trisvabhāvanirdeśa*), twelve points rely upon the extinction of two natures to manifest the distinctions between the stages of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

As that treatise states: "Because of the path of seeing, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, hence it is said that it is 'not obtained'; because of the path of cultivation, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is extinguished, hence it is said that it is 'not seen'."

Regarding the second nature, because both the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures are devoid of intrinsic nature, it is said that "one neither attains nor sees" them. Thirteenth,

according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises, the two types of afflictions— conceptual (*vikalpaja*) and innate (*sahaja*)— are used to manifest the distinctions between the stages of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) are assigned to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are assigned to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because there is a distinction between the coarse and subtle levels of these afflictions.

How is it known that this is merely an assignment of stages and not an actual abandonment? It is like the view of a self through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpātma-dṛṣṭi*), which relies upon three conditions.

"Birth" refers to false teachers, false teachings, and false reflections that involve the false conceptualization of [the self] as being either identical to or distinct from the aggregates, and so forth.

Although I am like a disciple of the Buddha who dwells in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because I rely upon a true teacher, true teachings, and true reflection, I not only fail to give rise to such attachments as that [the self is] identical to the aggregates, but I also aspire to and delight in the nature of non-self (*anātmatā*). How could such a person have already severed [the afflictions] and entered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?

If one says that although there is no active manifestation (*samudācāra*), it is not [the case that one] has entered the path of seeing because the seeds (*bīja*) exist—since there is no active manifestation, one should then have entered the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra*) or the application (*prayoga*).

Previously, regarding the cessation of afflictions according to stages, the Initial Teaching (*śāsana*) distinguished between the innate (*sahaja*) and the acquired (*vikalpa*); now, what is the point of this? [In this context,] we are precisely discussing actual severance.

Regarding the phrase "As for 'provisionally relying on' (*yiji*)," it is as explained below. First, the objection is established to clarify the reason for the provisional reliance; "as in the case of the Buddha" and so forth constitutes the formal presentation of the objection;
"if one says" and so forth constitutes the concession and subsequent refutation.

Since the meaning is not as [the opponent] claims, one should therefore know that the provisional reliance upon those arbitrary conceptualizations is intended to reveal the principle of selflessness (*anātman*) of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

The inverted gross afflictions are revealed by contrast; furthermore, because the spontaneously arising afflictions are subtle and difficult to sever, they are contrasted to reveal the gradual increase of distinctions during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
According to the true meaning, there is only a single category of affliction that possesses both gross and subtle aspects:
the gross are severed during the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the subtle are severed during the stage of cultivation.

In the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*), the distinction is made by way of the two stages of abandonment—those of *vikalpa* (conceptualized) and *sahaja* (innate)—corresponding to the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). This is because the capacities [of the practitioners] are coarse and the teachings are shallow;

it merely uses the distinction between coarse and subtle to show that conceptualized afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned on the path of seeing, while innate afflictions are abandoned on the path of cultivation.

However, since the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are only exhausted upon reaching the ultimate stage, one should know that [this teaching] is merely provisional.
Establishing its name based on this does not constitute actual abandonment.

For instance, the afflictions of the *manas* are abandoned throughout both stages. As the *Nirnimitta-śāstra* states: "The second grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*) and its associated dharmas are ultimately extinguished upon reaching the stage of *Arhat*.
If one perceives the [afflictions] of the fleshly eye, these are the afflictions of the consciousness and the mind."
When the Dharma attains the sixteen moments of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), the remaining residues are ultimately severed;

these belong solely to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and are termed the second "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Compendium of the Great Vehicle) explains this in the same way, as can be known from the passage cited above.
Regarding the *Kongmu* (Outline) which states that the afflictions of the *manas* are abandoned through both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*):

"If one says they are extinguished at the initial stage of the path of seeing, why would this obstruct the realization of the principle of selflessness? Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva states:
"Because one transforms the defiled *manas*, one attains the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*); at the time of the first clear observation (*abhisamaya*), [this occurs] first."
