"Having already attained realization, at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), that which becomes further purified and increasingly pure is the extinction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the second clinging consciousness, the 'signless' (*animitta*), it refers to the *manas* consciousness. Regarding the first consciousness, it refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
As for the associated dharmas, the *Kongmu* states: 'Once the *manas* arises, it continues in succession without ceasing, [associated] with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*)."
The four latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—namely, pride, self-love, and ignorance—correspond to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).

During the first fifteen moments of mind, one severs only the afflictions (*kleśa*) and their acquisitions (*prāpti*); at the sixteenth moment, one completely eradicates even the subtle seeds of the afflictions.
This is consistent with the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, which cites the *Nirākāra-śāstra* as its precedent.

14. Regarding the three conditions upon which the delusions of conceptual discrimination depend, these are metaphorically manifested as the distinctions within the stages of the three types of noble beings prior to the [ten] bhūmis—namely, the ten levels of understanding (*adhimukti*) and so forth.
One should know that these exclude false teachers and the like, corresponding respectively to each stage; furthermore, this is explained from the perspective of those who progress directly.

Moreover, those [delusions] arising from false teachers and false teachings are metaphorically assigned to the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra*), because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse; those arising from false reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) are assigned to the stage of application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), because the aspects of their practice are subtle, this is explained in reference to the *śrāvakas* who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna].

On the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi-pūrva*), the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are not established as formal stages, because faith is merely a form of practice and not a stage. Furthermore, the four preparatory practices (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*) are not opened up [at this point] because they differ from the Lesser Vehicle;

rather, they are explained in reference to those who proceed directly [to the path], for whom the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are opened up prior to the grounds.

The seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are identical to those of the Hīnayāna; therefore, they are explained here in reference to those who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
Regarding the fifteen [stages] within the innate [afflictions]: from the seventh stage onward, the afflictions of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses manifest only occasionally (*sāntarāya*);

from the eighth stage onward, they are forever suppressed and do not arise. This distinction is made to clarify the difference between the stages of intermittent and non-intermittent entry into meditative observation.

This explains that the first seven stages are divided from the eighth stage and beyond because, up through the seventh stage, the observation of the mind has intervals and there is the possibility of its active manifestation, whereas from the eighth stage onward, the observation of the mind is uninterrupted,
permanently suppressing [the afflictions] so they do not arise; thus, two positions are distinguished.
Sixteenth, furthermore, the afflictions of the six consciousnesses are relegated to the end of the fourth bhūmi, while the afflictions of the manas are relegated to the seventh bhūmi;

from the eighth bhūmi onward, there remains only the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This statement is also made in order to clarify the distinctions between worldly beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas.

The afflictions of the six consciousnesses are abandoned in the four stages, their mode of abandonment being similar to that of worldly beings; the afflictions of the manas are abandoned in the seventh stage, being similar to those of the two vehicles;
and from the eighth stage onward, they are abandoned in the rank of the bodhisattvas because they consist of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Seventeenth: because it is intended to manifest the distinct differences between each of the ten stages up to the Buddha-stage, the eleven types of ignorance are used as a counter-reflection to reveal them.
Since the stages are distinct, the afflictions are used as a counter-reflection to manifest the differences between the characteristics of those stages.
Eighteenth, in order to manifest the two types of wisdom—ultimate and conventional—at each stage (*bhūmi*), twenty-two forms of ignorance (*avidyā*) are employed as a means of manifestation.
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Because these twenty-two categories of delusion and eleven types of heavy obscurations (*dauṣṭhulya*) establish the various stages.
Since it says they "establish" them, we know this is a case of employing [ignorance] as a manifestation. These meanings are explained in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises explain that, for the most part, the preceding discussion is based on the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
In each stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes the ultimate truth through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and penetrates conventional reality through subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there are twenty-two types of ignorance (*moha*) and eleven types of heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*); these are abandoned upon the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), whereby the obstacles of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-āvaraṇa*) are destroyed.

1. On the Second Ground (*Vimalā-bhūmi*), one abandons the obscuration of wrong conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*) and the delusions of clinging to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa-moha*), the delusion of the defilements of the miserable destinies (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*), and the delusion of subtle transgressions (*sūkṣma-āpatti-vibhrama-moha*). 2.

On the Third Ground (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*), one abandons the obscuration of dullness and sluggishness (*dhandha-jāḍya-āvaraṇa*) and the delusions of attachment to desire (*kāmarāga-moha*), the delusion regarding the retention of what has been heard (*śruta-dhāraṇa-moha*), and the delusion regarding the breaking of [vows]. 3.
On the Fourth Ground (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), one abandons the obscuration of active afflictions (*samudācāra-kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the delusions regarding meditative attainments (*samāpatti-moha*).
1. On the *Pramuditā-bhūmi*, one abandons the obstacle of attachment to the Dharma and attachment to foolishness, as well as the obstacle of seeking parinirvāṇa through the Lesser Vehicle;

one destroys the delusion of turning away from the vehicle and the delusion of turning toward nirvāṇa. 2. On the *Vimalā-bhūmi*, one abandons the obstacle of coarse characteristics and the obstacle of the manifestation of signlessness;

one destroys the delusion of observing saṃsāra and the delusion of the manifestation of signlessness. 3. On the *Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*, one abandons the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics and destroys [the aforementioned delusions].

1. The delusion regarding the cycle of birth and death and the delusion regarding arising and ceasing are severed on the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), which eliminates the obstacle of non-additional application and the delusions regarding the breaking of application and mastery.

2. The obstacle to the lack of desire to act for the benefit of others is severed on the ninth stage, the Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), which eliminates the delusions regarding meaning, phrasing, and dhāraṇī, as well as the delusion regarding mastery of eloquence.
3. The obstacle to the non-attainment of mastery is severed on the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

The destruction of the delusion regarding great supernormal powers and the awakening to the entry into subtle delusions constitute the first obstacle on the Tathāgata stage, which is severed in the eleventh [moment].
This destroys the delusion of attachment to the knowable and the delusion of subtle hindrances. These [terms] below collectively refer to the preceding nine gates, as detailed in various treatises.
The above concludes the first nine gates; the following nine gates are summarized below.
All the aforementioned sections are gates of the Āgamas that rely on delusion to reveal the distinctions between the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Why is this? It is to protect the ten stages and to cause sentient beings to abandon prideful attachment regarding the ten stages.

Because the characteristics of these stages are extremely profound and exceedingly difficult to comprehend, the stages are revealed by relying on delusion so that pure faith may arise. Other meanings may be understood by applying this principle accordingly.
The *Kongmu* (Outline) states: "These various distinctions among the dharmas are for the sake of protecting the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Accordingly, through various gates of skillful means, they are explained in manifold ways to cause all sentient beings to abandon overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding the ten stages.
By manifesting the stages through the medium of delusion, they cause sentient beings to give rise to reverence and faith toward these ten stages."
If one relies on the sudden teaching (sudden vehicle), all afflictions are primordially and inherently detached; thus, it is ineffable whether they are severed or not severed.
As the *Dharmadhātusvabhāva-sūtra* states, the Buddha asked Mañjuśrī, "How do you instruct the sons of good family to resolve upon bodhicitta?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I resolve upon the mind of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Why? Because the limit of self-view is precisely..."
This passage serves as scriptural evidence for [the realization of] bodhi.
To prove that the essential nature of all afflictions is inherently detached, the *Dharmadhātuprakṛtisūtra* states:
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, "How do you, O man, and others, preach the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "Regarding those men..."

The *Commentary* (Sū) cited by the *Subcommentary* (Shu) regarding the teaching that "arousing the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is itself the preaching of the Dharma for them" is slightly different from the present text.

If one relies on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the essential nature (*tixing*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot be described; it is only in terms of their function (*yong*) that they are extremely [profound].

Because that which is profound, vast, and great consists of the fact that a single obstructed phenomenon is identical to all phenomena, being fully endowed with both the primary and its attendants, so too are the delusions that act as those obstructions.
Therefore, there is no distinction between the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the seeds (*bīja*), and their manifestation;

rather, just as in the *dharmadhātu*, by attaining one, all are attained. Consequently, when afflictions are severed, they are all severed at once. Thus, the "Universal Good" chapter clarifies this unity.
The meaning of "one severance severs all severances" is that which clarifies the section on the minor characteristics (*kṣudra-lakṣaṇa*) regarding the obstruction of all obstructions.
The *Kongmu* (Outline) states: "If one discusses the limits of the extinction of delusions, according to the *Samantabhadra-parivarta*, it is said that 'one obstruction obstructs all obstructions';
according to the *Kṣudra-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*, it is said that the limit of severing delusions is 'one severance severs all severances. This is due to those flowers."

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there are five hundred afflictions each within and without, as well as eighty-four thousand afflictions, which are universally extinguished rather than individually; thus it may be known.

Furthermore, regarding the boundaries of this abandonment of delusions, according to the preceding and following passages of the sūtra, there are four types: first, in terms of realization, namely the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Second, regarding the stages of interruption: it refers to the stage from the tenth abode (*bhūmi*) onward. Third, regarding the practice: it refers to the final mind-moment of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
Fourth, regarding the ultimate reality: there is nothing to be interrupted, because it is primordially pure; this is explained in detail as stated in the sutras.
Regarding realization, one should know that this refers to the meaning of suddenly severing delusions at the final moment of mind of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the stages, it is equivalent to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*) of the Three Vehicles, wherein [delusions] are severed while in the stage of the three worthies (*tri-satpuruṣa*). Regarding practice, it refers to the severance of both the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from the end of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) back to the stage of one's own nature.
Regarding reality, there is nothing to be severed, for its intrinsic nature is pure.

Furthermore, regarding the severance of delusions through the various gates of the three vehicles and so forth—if one obstruction is severed, all obstructions are severed, and if one is severed, all are severed—then one enters this teaching;
however, if the sequence follows the individual gates, these belong to the three vehicles and so forth. This refers to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).

The Essential Questions on Severing Delusions through the Various Gates state: "Within the *Samantabhadra* chapter, it is said that according to the Dharma of Samantabhadra, it is extremely profound and vast.

Furthermore, it says: 'If one relies on the Śrāvaka-vehicle treatises, from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*), and the defilements (*mala*) up to those included in the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-vyākaraṇa-yāna*), all these aforementioned delusions—whereby one delusion constitutes all obstacles and one severance constitutes the severance of all—are categorized under the One Vehicle teaching. If one follows [this]:..."
The following section distinguishes from what preceded by summarizing and assigning the categories.

If one considers the inclusion of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*), everything elucidated in the preceding teachings is subsumed within this, because these are the preparatory practices themselves, as well as their outflows and designations;
other points should be understood accordingly. This concludes the section on the elimination of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*).

Subsuming the aforementioned teachings fully encompasses the various doctrinal schools (*zong*). Regarding the meaning of the dependent origination of the "Common Teaching" (*tongjiao*), Qingliang [Zongmi] stated:

"The Perfect [Teaching] necessarily subsumes the four. The *Kongmu* says: "If one relies horizontally on the provisional gates of expedient means (*upāya*) for progress, there are two senses in which 'One Vehicle' (*ekayāna*) is spoken of in a general sense:
because it serves as an expedient for that ultimate, perfect One Vehicle, it is therefore called 'One Vehicle.'"
This concludes the section on the limits of severing delusions regarding the meaning of non-dual perfect penetration and mastery.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Shanxi of Lize. The seventh [section]:
There are six explanations regarding those of the Two Vehicles who turn their minds [toward Mahāyāna].

Regarding those who turn their minds, the *Kongmu* (Outline) states: "As for the meaning of turning the mind, there are generally two [categories]: first, based on those who have not yet entered the Buddha [Vehicle]..."

Regarding the Dharma, there are two bases for the transformation of the mind (*cittavivarta*): first, the stage of liberation-portion merit (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) which distinguishes the initial transformation of the mind for those who have not yet entered [the path], and second, the state of entering the stainless realm of the Buddha-dharma.
The former refers to those in the position of an *icchantika* who engage in "semblance practice" (*pratirūpaka-pratipatti*), universally honoring and recognizing evil dharmas;
such *icchantikas* are led to enter the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The details of this method are fully set forth in the Question and Answer.
The middle section clarifies this:
first, it may be that all followers of the two vehicles lack the aspiration to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], because they have no further goals to seek, as explained in the Hīnayāna.

Because those of the Lesser Vehicle do not know that the Great [Vehicle] exists, the *Kongmu* states: "If one considers the Śrāvakas, from the stage of non-retrogression onward, they do not turn back.

Alternatively, it may be that all followers of the Two Vehicles eventually turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], because the power of the Buddha-nature serves as the internal perfuming cause for all.
Because the Tathāgata’s power of great compassion does not abandon external conditions, because fundamental ignorance has not yet been exhausted,
and because the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna is not ultimate, there is nothing among all [beings] that does not turn their minds toward Great Bodhi.
This is explained according to the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-naya).
All turn back together toward the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the essence of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the sentient beings of the six realms.
Furthermore, it is said that "Buddha-nature" is explained through both dharma and metaphor;
Buddha-nature is the cause of all ordinary beings and sages, for all ordinary beings and sages are born from Buddha-nature.
The extended analogy is as follows: milk is the cause of curd; all curds grow and develop by depending upon milk.
Therefore, the *Kongmu* (Outline) below states: "If categorized according to the Final Teaching (*jiao*), everything is transformed."

Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, among the four alternatives regarding the attainment and non-attainment of the various consciousnesses, it is stated that for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who enter the nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), both the ālayavijñāna and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are no longer attained.

Since both the fundamental consciousness and the evolving consciousness have been extinguished without remainder, what serves as the cause for the subsequent arising of the mind? Is it without a cause?
Because it would be illogical for [the result] to arise [in that manner].
The *Kongmu* states: "In distinguishing between accomplishment and non-accomplishment, there are two senses of 'accomplishment' depending on the context:

first, the sense of accomplishment as distinguished within the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, accomplishment as distinguished according to the fundamental principle (*tattva*). Regarding the first, accomplishment in terms of characteristics, this is based on the manifest."
From the *Treatise on the Propagation of the Holy Teaching*: Question: If one accomplishes the *ālaya-vijñāna*, does one also accomplish the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*)?

One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, there are those who accomplish the *ālaya-vijñāna* but not the evolving consciousnesses—namely, those in mindless sleep, those in mindless fainting, those who have entered the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), those who have entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and those born in the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-āyatana*).

Regarding the celestial beings (*deva*), some accomplish the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) but not the *ālayavijñāna*—namely, those Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas who abide in the state of having a mind (*sacittaka-avasthā*). Some accomplish both—namely, the rest who abide in the state of having a mind.
Some accomplish neither—namely, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive [Bodhisattvas] [who abide in the state of being without mind].

Regarding the question: when Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu), since the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and so forth have ceased, what serves as the cause for the subsequent arising of the mind?
The answer is: That treatise relies on the gate of the Initial Teaching (shijiao) and cites the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna);

therefore, the characteristics of the ālayavijñāna it establishes are coarse and manifest, and because it does not arise from the Truth (tathatā), it says that it has cessation. Furthermore, in order to conform to the Small Vehicle, it also allows for their nirvāṇa to be non-final;
thus it says that once one has entered it, one does not arise again.

Therefore, it is said that there is "extinction" (*nirodha*). The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When the four virtues are perfected, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is entirely exhausted.

As for what is here called "extinction," the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "It is only the characteristics of mind (*cittalakṣaṇa*) that are extinguished, not the essence of mind (*cittasvabhāva*) that is extinguished.

The commentary explains: "Since the characteristics of mind are themselves empty, there is nothing to be extinguished; this is what is termed 'extinction'. For those who follow the Hīnayāna, this is because the Śrāvakas do not regress from their own [attainment].
After [attaining] that stage, one does not regress; this is now explained in accordance with the Mahāyāna teaching that after entering nirvāṇa, one does not arise again.

Now, speaking according to the ultimate truth within the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya), since the fundamental ignorance has already perfumed the Tathāgatagarbha to form the ālayavijñāna, how could those of the Two Vehicles—given that they have not yet severed or realized these two dharmas—possibly attain cessation?
Furthermore, since that [ālayavijñāna] has not been severed or realized, how could the nirvāṇa attained thereby be ultimate?
It would necessarily entail the error of being analogous to a "transformed city" (an illusory city). Moreover, it is due to the four aforementioned causes that the mind arises.
The Treatise says: "Because they rely upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is arising and ceasing; this arising and ceasing is precisely ignorance.
That which is called 'neither-arising-nor-ceasing' in conjunction with 'arising and ceasing,' being neither identical nor different, is named the *ālayavijñāna*.
This is because the true mind does not maintain its own nature, but follows conditioning influences to combine and form the *ālaya*. Now, these followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet..."
Although ignorance has been severed and true reality (*tathatā*) has not yet been realized, by what cause can the *ālayavijñāna* be extinguished?

Since there is neither severance nor realization, that which is attained is not the ultimate truth; it is like a "provisional city" (*pariṇāmika-nagara*) intended merely to bring one to rest. Thus, the sacred word remains unimpaired.

The four causes are precisely those mentioned in the preceding correct explanation: Buddha-nature, great compassion, ignorance, and nirvāṇa; therefore, one is able to give rise to the mind of dedication.
Question: Regarding the turning over of the mind (*cittotpāda-pariṇāmanā*), what are its temporal limits?
The *Kongmu* states: "Furthermore, the limits of the turning of the mind are manifold and unequal. There are those who enter the stage of the Śrāvaka from the state of an icchantika;
there are those who turn from the Śrāvaka toward the Pratyekabuddha and the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching); and there are those who turn from the Śrāvaka [toward other stages]."
Those who progress directly and those of the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya) may, in some cases, turn their minds toward the Sudden Teaching and the One Vehicle (ekayāna);
this meaning can be understood by analogy with these cases.
Answer: Because their faculties (indriya) are not equal, their progress is either slow or swift. Those who are slow take kalpas to attain [realization], as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "Tasting..."
Attached to the bliss of samādhi, they dwell peacefully in the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), neither attaining final liberation nor regressing.

They obtain bodies of various samādhis such that they remain unaware for as long as an eon; this awakening is like a person who has been intoxicated by wine, who only awakens once the alcohol has worn off.
The awakening of these dharmas is likewise so. This refers to the attainment of the supreme body of a Buddha. It should be understood that this passage explains only the general characteristics.
Citing the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* regarding those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] due to differences in their faculties:

because the capacities of the five vehicles differ in their superior or inferior levels, the ways in which they turn their minds are likewise distinct; thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra* provides general proof for this point below.
If explained according to their distinctions, those of sharp or dull faculties each reach the stage of the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after a different period of time;
as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Even for a *srotāpanna*, it is not fixed;
thus, after eighty thousand *kalpas*, they can attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," and so on, up to: "A *pratyekabuddha* attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after ten thousand *kalpas*."

Regarding "the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," the commentary explains that this clarifies the case of the most dull-witted *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), who enters nirvāṇa only after undergoing seven births.

Their minds and mental factors cease as if entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and only after the passage of eighty thousand *kalpas* do they regain their minds and receive the Buddha’s teaching, thereby giving rise to the bodhicitta.
If, however, one attains the second fruit within a single lifetime, they will undergo two births.
Having already entered parinirvāṇa, after sixty thousand kalpas have passed, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

If, in a single lifetime, one attains the third fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) and no longer returns to the desire realm, one enters parinirvāṇa; after forty thousand kalpas have passed, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

If, in a single lifetime, one attains arhatship, one immediately enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); after twenty thousand kalpas have passed, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. If [one is] solitary...
According to the *Jueli jing* (Sūtra on the Benefit of Awakening), it takes ten thousand kalpas to be able to resolve the mind [for enlightenment].

When these five types of people resolve their minds, they immediately enter the stage of the Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), and only then is it called "generating the mind for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

after the first five types of people have attained the small fruits from the mundane state and entered nirvāṇa, they subsequently arouse a turning-of-the-mind (*parāvṛtti-citta*) to cultivate the practices of the Ten Faiths; once the mind is perfected through these faiths, they are capable of entering [the path].
From the first stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) onward, according to whether their faculties are sharp or dull, they each pass through those respective eons;
it is not necessarily the case that they all remain exclusively within *nirvāṇa* for such a duration of eons.

Just as those who proceed directly fulfill their practice after ten thousand eons and are capable of generating the resolve for enlightenment, so too do these Pratyekabuddhas—whose faculties are most sharp—resemble those who proceed directly in passing through [the stages].

Furthermore, because there are differences among the four types of dull faculties over more than ten thousand *kalpas*, there are many distinctions in the duration of time. Thus far, the explanation has clarified those who are slow.
Citing the two initial passages from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as proof, it correctly explains that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states faculties have sharpness and dullness, and wisdom has priority and sequence;

even a *srotāpanna* who is extremely slow takes eighty thousand *kalpas* to arise in the *nirodha-samāpatti* and receive the Buddha’s transformative teaching, at which point they are immediately able to generate [the path].
From those who have attained realization of the first fruit up to the Pratyekabuddhas, after ten thousand kalpas have passed, they resolve upon Bodhicitta and realize that fruit.
Among these, even the most dull-witted and extremely slow may require as many kalpas; however, their faculties are not fixed.

Beyond these five types of persons, those who resolve upon the mind immediately enter the Mahāyāna and attain the stage of the Ten Faiths. Furthermore, there are two distinct meanings regarding the latter two categories. By means of...
The first five types of persons are certain to pass through such kalpas within *nirvāṇa*;

from the past remote kalpas until now, they enter the Śrāvaka vehicle from the stage of *icchantika* and only after turning their minds toward enlightenment and entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) do they experience those kalpas before attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, the two meanings of "turning the mind" are distinct.
If one is extremely swift [in realizing this], as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who do not hear this sutra;
they neither know nor realize the conduct of a bodhisattva, yet they give rise to the thought of parinirvāṇa regarding the merits they have attained and think they shall enter nirvana.
I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name, and these people, though having entered the state of parinirvāṇa..."
One conceives of entering nirvana and seeks the Buddha’s wisdom in that land;

upon hearing this sutra, one attains extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle, with no other vehicle existing—except for the skillful means employed by the Tathāgatas in preaching the Dharma. The above is explained according to the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya).
"Other lands" refers to the Land of Provisional Existence with Remainder among the four lands of Tiantai.

However, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that one attains extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle; it further says that within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma.
Thus, those who hear this sūtra in other lands know that they need not necessarily pass through so many kalpas [to attain liberation].

Third, regarding whether those of the two vehicles turn back or do not turn back: those of the definite lineage (*niyata-gotra*) who incline toward tranquility (*śama*) do not turn back, whereas those of the indefinite lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) all turn toward the Great [Vehicle].
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śrāvaka-viniścaya*, this refers to the introduction of the two vehicles according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
There are four types of śrāvakas: first, those who are fixed; second, those with overweening pride; third, those who have regressed from the bodhicitta;
and fourth, those who are emanations. "Fixed" refers to those who, for a long period of time, are oriented toward nirvāṇa.

Those with overweening pride, by means of mundane, outflow-tainted samādhis and samāpattis, falsely perceive that there is no true nirvāṇa and yet give rise to the notion that it exists. Thus it is said.
Those who have regressed from the bodhicitta are like Śāriputra, whom [the Buddha] had already taught at the sites of twenty thousand Buddhas;
now, he causes you all to remember your original vows and the path you have practiced.

As for those who manifest through transformation, such as Pūrṇa, who secretly maintains the conduct of a bodhisattva while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka, and Ānanda, who uses skillful means to serve as an attendant.

The *Rāhula-mi-hsing* (Practice of Rāhula’s Secret) refers to those śrāvakas who are all to be transformed; this is determined by excluding the other three types of indeterminate ones, as they have encountered the influence [of the teaching] but have not yet reached their own stage.

The fourth is neither turning back nor not turning back, because it is free from characteristics, as taught in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā* and other sūtras; this is explained according to the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). The sūtra states:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, and the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas..."
From the dharmas down to the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), none are apprehendable; why? Because they are ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

Fifth, some combine and include the preceding four explanations, asserting that this is because it is a skillful means (*upāya*) for this Great Dharma; thus, this is explained in terms of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) which subsumes all skillful means.
Regarding the "One Vehicle that subsumes expedient means," it subsumes the preceding four teachings as being of the same teaching (tongjiao).

The *Kongmu* states: "Because it serves as an expedient means for that ultimate, perfect One Vehicle, it is therefore called the 'One Vehicle,' yet this does not mean it possesses the meaning of immediate, perfect, and sovereign penetration."
Sixth, there are those for whom the preceding five [types of regression] are all severed; this has two kinds:

first, those who have nothing at all to turn back from among the two vehicles, because when viewed in light of the One Vehicle, they are all immediately empty and thus nothing can be turned back—such as those described in the sutras as being "like the deaf" or "like the blind."
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know that [all phenomena] are one, it is said that they are all "identical to emptiness.
Second, all followers of the Two Vehicles and others have already completed their turning back [from the Lesser Vehicle] and will never turn back again;

as stated in the sutra, "with the eye of Samantabhadra, he sees that all sentient beings have already reached ultimate perfection. These points are all explained according to the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle.

Samantabhadra and others, as the responsive instruments, obtain the ten eyes that see all sentient beings as originally and ultimately exhausted within the scope of Vairocana’s capacity for transformation;
therefore, these [passages] together conclude the two preceding meanings, both of which are explained according to the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagvidyā).

Question: Regarding the distinction between the turning of the mind within the skillful means encompassed by the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the turning of the mind within the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), what are the respective limits of the dharma-gates attained?

Answer: If one turns the mind within the Three Vehicles, one enters from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward and proceeds through the successive stages of cultivating the dharma-gates of the bodhicitta, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and so forth.
If one turns the mind within the One Vehicle, it is as described below in the section on the "Abandoning" [of the three vehicles].

Śāriputra, the bhikṣu Indrasena, and six thousand others turned their minds toward Mañjuśrī and immediately attained ten great Dharma-gates, as well as the realms and meanings of the ten eyes and ten ears;
this should be understood as the body of practice and realization pervading the five stages. Other meanings are as explained elsewhere.

Regarding the attainment gained through the "turning of the mind" (*cittavivarta*) in the One Vehicle’s Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) compared to that in the Three Vehicles’ turning of the mind:

as for the lower category of the Three Vehicles, according to the *Kongmu* (Key Index), those who possess the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) at the limit of the untainted (*anāsrava*) entry into the Buddha-dharma—when the Tathāgata skillfully establishes two gates, one refers to the initial gate.
This refers to the meaning of the parable of the poor son in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and so forth; they are indeed [regarded as] deluded.
In the *Dharmasamgīti-sūtra*, the text is judged to mean that [the poor son] is exhausted by hardship; yet, the very body of the impoverished son is originally that of the son of a wealthy elder.
In principle, this corresponds to the *dharmatā*, the true mark (*tathatā*), and the *tathāgatagarbha*. When one is "stained while being unstained," it refers to the subsequent stage;
if one turns the mind [toward awakening], it corresponds to realizing that *dharmatā*. This principle is precisely what is meant by "being stained while being unstained," which is termed the "King."
The "Species" (gotra) is noble; the "One Vehicle" (ekayāna) is explained below according to its ultimate meaning.

The Great Wisdom Śāriputra and five hundred bhikṣus, while physically within the Buddha-dharma, were by right of their intelligence in a position to turn [toward the Mahāyāna]. At that time, they immediately attained the ten kinds of great dharmas, such as seeing, hearing, understanding, practicing, and realizing.
This present stage is that of their practice and realization (*śruta-caryā*). If one wishes to recognize the flowers:
Regarding the inexhaustible teachings and meanings of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, one should understand them through the six aspects (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) and the subtle wisdom of the *Indra-jāla* (net of Indra);
other meanings are as explained in the *Kongmu-zhang*.

Eighth, regarding the characteristics of the meaning of the fruit of Buddhahood, there are two parts: first, clarifying the meaning of permanence and impermanence; second, clarifying the characteristics.
This is a distinction of excellence.
Because the physical characteristics of the Buddha’s bodies are manifested differently according to their resultant virtues, they are divided into two types.
Within the former, if one follows the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the fruit of Buddhahood is exclusively impermanent, because its intrinsic virtuous qualities are not taught.

The *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) states: "In the Hīnayāna, there is no attainment of Buddha-nature by nature; there is only attainment through cultivation. The *Kongmu* (Comprehensive Catalogue) states:
"First, one must understand the teachings established to convey the Buddha’s intent. In the Hīnayāna, there are only two Buddhas:
first, the birth-body Buddha (*janmakāya-buddha*), and second, the transformation-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*). The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics belong to [the latter]."
The Buddha in his birth-body among humans and devas is also identical to the reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), with the sole distinction being the presence of self versus the absence of self;
this is because he does not speak of the merits of the primordially existing dharmakāya, but speaks only of those manifested through cultivation and arising.

If, in the initial teaching of the Three Vehicles, the *dharmakāya* is said to be eternal because of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is also said to be impermanent because of its separation or non-separation [from adventitious defilements].
The merit produced through cultivation is impermanent because it arises from causes and conditions;
yet, as it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it may also be considered eternal because it is uninterrupted and arises in continuous succession.
The dialogue states: "According to the Three Vehicles, the Buddha is both eternal and non-eternal. Because the *dharmakāya* Buddha is ultimate, it is eternal;
because it is neither separate nor inseparable [from phenomena], it is non-eternal. The *saṃbhogakāya* is eternal because its realization is ultimate;

it is non-eternal because it appears with increase or decrease according to the capacities of those below it, such as *śrāvakas* and ordinary beings. The *nirmāṇakāya* is like fire: it burns in some places and not in others."
Because there is cessation in some respects, it is impermanent; because the transformative merit continues in succession, it is said to be permanent.
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "By nature, through uninterrupted continuity, the three Buddhas are all eternally abiding," and so forth.
The Treatise states that there are three kinds of permanence: first, the permanence of essential nature (*svabhāva-śāśvata*), because the *svabhāvakāya* is eternally abiding by its very nature;
second, the permanence of non-interruption (*anupaccheda-śāśvata*), because the *saṃbhogakāya* constantly experiences the joy of the Dharma without interruption;

and third, the permanence of continuity (*prabandha-śāśvata*), because the *nirmāṇakāya*, having disappeared, manifests again, its transformations being inexhaustible. Thus it is said that the three Buddhas are all permanent.
Regarding "permanently abiding" and so forth:
according to the Final Teaching (Jiǒngjiào), there are two meanings—the first is explained individually, and the second is stated collectively;
this may be understood.

The merits produced through cultivation within the distinct [teachings] are impermanent because they are produced through cultivation; yet they are also permanent, for once attained, they are identical with True Suchness (tathatā).
Why is this? Because they originally flow from the Truth, and once ignorance has been exhausted, they return to the essence of the Truth.

Regarding "produced through cultivation": because roots of goodness such as faith have not previously manifested and only arise for the first time by relying on conditions, they are said to be produced through cultivation;

thus, they are impermanent, yet they are also permanent. As for the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which was previously hidden within the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), it now manifests the Dharmakāya through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) upon emerging from those entanglements and becoming pure. Why is this so? The following provides two reasons.

Therefore, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharmakāya, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this Dharmakāya.
This principle is extensively established in works such as the *Ratnagotravibhāga* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*; it should be understood according to those texts.
Since all phenomena, whether defiled or pure, flow forth from True Suchness (tathatā) and return to True Suchness,
the *Ratnagotravibhāga* correctly explains the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* to establish this meaning.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Why is it that *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) does not conjoin with the three periods of time?

Because the past and so forth are illusory and subject to arising and ceasing, whereas *sarvajñā* is a real dharma and is not subject to arising and ceasing. The commentary explains: "*Sarvajñā*" is translated here as "all-knowledge";
it is the perfected wisdom of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), which is identical to *tathatā* (suchness), and therefore is not subject to arising and ceasing.
That the Buddha’s wisdom is identical to True Suchness (tathatā) is because True Suchness is neither diminished by defilement nor purity, and is never altered from beginning to end;
therefore, it does not coincide with the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Just as space pervades all limits of form and is without arising, ceasing, or transformation, so too is the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
it pervades all that is knowable and is without error or transformation.

Therefore, one should know that it is not merely because of being uninterrupted that it is considered eternal, but rather that it is likewise unchanging and constant, identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Just as space pervades all places yet does not combine with form, so too the perfection of the Buddha-fruit pervades the limits of all realms of form and formlessness, yet remains without change; therefore, it is called "eternal."
The Dharma-body is eternal because it does not change its own nature even when following conditions; yet it is also impermanent because it arises in accordance with defiled conditions.
Why is this? Because all merits are equally both true and real, the arising of their function is exclusively the work of the True.
The *Dharmakāya* is that which is encompassed by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, stainless and unimpeded wisdom is termed the *Dharmakāya*.
In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is called the *Dharmakāya*, and so forth.

Because the *Dharmakāya* manifests all phenomena according to conditions without losing its own intrinsic nature, and because it responds simultaneously to all directions as many capacities are instantly moved, it is categorized as impermanent.
All merits arise based on the True [Suchness] (*tathatā*); because they are subsumed within its functioning and return to the True, they are established as permanent.

Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* explains that the two bodies—the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—belong to the Great Function of True Suchness. Furthermore, the treatise states:

"When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the images of the Dharma-body appear," and again: "Furthermore, original enlightenment, following along with defilement, gives rise to two kinds of discrimination."

The various characteristics are inseparable from that original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya-parivṛtti), being described as "one" [with it]—namely, first, the characteristic of the purity of wisdom, and second, the characteristic of inconceivable activity—and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding the arising of the function of the Great Vehicle, the two bodies of the Buddha—the retributive body (saṃbhoga-kāya) and the transformation body (nirmāṇa-kāya)—are distinguished; for that function of the Great Vehicle arises based upon the essence and characteristics.
Because the functions return to the essence, if the minds of sentient beings possess defiled dharmas, the *dharmakāya* does not manifest;
when the minds of sentient beings are pure, it naturally appears. Furthermore, since this occurs within the section on "following defilement," it is said that two kinds of marks arise.
Because these marks, once arisen, do not depart from the essence of awakening (*bodhi*), we know that the "pure mark" clarifies how original awakening follows defilement and returns to purity.
Regarding the inconceivable characteristics, this clarifies the characteristics of the functional activity (*karmayoga*) of the fundamentally enlightened awareness that returns to purity.
Second, regarding the general explanation: because this *dharmakāya* follows conditions (*pratyaya*), the differentiation of its merits is thereby established;
yet because it is immutable, there is no merit that is not identical to *tathatā*, as the entire substance follows conditions while its total aspect remains unaltered.
Because the two meanings of transformation are fused without obstruction, the fruit of Buddhahood is both permanent and impermanent;
it is fully endowed with the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) or is beyond the four propositions, as should be understood according to the specific sense.
Because the two meanings of "unchanging while following conditions" mutually support one another, the Buddha-body is both eternal and non-eternal;
furthermore, because these two meanings are fused and integrated without obstruction or hindrance, it is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Question: If this is so, why can it be said that they are neither identical nor different?
Since they are fused and unimpeded, why further say they are neither identical nor different?

Answer: In the Initial Teaching (Śāstra), because True Suchness (tathatā) is all-pervasive and wisdom realizes True Suchness, they are not different; yet, [they are also not identical] because of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not identical [to the conditioned], they are not one.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is that which is realized, while wisdom (*jñāna*) is that which realizes; because the object and the subject have merged and been extinguished, they are not different.
This principle is unconditioned, whereas wisdom is conditioned; because these two meanings—conditioned and unconditioned—are distinct, they are not one.

In the Final Teaching (Jōgyō), there are two meanings regarding merit: first, the meaning of the manifestation of dependent origination, because the merit accumulated over three incalculable eons is not in vain;
second, the meaning of the absence of self-nature, because apart from True Suchness (Tathatā), there is no intrinsic substance.
Because the merit of the Dharma-body manifesting distinctions in meaning according to conditions is not in vain;

because the Dharma-body is unchanging, profoundly still, and eternally present, its essence being without transformation; and because it is precisely by taking its entire essence to follow conditions that it achieves non-change—since it is through this non-change that it is able to follow conditions—it is therefore essential that its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) be manifested only within conditions.
Among these, the first meaning [of the dharmakāya] corresponds to its conformity with conditions (*anuparivartin*), while the latter meaning corresponds to its immutability (*avikāra*);

these are different perspectives because they take up the entire substance in its totality. Furthermore, this first meaning is not identical to its immutability, and the latter meaning is not identical to its conformity with conditions;
these are not one perspective because their meanings are distinct. This clarifies that while it is immovable, it is not non-different; reflect upon this.

It is seen that, by virtue of the meaning of dependent origination, it accords with the dharmakāya through its capacity to follow conditions; and by virtue of the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature, it accords with the dharmakāya through its immutability.
These are not different gates: because it is dependently originated, it is precisely immutable; and because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is precisely able to follow conditions.
This is not a single gate; therefore, by not destroying their non-identity, they achieve a state that is not one.

If one relies on the Sudden Teaching, because characteristics are exhausted and thought is transcended, there is only the single, true Dharma-body, which is perfectly equal and cannot be said to have distinctions of merit, nor can it be said to be either permanent or impermanent.
If one relies on the Sudden Teaching (dun-jiao), then the physical characteristics and appearances of all Buddha-bodies are ineffable because they are without marks (animitta).
If, however, one seeks to manifest them through words, it is as the sutra says: "This body of mine is itself the Dharma-body," and as another sutra says:
"The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body. One should understand it according to these principles.
The text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* manifests the Dharma through transformation; thus, Qingliang (Jizang) cites it to explain the Final Teaching (*zhōngjiào*), saying:

"This body of mine is now the eternal body. He feared that people might say this is merely an unceasing eternity rather than an immutable eternity, for the immutable eternity is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, regarding the passage on "the single mind and the power of single wisdom," etc., [it refers to] the power of the single mind and single wisdom.
The same applies to "fearlessness," which refers to the *Vidyādhara-paṭala*. The *Kongmu* states: "This is explained according to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.
If one relies on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are three explanations regarding the meaning of the Buddha-fruit’s permanence and so forth."

Because the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is the One Vehicle of the Buddha, it speaks of two kinds of ten bodies: the ten bodies that fuse with the three worlds, and the Buddha-body which inherently possesses the ten bodies.
Now, these are explained according to the three meanings of essence, attributes, and function.

First, regarding the function: since the Buddha-fruit universally encompasses all phenomena, including the three worlds and so forth, it possesses the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) such as permanence and so on.
The meaning of the four propositions—such as whether the One Vehicle and the ten Buddhas are permanent or impermanent—is precisely that of the Perfect Teaching (paripūrṇa-deśanā) of the One Vehicle.

According to the common teachings, the two—referring to the Buddha-fruit in terms of its qualities—possess four meanings: first, that which is produced through cultivation; second, that which exists inherently; third, that which both exists inherently and is produced through cultivation;

and fourth, that which is produced through cultivation and exists inherently, being perfectly interfused and unimpeded, and endowed with boundless virtues. For this reason, it is also said to be "common" (tong) with the [Buddha-]qualities.
Regarding the fourfold sets, the meaning of the first two and the latter four can be understood by reflecting upon them.

Zhixiang said: "Based on the teaching of the One Vehicle, there are the 'originally existing' and the 'originally existing produced through cultivation,' as well as the 'produced through cultivation and originally existing.

Therefore, possessing the nature-merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is the meaning of the 'same teaching' (tongjiao). If the One Vehicle is explained according to its practice, it is not [the same]."
This is because it encompasses the meanings of both that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-ja*) and that which is innate (*sahaja*).
Thirdly, regarding its essence, it also admits of four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, in this sutra, it is manifested as "ineffable" (*anabhilāpya*), thus it is eternal;
yet, because it accords with the *Āgamas*, it is impermanent. Since these two meanings are non-obstructive, both exist simultaneously at the limit of arising according to conditions.
Therefore, both [positions] are incorrect.
One must ask: Are the One Vehicle and the ten Buddhas permanent, impermanent, neither permanent nor impermanent, or neither used nor not used?
Because they are spoken of as being spoken, the Buddha is permanent; because he accords with the *Āgamas*, he is impermanent, arising in accordance with conditions.
Because they reach the ultimate limit, they are neither eternal nor impermanent.

Regarding these three aforementioned meanings, whether it be the identity of essence (*tattva*) or the simultaneous identity of essence, up to the simultaneous application of function (*vṛtti*), because they are fused and subsumed without obstruction,
one should contemplate that all possess the unobstructed nature of permanence and so forth.
The above three points conclude the general clarification that the fundamental dharmas of dependent origination mutually encompass one another without obstruction.
Second, regarding the distinctions of the marks and signs: according to the Hīnayāna, the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs are substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*).

The question must be asked: According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, seeing the Buddha’s physical body with its thirty-two marks and so forth is considered seeing the reality, and is thus called "seeing the Buddha.
However, within the Three Vehicles, it is sometimes taught that these thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics are merely the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
The principle that "phenomena are themselves emptiness" is as explained in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and other treatises;
this refers to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), which is presented here according to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Furthermore, it says: "If one relies on the Three Vehicles and perceives the Buddha’s actual form-body (*rūpakāya*) and its thirty-two marks, this is not called 'seeing'."
Because the Buddha is conjoined with conceptualization and pervasive imagination, even if one sees a semblance of his appearance, this is merely a semblance and not seeing the Buddha.
If one knows that he is without intrinsic nature and without the marks of coming or going, this is called seeing the Buddha.
As the Tathāgata said in the *Vajracchedikā*, "The thirty-two marks are indeed no thirty-two marks," and so forth; this refers to the beginning.
The teaching resembles that of the Hīnayāna.

Alternatively, it may be explained in reference to the *saṃbhogakāya*, wherein the eighty-four thousand marks are all actual virtues; this is explained according to the *zhíjìn* (direct-advancing) and the *zhōngjiào* (final teaching), etc.

Regarding "actual virtues" (*bhūtadharma*) below: the cultivated (*bhāvanā-maya*) and the innate (*upapatti-lābhika*) are both actual virtues; because in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), the Direct Progression (*pratyakṣa-praveśa*), the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), and so forth, there is only the single *tathatā*.

Question: For what reason do works such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explain that [the Buddha’s] experiences in this *nirmāṇakāya*, such as the golden spikes and the barley meal, were caused by past karma?
Do the thirty-two marks and so forth each have their own causes?

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Buddha’s transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) undergoes nine instances of affliction and suffering: first, six years of ascetic practice; second, the slander by Sundarī;
third, the golden spikes; fourth, the horse-barley; fifth, the killing of the Śākya clan by King Virūḍhaka; and sixth, the headache of the Tathāgata.

1. The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana); 2. A Brahmin country where he returned with an empty bowl after begging for alms; 3. The seven Jāñcā women who slandered him by covering his bowl; 4. Devadatta pushing down a mountain; 5.
Cold winds and the request for clothing; 6. The barley and gold at Verañjā; these are all fully set forth in the *Udānavarga* (Scripture on the Arising of Deeds).
Since past karma has emerged as its cause, how can one say it is immediately empty?

The answer is: It was taught that the fruits of present karma do not perish in order to lead the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) down to a common level; thus, while the Noble Path severs delusions, it does not extinguish retributive results.

This is also the case for Arhats consuming sand or golden gruel. The Lesser Vehicle regards this as the actual beginning of the teaching, whereas the Initial Teaching explains it through the doctrine of emptiness as a skillful means (*upāya*).
One should know that this is explained as a skillful means in the Mahāyāna *Upāya-sūtra*.

The Mahāyāna was taught to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle [to understand] that karmic results do not perish; furthermore, it is through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) that afflictions are severed, not by extinguishing karmic retribution.

Each chapter of the *Kongmu* states that the "teachings of the initial gate" regarding defilement and purity as being empty belong to the teachings on the Truth of Suffering of the Śrāvaka vehicle of the "Dull-Witted" (*bāla*).
The tenets concerning real dharmas, such as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are all of differing meanings and principles.
These are distinct.
Regarding the manifestation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), there are two meanings:

first, as a skillful means (*upāya*) to attract those of the Two Vehicles, he displays the supreme cause and effect within this very body, for the true recompense body (*vipāka-kāya*) is not seen by them; second, these [marks and signs] are also themselves...
Because the characteristics of the true recompense body (*sambhogakāya*) are manifested and displayed herein, the cause for its emergence can be discerned.

There are two reasons for the emergence of that transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): first, to lead those of the Two Vehicles toward the lower [teachings], as the true recompense body is not within their field of vision;
second, to demonstrate the true recompense body by means of the transformation body.
Question: Why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that the thirty-two marks and so forth are included among the merits of the Dharma-body?
Previously, you addressed the question of how the transformation body might be confused with the retribution body; why now do you speak of the transformation body being confused with the Dharma-body?

The answer to this also has two meanings: first, as a skillful means to turn those of the Two Vehicles toward the gradual teaching of the true *dharmakāya*, fearing they might find it difficult to believe, these merits are described as the *dharmakāya* so that they may easily accept and believe it, because it is something perceived through direct experience;
second, since they regard these merits as the *dharmakāya*, they are subsumed within that [category]. Both of the above points pertain to the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*).
If one relies on the Hīnayāna, there are two types of Buddhas: the birth-body Buddha (*janma-kāya-buddha*) and the transformation-body Buddha (*nirmāṇa-kāya-buddha*).

Now, in the Initial Teaching, the thirty-two marks are used as a provisional manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) to skillfully entice and lead beings so that they may easily believe and accept it;
furthermore, the merits of true retribution are subsumed within the Dharma-body and thus included among these marks.
Furthermore, the thirty-two marks and so forth are themselves without intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are also the *tathatā* (suchness) *dharmakāya*.
This is explained according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-deśanā*).
It must be asked: if one knows that there is no intrinsic nature and no characteristics of coming or going, then form is emptiness; it is not that form is extinguished to become empty.
This is explained according to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).
If one relies on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there are as many marks as there are atoms in ten oceans of *padma-garbha* world-systems;

each and every mark pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, and their functional activity (*karma-yoga*) is likewise. The reason for speaking of "ten" is to manifest their inexhaustibility, just as with the marks themselves.
The "Chapter on the Ocean" states:

In this sutra, within the Lotus Treasury World—which is the infinite Indra’s net of the Buddha’s perfect fusion of defilement and purity—the environment and its inhabitants are harmoniously integrated, possessing as many marks as there are atoms in the three worlds.
These marks are not merely virtuous qualities, nor are they merely non-virtuous qualities; they are both virtue and non-virtue. By means of these, [the Buddha]...
Because the principle of dependent origination is fully endowed with the characteristics and functions of merit in both direct and reverse order, they are all inexhaustible.
Furthermore, in the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are divided into three sections based on these three principles.
Regarding the statement that there are three vehicles (yāna) as the fundamental tenets, some claim that this refers to the scriptures of the three vehicles; however, this is incorrect.
The "three vehicles as fundamental tenets" refers to the three schools: the Hīnayāna, the Triyāna, and the Ekayāna.
Therefore, that sutra says: "The most concise of the concise—I shall now, for the sake of the great assembly in this gathering and for King Śuddhodana, briefly explain the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because he was born among humans and manifested the same activities as a human being, he is said to possess the thirty-two marks;

because he surpasses all devas, he is said to possess the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). For the sake of the bodhisattvas, I shall explain the eighty-four thousand [dharmaskandhas]."
The Buddha of Sublime Marks and Features truly possesses sublime marks and features;

I have already extensively explained this in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for the sake of Samantabhadra, Bhadramukha, and other great bodhisattvas at the site of enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha when I first attained the Way.

Regarding the marks of the *sabhāgatā* (commonality) of persons, one must ask: if, according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the marks of a person are taken as the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth, then these would belong to the category of phenomena (*dharma*). The rest of the text is clear.

The commentary states: "In this context, the thirty-two marks and so forth are the most abbreviated of the abbreviated [teachings], intended for the sake of humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles."
The meaning of "eighty-four thousand" and so forth from the beginning refers only to the brief exposition for the sake of the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles.
The meaning of the Buddha’s true marks and excellences as explained in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra* (the *Avataṃsaka*) refers to the extensive exposition;

that is to say, it refers to what is taught in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasāgaravyūha-parivarta*) of this *Avataṃsaka*. This exposition of the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle is different from the final [teaching]. Since the *Saṃpuṣpita* is...
Because this is the *Avataṃsaka*, other meanings can be understood accordingly; that is,
the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies" enumerates ninety-seven marks of a Great Man, which,
when combined with those numbering as many as the atoms in ten lotus-treasury world-oceans, all pervade the Dharma-realm.
The ninth section clarifies the scope of the transformation and guidance [of sentient beings].
According to the Hīnayāna, this Sahā world-system of impurities alone is the retributive land (vipākakṣetra) of the Buddha;
within it, this Jambudvīpa is the locus of the retributive Buddha, while the remaining ten billion [worlds] and so forth constitute the scope of his transformative domain (nirmāṇaviṣaya).
"Saha" (娑婆), when its profound meaning is explored, is translated as "Endurance" (堪忍); "Jambudvīpa" (閻浮提) is translated here as "Supreme Gold" (勝金).

It is only this Jambudvīpa that serves as the locus for Śākyamuni’s true retributive reward. "A billion" refers to the trichiliocosm, which constitutes the entirety of his realm of conversion and transformation.
If one were to speak of the lands within the Three Vehicles, the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (dharma-nature land) and the *svasaṃbhoga-kṣetra* (self-enjoyment land) are not discussed here.

Within the Three Vehicles, there are three kinds of lands: first, the *dharmatā-kṣetra*; second, the *vipākaphala-kṣetra* (land of true retribution); and third, the *nirmāṇa-kṣetra* (land of transformation).

Alternatively, four lands are taught, by dividing the *vipākaphala-kṣetra* into the *svasaṃbhoga-kṣetra* and the *parasaṃbhoga-kṣetra* (other-enjoyment land). Here, in the following section, the first two are excluded.
The Land.

Regarding the *sāmbhogika* (enjoyment) and *nairmāṇika* (emanation) pure lands of Śākyamuni Buddha that correspond to others' reception of benefit: some say they are located in the realm of Maheśvara;
others say his emanations fill ten billion Jambudvīpas. These are the boundaries of what is transformed, as described in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other texts.
It should be understood that the *Abhidharmakośa* and other such treatises explain this according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states that the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) resides in the palace of Śūra-deva;

it says, "Upon a thousand lotuses surrounding [the central one], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis," which refers to the Great Transformation. Furthermore, it says, "Within each of the ten billion lands upon a single lotus, there is a Śākyamuni," which refers to—

The "small transformation" refers to a single set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*). The "great transformation" encompasses a total of ten billion such worlds. The *Fanwang jing shu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Sūtra) states:

"If one enters the Mahāyāna, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* explains that upon the realm of Maheśvara there is a single Buddha of true retribution who takes one great trichiliocosm as his objective field; he manifests ten billion Śākyamunis, all attaining Buddhahood simultaneously."
Why is this? Because the teaching for the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) regards the body of Śākyamuni as a body of true retribution (*vipākaphala-kāya*);
here, we now overturn that view to reveal that it is actually a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Therefore, a distinct body of true retribution is established for those heavens.

Furthermore, fearing that the followers of the Two Vehicles would not believe in the existence of a truly pure land outside the triple world (*dhātu*), [the Buddha] relies upon the most supreme location within the world to speak of his transformation body, which merely fills ten billion worlds and so forth.
This follows that explanation.
The realm of Akaniṣṭha is described in terms of the retribution of karmic results in order to inspire pure faith in the followers of the Two Vehicles,
because the initial gateway of the Mahāyāna contains many shadow-like appearances.
Some say that Śākyamuni Buddha’s land of retribution is outside the triple world; as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"To the west, beyond lands equal to thirty-two Ganges-sands from here, there is a world named Unconquerable (*Anabhibhūta*), which is the true land of retribution and purity of Śākyamuni Buddha.
This is explained according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-vyavasthāna*).
The *Yanyi* (Exposition of the Meaning) quotes the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-four, "The Noble King of Virtue":
"To the west of here, beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named 'Invincible' (*Anabhibhūta*).
Why is that land named 'Invincible'? Because all the adornments within that land are entirely equal and without distinction."
There are distinctions, such as the Western World of Ultimate Bliss and others; the statement that it is "thirty-two [yojanas] from here" now is likely a scribal error.

Because it does not follow what is said below, and in order to manifest that this Sahā world is solely a transformation, one should therefore know that [this refers to] the Peak of Form (*rūpāvacara*).
This body is also not a true retribution-body.
Now, by distinguishing between internal and external realms, we differentiate the provisional and the real.

Or, it is said that the transformed realm is not merely ten billion worlds; as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is taken [as the scope].
Counting this [number] repeatedly until it reaches as many as the sands of the Ganges constitutes one world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Counting these again until they reach as many as the sands of the Ganges constitutes one world-ocean (*lokasamudra*). Counting these again until they reach immeasurable Ganges-sands constitutes one world-lineage (*lokadhātujāti*).

Counting these again until they reach as many as the sands of the Ganges in the immeasurable ten directions constitutes the extent of the realm of conversion for a single Buddha-world. This, too, is...
According to the teaching of the Final Vehicle (niṣṭhā-yāna), the scope of those to be gathered and transformed (*saṃgraha-vinaya*) is broader than previously stated.

The inquiry thus asks: if, according to the Final Vehicle of the Three Vehicles, Buddhas manifest their enlightenment in identical worlds numbering three thousandfold, are these all transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)?

Now, citing the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), it is proven that the limits of those gathered and transformed are even more extensive than what was previously established by the Final Vehicle.

Furthermore, it is taught solely with reference to the world-system of Mount Sumeru; because this is restricted to this particular realm and does not yet speak of world-systems shaped like trees and so forth,
it is not the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
However, this is not the latter teaching, as it speaks only of one type of world-system and does not mention other types of realms.

Alternatively, it is said that Śākyamuni’s reward land (vipākakṣetra) is on Vulture Peak; as the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "I am always on Vulture Peak," and the commentator of the *Lotus Sūtra Treatise* explains this as the reward-body (vipākakāya) bodhi.
One should know that this is explained according to the common teaching (sāmānyanaya) of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "clouds and so forth," as well as when sentient beings in other abodes see this kalpa-ending great fire burning everything, my land remains peaceful and secure, constantly filled with devas and humans.
Tianqin (Maitreya) explains that this refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) Bodhi; this is the manifestation of the reward body through means of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

Why is this? Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also reveals the One Vehicle; since in that teaching defilement is immediately transformed into purity, the place where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached is itself the reality.
Because the One Vehicle revealed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is identical to that of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is a teaching of common import (*tongjiao*).
Just as the place where the *Avataṃsaka* was preached beneath the Bodhi tree is the realm of the ten bodies within the Lotus Treasury World, so too is it with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
because it gradually becomes identical to this, it is a teaching of common import.

Just as the *Avataṃsaka* is taught in a defiled land—specifically in the kingdom of Magadha—and yet is identical to the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean, complete with its primary and attendant teachings and the Indra’s Net of phenomena, so too is it with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. It reveals purity through impurity and gradually accords with the *Avataṃsaka*;
therefore, it is called "teaching-in-common" (*tongjiao*).
However, because it has not yet been taught that those very places constitute the Ten Lotus Treasuries and the Indra-worlds and so forth, it is not a distinct teaching.
Furthermore,

although the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of returning from defilement to purity and teaches the meaning of the One Vehicle, its primary and secondary elements (the principal and its attendants) are not fully complete.

However, because it does not state that the Ten Lotus Treasury [Buddhas] and others are excluded from being of the Separate Teaching (pratyekavyākaraṇa), some say that this body of Śākyamuni is itself the Body of Enjoyment of True Reward (*sambhogakāya*).
For example, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states at its beginning that this Buddha Śākyamuni possesses twenty-one kinds of merits of true reward; that treatise explains this as the "Enjoyment" [body].
Regarding the "use of the body," this is also explained according to the *tongjiao* (teachings of commonality).
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* indicates that Śākyamuni himself possesses twenty-one kinds of sublime merits,
which the Bodhisattva Sthiramati explains as the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of enlightenment.

For what reason? If this Śākyamuni Buddha, within the Three Vehicles, is merely a *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), yet according to the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle he is the ultimate body of the ten Buddhas, why is Śākyamuni designated as the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body)?
If he is considered an emanation within the Three Vehicles, yet [is otherwise] in the Separate [Teaching]...

If the teaching were simply the ten bodies, then manifesting through transformation (nirmāṇa) to reveal the retribution body (vipākakāya) would accord with the meaning of the "Shared Teaching" (tongjiao).
However, this present expedient means encourages those of the three vehicles to clarify that the body of Śākyamuni is not merely a transformation body;

for fear that they might find it difficult to believe and accept, that sutra—focusing on the section concerning the profound merits of the Buddha-fruit—clarifies that the Buddha-body conforms to the teaching and is thus provisional (upāya).
The ultimate reality is explained as the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Now, because the three vehicles are integrated into the one vehicle, and because the explicit teaching in that sutra is profound and subtle, it is said that the Buddha-body is provisional in its manifestation but returns to the ultimate reality.

When the One Vehicle Dharma of the *Avataṃsaka* is skillfully revealed and expounded, this body of Śākyamuni also conforms to that teaching as the ultimate Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) of the ten Buddhas.
Therefore, it is subsumed under the category of the "Teaching of Commonality" (*tongjiao*).
As it is said, when the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma is being expounded, even when Śākyamuni is mentioned, he is immediately the Ten Bodies;

yet, because this [present teaching] involves returning the provisional to the real, and because the inexhaustible bodies have not yet been revealed, it is distinguished as not being the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). Question:
